Bath & Body Works is spritzing up its stores with new layouts and signage designed to help shoppers more easily discover its fragrances and personal care products.

The retailer - which has become a staple in malls - is redesigning its U.S. and Canadian locations with a more streamlined shopping experience, organizing products around scent categories rather than traditional displays, the company told Retail Dive.

Shoppers will now be able to browse fragrances by categories such as botanicals and blooms, fresh and clean, fruity and bright, treats and sweets, and warm and woodsy. Products will also be grouped by key categories, including body care, hand soaps and home fragrance.

The updated stores will feature dedicated “body care zones” where customers can shop products for their daily routines, with signs highlighting fragrance notes and product benefits. Popular collections like Fruit Fusion, Everyday Luxuries and Aromatherapy will be displayed together to make it easier for shoppers to find and explore new scents.

Seasonal products will get their own dedicated displays, while everyday favorites will remain along store walls for easier browsing. Store layouts may vary by location, and Bath & Body Works plans to collect customer feedback to help shape future updates.

open image in gallery The new Bath & Body Works layout will use dedicated displays for seasonal products, while year-round favorites will remain on store walls ( Getty Images )

The redesign is part of the retailer’s broader “Consumer First Formula” strategy, which aims to drive long-term growth by refreshing the brand, improving the in-store experience and making shopping more engaging.

The effort builds on the company’s newer “Gingham+” store concept, which features scent-testing areas, softer lighting and a more modern design meant to create a more immersive experience.

The overhaul comes as Bath & Body Works works to win back shoppers amid recent sales challenges. The company’s stock, which trades on the NYSE under the ticker BBWI, has declined in recent weeks, falling from about $22.37 at the start of July to $19.47 as of Friday. In its latest earnings report, the retailer said net sales dropped 3 percent year over year to $1.4 billion, while first-quarter net income increased more than 74 percent to $183 million.

Beyond updating its stores, the company is expanding its reach through a new Amazon storefront and a partnership with Ulta Beauty, where Bath & Body Works products are available in more than 600 stores nationwide and online.

The brand is also leaning into celebrity partnerships as part of its refresh. Earlier this month, singer and actress Hilary Duff became Bath & Body Works’ first-ever celebrity brand ambassador and creative partner, helping launch the Fruit Fusion body care collection.

News.title: Father who murdered four-week-old son in ‘fit of anger’ jailed for life
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A father who murdered his four-week-old son by shaking him has been jailed for a minimum of 18 years.

Atticus Bartlett died in hospital after collapsing at his family home in Chard, Somerset, on July 16, 2022.

Tony Bartlett, 39, from Axminster, Devon, was convicted of murder following a trial at Bristol Crown Court.

The jury found Bartlett violently shook Atticus, causing severe internal injuries to the baby’s brain and spinal cord.

Mr Justice Cavanagh sentenced Bartlett, formerly a postman, to life imprisonment and ordered him to serve a minimum of 18 years.

The judge told Bartlett he was “very drunk” when he carried out the fatal attack on Atticus, adding: “I have no doubt that this terrible tragedy would not have happened if you were not so heavily intoxicated.”

open image in gallery Atticus Bartlett died in hospital after collapsing at his family home in Chard, Somerset, on July 16 2022 ( Avon & Somerset Police )

He said Bartlett had been feeding Atticus with a bottle and the baby was bringing up the milk.

“In your drunken state, Atticus’s inability to take the bottle as well as you thought he should enraged you,” the judge said.

“You had a sudden fit of anger. You vented that anger on your tiny baby son. You shook him very violently indeed, gripping him very tightly round his ribcage.

“This only lasted a few seconds or at most a minute or so. Just in that brief moment, you wanted to cause Atticus serious injury.

“As suddenly as you began, you stopped, your anger evaporated, and then you dozed off.”

During the trial, Charles Row KC said Bartlett had been “drunk and frustrated” when he attacked his newborn son.

Bartlett and his then-partner, Evelyn Ballentyne, Atticus’s mother, had gone to a pub and comedy club that evening.

open image in gallery The judge told Bartlett he was ‘very drunk’ when he carried out the fatal attack on Atticus ( Ben Birchall/PA )

Ms Ballentyne’s mother Rachel Donovan and her husband went to the family’s home on Darcis Row, Chard, to care for Atticus.

Over the evening, Bartlett drank 8.5 pints of lager before returning home with Ms Ballentyne.

Mr Row told the court: “Evelyn Ballentyne went upstairs for a few minutes, leaving Atticus in the defendant’s sole care.

“When she returned, Atticus was lying face down across the defendant’s lap.

“She said ‘he’s dead, he’s not breathing’. She noted that the defendant appeared to be asleep or at least his eyes were closed.

“The defendant flipped Atticus over. Atticus released two gasps and appeared to be floppy and lifeless.”

Emergency services attended the property and Atticus was taken to Musgrove Park Hospital before being transferred to Bristol Royal Hospital for Children.

His brain damage was so severe he did not regain consciousness or breathe for himself.

Atticus died just before midnight on July 23 2022.

Experts said the injuries suffered by Atticus were associated with “vigorous shaking”, with his rib fractures caused by “gripping and squeezing” during that attack, Mr Row told the court.

In a victim personal statement, Ms Ballentyne described how she had been left with “severe anxiety” following Atticus’s death.

open image in gallery The trial took place at Bristol Crown Court ( Ben Birchall/PA )

“I will never know what kind of person Atticus would have become,” she said.

“I will never see him hit milestones. I will never see him go to school. I will never see him grow up and have a family of his own.”

She continued: “Who plans their baby’s funeral? Who goes to the chapel of rest?

“I had to wait 11 hours and 18 minutes for Atticus to die. It was horrendous. I was scared to go out, I was scared to stay in.

“I don’t enjoy any moments because I have a dead son. It is mentally and emotionally draining all the time. It is awful.”

Her mother, Mrs Donovan, told the court how she wondered what Atticus would look like now and what toys he would like to play with.

“I just want one more day with Atticus,” she said.

“I’m glad I had Atticus that night. He was loved and cuddled and had a lovely night with us.

“I just hope and pray he never knew what happened to him.”

Representing Bartlett, Nigel Power KC said his client had previously been a “good and caring parent” to his son.

“This is not a case where there is intention to kill or premeditation,” Mr Power said.

Detective Sergeant Sarah Bowden, from the Major Crime Investigation Team at Avon and Somerset Police, said: “Tony Bartlett was alone with Atticus when he suffered these horrendous injuries and the medical evidence gathered during the investigation proves he was solely responsible for causing them, despite his claims of innocence.

“This is a devastating case in which a very young baby has lost his life as the direct result of a cruel act by a man who was supposed to provide him with the protection and care he needed.

“The loss of Atticus has had a profound effect on all those who loved him. Our thoughts are very much with Atticus’ family who’ve had to endure a lengthy and complex police investigation, followed by a trial. They’ve shown great dignity and courage throughout.

“Investigations like this are extremely harrowing and I’d like to thank all those who provided evidence and supported our investigation to establish the facts behind Atticus’ tragic death.”

Hundreds of thousands of disabled benefit claimants will soon face intrusive reassessments despite claiming for over a decade, as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) restarts a changeover scheme.

As part of the closure of adult Disability Living Allowance (DLA) claims, these individuals will be moved to the Personal Independence Payment (Pip) – the benefit currently at the centre of a government review.

Although still open for child claimants, adults have not been able to claim DLA since 2013, when Pip was introduced as its replacement.

The DWP began inviting adult DLA claimants of the benefit to move over to the newer benefit in the same year, but this lengthy process was paused in 2020 in response to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Around 153,000 adult DLA claimants still remain, the DWP has said, all of whom will now be invited to move to Pip.

If they fail to respond to this invitation and make a claim, they will lose their current benefit entitlement.

open image in gallery Around 153,000 adult DLA claimants will be moved to Pip, the DWP has said ( Getty )

It is understood that most of these DLA claimants received lifetime awards, meaning there was an acknowledgement that their conditions would not change and so they would not be subject to further assessments.

Most adult DLA claimants post-2013 have had to move to Pip when their award comes up for review, but this does not happen for these claimants.

But they will now instead be assessed under Pip rules, meaning a new form must be filled out, likely followed by a health assessment to determine eligibility.

This process is often described as “dehumanising”, “soul-destroying”, and “degrading”, disability minister Sir Stephen Timms recently found in his interim report into Pip.

The authors add that applicants are often required to share “intimate details” with assessors only for them to feel these are later “misrepresented or dismissed”.

Although the final report and recommendations are not expected until the autumn, the review team added that “bold changes” will be made to the benefit which was at the centre of Labour’s welfare fallout last year.

open image in gallery The review into Poip is being led by disability minister Sir Stephen Timms ( PA Archive )

These will not be implemented before the DLA to Pip transfer scheme resumes, however. The DWP has said it will begin with 3,000 randomly-chosen cases from September before any wider rollout.

James Taylor, director of strategy at disability equality charity Scope, said: “The DWP needs to make sure they don’t penalise disabled people whose extra costs are only likely to rise.”

Current DLA claimants need to “make sure they respond when the DWP gets in contact,” he added.

“Disabled people know that the current system for PIP is not working and too many have to endure assessments that feel dehumanising and confrontational.”

The DWP has been approached for comment.

The number of measles cases in the U.S. has surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025, with five more months of 2026 still to come.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention logged 2,318 cases of measles as of Thursday, according to an agency update on Friday.

The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades. Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.’s worst year for measles since 1991, as major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona have sickened hundreds and smaller clusters of cases sparked in other states.

In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The U.S. eliminated local measles spread in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, which have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

Measles cases are undercounted

While measles cases in the U.S. are climbing, it may be impossible to say exactly how far-reaching the spread is. Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts are incomplete, because some people get sick and don’t seek out treatment — something not unique to measles.

Furthermore, experts say the spread might be greater than what’s known because the virus is one of the most contagious known to medicine and vaccination rates nationwide have declined. National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5% among kindergartners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2% in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities.

In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has sickened more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department. Experts relying on mathematical modeling and genetic analyses indicate that a large outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be around three to four times bigger than what’s currently known, state epidemiologist Dr. Leisha Nolen said.

The picture is muddier in South Carolina, which had the nation’s largest outbreak in 35 years. There, the 997 total is likely an undercount, the state health department has said, but it doesn’t know by how much.

Dr. Brannon Traxler, acting director of the state department of health, said the undercount is “impossible to know and may vary during the course of an outbreak.”

Data gaps can make it hard to reliably estimate an outbreak’s true scope. Experts say hospitalization rates can be a good barometer, but measles hospitalizations are not required to be reported in every state.

“If we really had some kind of solid gold standard for the percentage of all cases that have hospitalization or some measure of severity, then that would be another way of estimating the outbreak size that we could see if it’s consistent with these other methods,” said Damon Toth, an applied mathematician at the University of Utah’s medical school who is working on one of the Utah outbreak analyses.

Researchers are still analyzing the 2025 Texas outbreak

In Texas, researchers are still working to estimate the size of the state’s 2025 outbreak and early findings show it might have been nearly twice the size of the 762 known cases.

Rémy Pasco, a mathematical epidemiologist at the University of Colorado Boulder who is working on the analysis, said the undercounts were unsurprising. In the absence of an adequate community vaccination rate — 95% according to health experts — “there’s just not much you can do about measles once you have it,” he said.

The CDC defines an outbreak as three or more linked cases. But by the time three such cases are identified in communities with low vaccination rates and less disease surveillance, “either you missed the previous ones or you’re going to have a lot more,” he added.

Dr. Varun Shetty, Texas’ chief state epidemiologist, said there were instances where people tested positive for measles but health officials couldn’t confirm who else was in the person’s household or if they were sick.

“What we’re able to count and report is almost always an underestimate of what actually occurred, because it relies on people being willing to be able to get tested, to share information with healthcare providers and with public health,” Shetty said. “Sometimes that just doesn’t happen.”

The state health department previously reported that 182 probable measles cases went unconfirmed in March 2025 among minors in Gaines County — the epicenter of the outbreak — due to a lack of information. The confirmed case count for the western Texas county for the whole outbreak is 414.

Shetty expects to keep seeing measles cases and even outbreaks because so many people are unprotected.

“It’s really critical, not only for individual people, but for communities, to have high vaccination coverage,” he said.

Vaccination is about protecting others, physician says

Dr. Mark Roberts, retired director of the Public Health Dynamics Lab at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health, worries most for the people he calls “innocent bystanders.”

Research and measles modeling by his team shows those who cannot get vaccinated — young babies, people with weak immune systems and those who rarely don’t get robust immunity from the vaccine — bear the brunt of outbreaks early on.

Some people see skipping vaccination as like deciding not to wear a seat belt in a car, Roberts said.

“Not vaccinating your kid is like saying, ‘I don’t want my car to have brakes,’” he said. “Because it’s other people that you can hit. It’s not just you in your car. It’s other people.”

News.title: The AI gold rush: the technology transforming Britain’s small businesses
News.content:
Artificial intelligence has rapidly transitioned from the margins of business to the mainstream. More than half of UK firms (54 per cent) are now actively using AI in their operations, according to the British Chambers of Commerce – a vast leap from just 23 per cent three years ago.

“Consumers are using it non-stop, large corporates are heavily investing, and now SMEs too need to apply the widespread benefits to their businesses – to avoid falling behind,” says Ruchir Rodrigues, Client Strategy & Commercial Director at Lloyds Business and Commercial.

Ruchir Rodrigues, Client Strategy & Commercial Director at Lloyds Business and Commercial ( Lloyds )

Two-thirds of UK businesses have invested in AI, according to the Lloyds Business Barometer, with most companies spending less than £25,000 on the technology. For many, these relatively modest investments are already translating into tangible day-to-day productivity gains.

“But our findings suggest only 7.5 per cent of SMEs engaging with AI are very confident in understanding the benefits for their business,” Rodrigues adds. “A lot of our one million business clients say, ‘it'll help productivity, but how do I put a number on it?’”

A quarter of small and medium-sized enterprises cite uncertainty around return on investment (ROI) as a primary barrier to AI adoption, according to a YouGov survey of over 1,000 IT decision-makers. However, Lloyds’ own customer research reveals that trust has emerged as an equally formidable hurdle.

For many SMEs, the hesitation isn't just about whether AI technology works, but whether they can trust it with their proprietary data ( Getty Images )

In a crowded market filled with rapidly evolving players – including Google’s Gemini, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Perplexity – business owners are struggling to know which tools to trust and where to safely invest.

This trust deficit is heavily compounded by deep concerns over data privacy and security, alongside a growing realisation that many firms lack the strong underlying data foundations needed to deploy these tools safely.

These issues stand alongside a persistent digital skills gap as critical barriers. For many SMEs, the hesitation isn't just about whether the technology works, but whether they can trust it with their proprietary data.

From soil mapping to automated fabrication

“We have agricultural businesses using the technology to upload images of soil [and] analyse its content,” Rodrigues says ( Michela Ravasio/Stocksy - stock.adobe.com )

However, Rodrigues sees a more optimistic picture, thanks to the real-world use cases Lloyds’ 700 relationship managers across the UK are seeing British companies deploy.

“We have agricultural businesses using the technology to upload images of soil, analyse its content, and cross-reference weather patterns to decide which crops to plant each season – resulting in a more profitable harvest, year after year,” he explains.

Lloyds has partnered with Soil Association Exchange (SAX) to build a major farm environmental dataset, applying AI-driven mapping and analytics to generate insights on risk, resilience and investment opportunities.

In a second example, an advanced manufacturing client is building an entirely new business model around the technology.

“Clients upload images of what they want made, the AI generates a design and a 3D printer produces it,” Rodrigues adds.

The company has partnered with the Lloyds-backed Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, which offers expert support to help SMEs adopt advanced digital technologies such as AI-powered design tools, robotics and automation.

As Rodrigues points out: “Access to data and vastly improving processes are helping manufacturers come up with better solutions for swathes of industries.”

Navigating the AI maturity spectrum

More than six in 10 businesses are using AI for the creation of marketing content, according to a Lloyds customer survey* ( Getty Images )

For SMEs, AI maturity exists on a spectrum. At one end, businesses are simply dipping a toe in. Legal and professional services companies are using embedded AI systems to rapidly redact personal information from documents, for example, while others deploy large language models for content writing or to generate marketing ideas.

Indeed, more than six in 10 businesses are using AI for the creation of marketing content, according to a Lloyds customer survey*.

“In the middle, we see SMEs starting to integrate AI into processes to automate repetitive tasks,” Rodrigues adds, “while at the far end, the most sophisticated operators are building agentic AI systems: technology that doesn't just assist humans but independently executes complex tasks.”

Lloyds uses its own experience to help its customers with the technology. Its senior leaders are currently enrolled on a six-month programme with Cambridge University focused on agentic AI, helping the bank rank on the Global Evidence AI Index as one of the world's most AI-literate financial institutions.

More widely, Rodrigues represents Lloyds on the SME Digital Adoption Taskforce, a joint government-industry group specifically designed to help businesses break down these very barriers. By identifying practical, scalable solutions to overcome hurdles like the skills gap, security anxieties and ROI uncertainty, the taskforce acts as a vital bridge – helping SMEs confidently adopt productivity-enhancing digital technologies and accelerate their AI journey.

Internally, the bank saw the technology’s practical power when dealing with its thousands of property developer clients. Previously, these clients submitted tenancy statements and cash flow forecasts to secure lending in hundreds of different formats, meaning relationship managers devoted hours to reconciling the information.

“Now that’s all automated,” Rodrigues says. “It’s gone from a whole afternoon of work to a few minutes – across our whole business, that has a huge impact – and we’re helping clients roll out that productivity boost.”

Far from replacing human roles, this shift seems to have freed up relationship managers from administrative bottlenecks, allowing them to dedicate more time to strategic, face-to-face client support.

Why fundamental data is key

For AI to scale safely and sustainably, businesses must implement rigorous controls, safeguards and responsible use policies ( Getty Images )

There is, however, a sobering note to Rodrigues' optimism: AI is only as good as the data feeding it.

“People get caught in the hype of AI but forget that fundamental data and strong governance is key: without that, it falls on its face.”

For AI to scale safely and sustainably, businesses must move beyond experimentation and implement rigorous controls, safeguards, and responsible use policies. Establishing these frameworks is what ultimately builds long-term customer trust.

Lloyds uses its own scale to lead by example. The bank is currently undertaking a significant cloud migration to unlock the value of its data. Crucially, the bank does not feed customer data into public models; instead, it adopts models from the likes of OpenAI or Google and pulls them inside its own secure systems, running the models internally to guarantee data privacy.

For an SME, leading by example looks remarkably similar, just on a different scale. Instead of massive custom infrastructure, it means ensuring that internal documents, client emails and financial spreadsheets are cleanly organised within secure, commercial versions of everyday software. By opting for business-grade subscriptions, a small firm can ring-fence its data just as securely as a major bank, ensuring proprietary information never leaks into the public domain.

Bridging the trust and capability gap

Alongside its work with the SME Digital Adoption Taskforce, Lloyds provides targeted backing to advanced tech hubs such as the MTC ( MTC Training )

For smaller businesses without that scale of infrastructure, navigating these governance and security hurdles can feel overwhelming. Lloyds’ approach is sequential: build the data strategy first, then find models you can use internally. But the bank isn’t leaving SMEs to figure it out alone. Instead, it is actively deploying its network, finance, and expertise to bridge the trust and capability gaps.

“You want everyone in your business to know about AI, but you also need a small pocket of expertise that understands it deeper: get an expert in your business,” says Rodrigues.

To help businesses build that internal capability, the Lloyds Bank Academy provides free, on-demand online skills training and masterclasses. This practical guidance cuts through the market noise, showing SMEs how to build robust AI strategies while explicitly highlighting the cyber risks and data-security dangers of feeding sensitive information into public AI tools.

Beyond training, Lloyds addresses financial and structural barriers through its broader industry ecosystem. Alongside its ongoing work with the SME Digital Adoption Taskforce, the bank provides targeted backing to advanced tech hubs like the MTC. This ensures SMEs have a direct pipeline to the expert support, technical advice, and foundational funding pathways needed to adopt AI-powered digital tools confidently.

Further ahead, Rodrigues sees AI combining with other emerging technologies, such as tokenisation – the process of representing real-world assets digitally on a blockchain – to help address long-standing financial challenges.

“Combining AI with tokenisation unlocks huge knowledge about the patterns of how money moves,” he says. While it has not fully reached SMEs yet, the implications for speeding up trade finance and cross-border payments are significant.

The competitive advantage of acting now

Those businesses who embrace AI technology will be far better placed than those that do not, Rodrigues believes ( Getty Images )

For now, Rodrigues’ message to SMEs is a simple one: start. Those who embrace the technology, however modestly, will be far better placed than those that do not.

“It’s transforming everything: every industry, every business’ way to both drive revenue and remove costs. It affects both sides of the balance sheet.”

Ultimately, the true return on investment for Britain’s SMEs may not just be measured in pounds and pence, but in time. By taking care of the repetitive, administrative heavy lifting, AI is giving business owners and their teams the freedom to return to the things that matter most: their core expertise, human creativity and building lasting relationships with their customers.

*Lloyds Business and Commercial Banking Customer 360 Survey

News.title: Wildfires force 80,000 to flee in France and Spain as Cap Ferret evacuated
News.content:

Massive forest fires are raging across southwestern France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 80,000 people from their homes. In France, some residents were compelled to flee by boat as flames engulfed the popular Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast.

The blaze near Cap Ferret, located just 60 kilometres (37 miles) from Bordeaux, has consumed approximately 100 square kilometres (38 square miles) since Wednesday. This area, usually celebrated for its stunning landscapes, sandy beaches, oyster-farming villages, and upmarket resorts, is now under severe threat. Over 60,000 French residents have been displaced.

Both France and Spain have appealed to fellow European Union member states for urgent assistance to combat the escalating infernos.

open image in gallery Firefighters work to extinguish flames during a wildfire in Lege-Cap-Ferret in the Gironde department, amongst worsening drought conditions following a heatwave and water shortages across much of France. ( Reuters )

Hundreds of French firefighters have been deployed and additional ground and aerial reinforcements were sent Friday to tackle the blaze. Meanwhile, another major wildfire burned further south down the coast. It remained uncontained as strong winds did not help firefighters.

Authorities believe the cause of both fires was accidental.

France’s Interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said 40,000 people have been evacuated in the Gironde department, and 23,000 in the Landes.

French President Emmanuel Macron said France will receive EU reinforcements including two Croatian Canadair firefighting aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractor aircraft, and two heavy-lift Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said that Italy and Greece are each sending two Canadair water-dumping airplanes.

The Clouds became ‘Darker and darker’

In southwest France, authorities sent boats to help the evacuation and a total of about 63,000 people, many of them tourists, were told to get out as two major, separate fires threatened homes and campsites, officials said.

"From our home, we had a view of the fires ... We could see the clouds becoming darker and darker," said Yoan Urien, who left late on Thursday after police told everyone in his neighbourhood in the town of Biscarrosse to leave. "I was able to find ‌somewhere to take shelter with my pets, but ... it's quite a shock," the 26-year-old told Reuters.

open image in gallery Holidaymakers from Lege-Cap-Ferret disembark from a boat upon their arrival in Arcachon during an evacuation operation of the entire Cap-Ferret peninsula ( AFP/Getty )

The other major fire, which began in nearby Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, is threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula and is the largest so far this season in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television. It has ‌torn through more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of forest and burned 80 homes, completely destroying about 50 ‌of them, he said.

"It breaks my heart. Because it's such a pleasant place to live, seeing it go up in smoke is truly sad," said family caregiver Corinne Paillaube. "It's totally apocalyptic," said Ambre Dubos, from the nearby Landes region.

Mapped: Cap Ferret peninsula

Spain struggles to tackle multiple fires amid a heatwave

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency for wildfires for the first time as the blazes in Madrid and the nearby province of Ávila prompted the evacuation of some 20,000 people from towns.

The national emergency means that the nation’s interior ministry, which controls police and security forces, has taken charge of overseeing the firefighting efforts that are being fanned by a heat wave. Temperatures are expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit) in parts of Spain.

The two major fires west of Madrid merged into one single blaze that had quickly charred 30 square kilometers (11.5 square miles) by Friday afternoon. Regional president Isabel Díaz-Ayuso called it the worst in Madrid's history.

The regional government of Madrid, which spans a wide area around the city, said that around 18,000 people had been evacuated from different villages and towns west of the capital.

open image in gallery Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near La Adrada, Ávila province, Spain. ( AP )

Meanwhile, a blaze in Ávila, less than two hours northwest of Madrid, had consumed 90 square kilometers (34 square miles), causing another 1,500 people to flee.

“In my 60 years I have never seen something like this in my village, I have never seen fire of these dimensions,” Francisco Martínez, the mayor of Burgohondo, whose residents were preventively evacuated in Ávila, told Spain’s national broadcaster TVE.

Spanish television showed video taken by retreating residents of walls of flames topped by long plumes of smoke advancing through woods and scrublands. High winds and hilly terrain complicated efforts by firefighters, who combated the blazes with firetrucks and bulldozers.

“All around the town was smoke and fire, I was scared. Everything was fire and smoke, people were nervous,” 33-year-old Joaquin Espinosa told The Associated Press before he and his neighbors were evacuated fromF the village of Chapinería, located less than an hour's drive west of Madrid.

Strong winds complicate efforts

In one week, Spain has had the worst fires on record for both the regions of Castilla La Mancha and Madrid.

Firefighters were still trying to extinguish Spain’s second-largest ever fire in the Guadalajara province of Castilla La Mancha after it had destroyed some 320 square kilometers (120 square miles) over the last week. Thirteen people were also killed in a fire in southern Spain earlier this month, the deadliest fire in recent memory for Spain.

Spanish Minister for the Ecological Transition Sara Aagesen said that Spain has seen 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) already burned this year, more than five times the burned terrain it had through the first half of 2025.

open image in gallery Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Ávila province, Spain. ( AP )

Grande-Marlaska said that in addition to the major fires in Madrid and in Ávila that have required the national government to get directly involved, there are nine serious fires in other parts of Spain.

“The day has been complicated by winds that reach 50 kph (31 mph) and high temperatures,” Grande-Marlaska said.

Sánchez called on Wednesday for a pact between political parties to fight climate change that he said is key to adapting to a more fire-prone climate. Spain has experienced record temperatures in recent summers and forest fires of increasing violence.

Sicily is burning

In Italy, wildfires continued to ravage parts of Sicily, with the central-western province of Agrigento particularly hard hit.

open image in gallery A Canadair drops water over a burning area as a wildfire flares in Sagana in the territory of Monreale, Sicily ( AFP/Getty )

Fueled by temperatures that have topped 40C (104F), low humidity and winds, the blazes have forced scattered evacuations and were blamed for the death of a firefighter responding to a fire in Caltanissetta.

Globally, 2025 was the third-hottest year on record, bringing severe heat waves across Europe. Scientists warn that climate change is exacerbating the frequency and intensity of heat and dryness especially in southeastern Europe, making the region more vulnerable to health impacts and wildfires.

A powerful Hurricane Fausto has intensified into a Category 2 storm in the Pacific Ocean, with forecasters predicting its approach towards the Hawaiian Islands next week.

The National Hurricane Center in Miami warned on Friday that while the risk of wind and rainfall impacts in the region is growing, it remains too early to pinpoint the precise location or potential severity of the storm's effects.

Fausto is currently situated far from any landmass, approximately 1,300 miles (2,090 kilometers) west of Mexico's Baja California peninsula and about 1,600 miles (2,575 kilometers) east of Hilo, Hawaii.

The hurricane is sustaining maximum winds of around 100 mph (161 kph).

open image in gallery Fausto is set to approach the Hawaiian islands and could also bring severe weather to Southern California ( NOAA via AP )

Beyond Hawaii, the hurricane center also issued a warning that swells generated by Fausto could lead to dangerous surf and rip tides along parts of southern California's coastline.

Tropical Storm Bertha dissipates

This Pacific system develops as Tropical Storm Bertha, which recently brought significant surf and flooding to southern Louisiana and Texas after making a second landfall, has now dissipated.

It made two landfalls along the Gulf Coast, bringing heavy surf and some flooding to southern Louisiana and Texas. The system, which rapidly weakened on Thursday, left behind a lingering risk of flash flooding from its remnants across the region.

The National Hurricane Center confirmed Bertha's dissipation by late Thursday evening, though it noted that wind gusts of tropical storm force were still possible along the upper Texas coast. Water levels in the area were also expected to remain elevated due to storm surge. Its remnants are now projected to produce 1 to 3 inches of rainfall, with isolated totals reaching up to 4 inches, posing a flash flood threat for coastal and south Texas.

Bertha first impacted southern Louisiana on Wednesday, moving slowly westward. It made its second landfall on Thursday afternoon, approximately 75 miles northeast of Galveston, Texas, already having weakened considerably. The system remained a tropical storm for only a few hours before being downgraded to a depression, characterized by maximum sustained winds of 38 mph or less.

open image in gallery Children play near breaking waves on West End Pier on Lake Pontchartrain as Tropical Storm Bertha approaches the Louisiana Coast Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in New Orleans ( AP Photo/Gerald Herbert )

The storm's thick cloud cover also led to the postponement of SpaceX's planned Starship launch from the southern tip of Texas. The space-skimming test flight was subsequently rescheduled for Friday, anticipating clearer skies for the operation.

No deaths or significant damage have been reported since Bertha formed on Monday in the Gulf of Mexico south of the Florida Panhandle. While its center caused some coastal flooding during its initial strike in Louisiana southwest of New Orleans, the heaviest rains largely remained over Gulf waters before moving inland along Texas's southeastern coast on Thursday afternoon. Tropical storm force winds on Thursday extended as far as 140 miles from the storm’s center.

By evening, a tropical storm warning from Sargent, Texas, to the Vermilion and Cameron Parish line in Louisiana was officially discontinued, signaling the immediate threat had passed.

News.title: Eleanor Cardwell: ‘Comfortable sportswear should not be expensive’
News.content:
What sports shoes do you recommend?

Robert, South West

The sports shoes that I’m currently wearing are from Puma. They’re very comfortable and have support. I actually wear a basketball shoe at the minute to have more support up the ankle.

A lot of the girls wear Asics as well, which I know is the netball shoe. I’ve worn Puma for the last four years, so I would recommend them.

But honestly, whatever works best for you, you have to try them out. Whatever is best for your instep and whatever is comfiest. And if you need more ankle support, you can put some ankle braces on.

How has playing for Manchester Thunder helped you develop as a player?

Jason, London

Manchester has massively helped me develop as a player. I’ve been playing here since 2012. As a young girl, it created me as a person, to be honest with you. It’s such a family environment that I think a lot of my values come from this club. So my family values, being connected, creating energy – all those things come rooted from this club, which is incredible.

I think whatever step you are in your career, whether you’re a young athlete or senior, they help you develop. Even now I’m 31, they’re still helping me learn new things on the court. The coaches are incredible, and I’m constantly learning and being inspired by them every single week.

Do players retire from elite netball quite young?

Helen, South West

I think it depends on the athlete. Some can retire at 40, and that’s because their bodies are so conditioned, and they might not have had any major injuries in their career. They’re able to continue to push themselves all the way until 40.

But I’d say the average is probably mid-30s. Now the Super League has become professional, the younger athletes are getting better training from a younger age. We want to keep pushing ourselves to play as long as possible.

How can netball get more coverage when women’s football is constantly pushed?

Sarah, South West

I think netball needs to have more sponsors to get more media coverage. Bigger sponsors.

Players need to put their personalities more out there on social media, so brands will want to work with us. Everyone’s got amazing personalities in netball. They [brands] should want to be a part of the netball players’ stories and the netball teams.

But it’s about getting as much exposure as possible, and making sure that everyone is going on YouTube or BBC, so more people are able to learn about the sport.

I loved netball at school. How do I get involved now in my 60s?

Sue, Yorkshire

Netball is for everyone. I personally love going to walking netball sessions and taking them through classes. You can go to the England Netball website and find out where you can play locally.

There’s also Back to Netball, depending on your ability and what you want to get out of it. Personally, I think walking netball is so much fun. The women who are in those sessions are a huge laugh, and I know when I retire, I’m going to be joining a group, for sure.

Apart from netball, what other hobbies do you have? How do they help you relieve the pressure of competition?

George, London

I feel like over the past few years I’ve really got into some new hobbies. I love reading. I love fantasy reading, like Throne of Glass. I love BookTok, so I’ve really got into that.

I’m also very crafty. I like making things – I’ve made little crochet bees for all the girls, and I like drawing, and painting occasionally – just wholesome activities to take me away from netball life. As soon as I zone in on an activity, I’m locked in and I have to complete it.

News.title: Africa improves health defences, but it remains vulnerable to pandemics
News.content:
Africa is significantly better prepared for a pandemic than it was five years ago, a major review of the continent’s health security has found.

The review, which tracked dozens of health metrics across the continent, found that local and international investments in Africa’s health sector since the pandemic have “paid off.”

Published by the Brown University Pandemic Centre and the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US non-profit, the report is the third of its kind and provides an update on two previous reviews from 2019 and 2021.

Investment in health by African governments grew rapidly during the pandemic. Post-pandemic, the average spend now sits at around 7.4 per cent of GDP, roughly $135 billion per year across the continent.

That figure still falls significantly below those of high-income countries, where the average spend on health sits at around 11.2 per cent of GDP.

The new African Health Security Index report found that almost every African country – 53 out of 54, excluding only the Republic of the Congo – has improved its ability to prevent, detect, and respond to disease outbreaks since 2021, the last time the index was updated.

Overall, the continent scores 41.2 out of 100 on its health security – up from 32.9 five years ago.

The score is built from hundreds of specific indicators covering things like how far people live from a hospital, how well infectious patients can be isolated, the size and training level of the health workforce, laboratory capacity, and the availability of vaccines and other critical medicines during an outbreak.

News.title: Ebola death toll passes 1,000 as outbreak shows no signs of slowing
News.content:
More than 1,000 people have now died in the outbreak of Ebola in the Congo, as medics struggle to curb the fastest-growing epidemic of the virus.

Dozens of deaths are being recorded each day and modelling has forecast that, in a worst case scenario, it could become the worst Ebola outbreak in history.

The outbreak, centred on the north east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), passed the four-figure death milestone little more than two months after it was first declared.

By contrast, the worst outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever on record, which struck West Africa from 2014 to 2016, took eight months from the first case to reach 1,000 deaths. It went on to kill 11,000 people.

The latest figures from the DRC’s national public health institute show 2,536 confirmed Ebola cases and 1,033 deaths, with at least 738 patients in isolation or hospitalised.

News.title: Inflation fall a ‘false dawn’, Burnham warned
News.content:
Falling inflation is a “false dawn” for Andy Burnham, economists warned after the pace of price rises slowed in June.

The consumer prices index (CPI) fell from 2.8pc in May to 2.6pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating economists’ expectations of a drop to 2.7pc to mark the lowest rate in 15 months.

Lower petrol and diesel prices drove the slowdown amid a short-lived peace deal between the US and Iran, while price pressures from chocolate, oils and fats, dairy and meat also weakened.

However, economists warned a rise in household energy bills in July may already have pushed inflation back up above 3pc.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants, said: “June’s slowdown is a false dawn as it may have already been reversed this month with higher energy bills, following Ofgem’s energy price cap rise, likely to have lifted inflation above 3pc.”

July’s 13pc increase in the energy price cap has pushed typical annual bills to around £1,862, while renewed fighting between the US and Iran has reignited concerns over oil and gas supplies.

Mr Thiru said elevated inflation would create a fresh headache for John Healey, the newly appointed Chancellor, by squeezing household budgets, raising government borrowing costs and limiting his room for tax cuts or spending increases.

Charlotte O’Leary, at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “June’s peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil and gas prices helped cool consumer price inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new Prime Minister’s premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived.”

The Bank of England will also be watching closely as it weighs further interest rate cuts, though economists warned renewed instability in the Middle East and higher energy bills could keep inflation close to 3pc for the rest of the year.

Mr Healey said: “Falling inflation is news families want to hear, but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need.”

News.title: Russia destroys Ukraine HIV warehouse
News.content:
A Russian missile strike has destroyed $2.6m (£1.9m) worth of HIV prevention supplies in Ukraine, according to an international aid group.

The Alliance for Public Health said the attack on Sunday night near Kyiv hit a warehouse holding 62 million prevention items earmarked for Ukraine’s harm reduction programmes next year. It includes syringes, needles, alcohol wipes, and condoms intended to support more than 300,000 people.

“This is not just another strike. It is an attack on 300,000 Ukrainians who depend on HIV prevention services and on their fundamental right to health,” said Andriy Klepikov, executive director of the Alliance for Public Health.

Efforts to prevent the spread of HIV rely heavily on harm reduction programmes that supply sterile syringes and needles to people who inject drugs, alongside condoms and other supplies that help curb sexual transmission.

Mr Klepikov said the destruction of the warehouse would not immediately disrupt services, because his organisation had moved its supplies for the rest of the year out of central storage and into regional distribution centres several weeks ago as part of contingency planning.

“Russia failed,” he said, adding that the Alliance had notified international partners and appealed for urgent support to rebuild next year’s inventory.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

Sports.title: England captain Harry Kane ‘opens talks with Bayern Munich over lucrative new deal despite Barcelona transfer interest’

HARRY KANE is set to open talks with German giants Bayern Munich over a new contract.

United recently enquired about Aurelien Tchouameni as Real Madrid would like to sign Rodri from Manchester City.

That tallies with reports early this year when United were monitoring Elliot Anderson, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali before their costly transfers.



Alex Scott, Carlos Baleba and Adam Wharton are three other midfielders United have tracked.

Tchouameni appeals to United as he is an outright defensive midfielder, something they are completely devoid of with Manuel Ugarte sidelined for the remainder of the calendar year.



United are bound to cover themselves and not promise a third midfield incoming.

Twenty years ago, the United chief executive David Gill promised “two world-class signings”.

United bought Michael Carrick and Tomasz Kuszcak, who were not world-class.

TICKED OFF PART ONE

THE FALLOUT continues from the Manchester United season ticket fiasco after several fans were locked out of their accounts.

United’s attempted clampdown was to target bots and established touts but, as reported in the week, many season ticket holders log in on multiple accounts for various reasons, such as to help family and friends.

Multiple United fans we have spoken to have taken umbrage with the club’s claim that there is no ticketing process that requires a supporter to access another person’s account.

One season-ticket holder does for relatives and friends to apply for away games.

They said: “It spreads the opportunity of getting away tickets and all are valid applications.”



Another fan has delayed their appeal before the deadline in the hope that there is a satisfactory resolution.

Two fans had suspensions overturned as they were logged into one account on multiple devices and were able to prove their whereabouts.

Many instances that have led to the suspension of accounts have been when more than one account logged into one device, which has been classed as “sustained activity.”

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust has been “inundated” with complaints by supporters affected.

There is also concern among supporters that the club will not refund those affected.



Well-placed sources say the fan groups are privately “hammering” the club and certain figures now understand and realise the damage they have inflicted.

TICKED OFF PART TWO

UNITED are struggling to shift tickets for their pre-season friendlies in Scandinavia.

Nearly 11,000 tickets are still available for their match against Rosenborg in Norway on Friday.



The Lerkendal Stadium has a capacity of 28,569 and 10,805 tickets remain unsold 24 hours before kick-off.

The most expensive non-VIP ticket is priced at 1,495 Norwegian Krone – £116.43. The cheapest ticket is 945 Norwegian Krona (£73.60).

The decision to play four friendlies in Scandinavia has risked tour fatigue as this is the fifth summer running that United have played in the region.

United faced Rosenborg in Trondheim at the start of their pre-season schedule two years ago and lost 1-0. Then-manager Erik ten Hag was critical of United’s performance after he picked two different XIs for each half.

With United’s squad still depleted as they wait for their World Cup participants to return, they have named a similar squad to the one that travelled to Helsinki for the 1-0 defeat to Wrexham last week.



The expectation is that Carrick will again field two different XIs for each half against Norway’s most successful club.

United decided to remain in Europe in pre-season for the first time since 2002, excluding the Covid-affected summers of 2020 and 2021, having toured the United States for the last three years.

The club had the offer to tour Asia but declined.



A source familiar with United’s ticketing strategy said the unusual tour schedule has been a “reality check.”

United’s 1-0 defeat to Wrexham in Helsinki last week drew a crowd of 20,069 and 19,000 tickets had to be sold to turn a profit.

With United due to take on more eminent sides in Atletico Madrid, Paris Saint-Germain, Leeds United and AC Milan next month, their opening Scandinavian friendlies have served little purpose other than to provide the players with minutes and rake in income.

Tens of thousands of tickets are available for the friendly with Atletico in Stockholm next week. Just 16 blocks are sold out at the 50,000-seater Strawberry Arena, where United drew 0-0 with Leeds last year.

There have been better sales for the match with PSG in Gothenburg on August 8. United have not played in Gothenburg for ten years and around 30,000 tickets have been flogged at the 43,000-capacity Ullevi stadium.



The presence of back-to-back Champions League winners PSG will have bolstered sales, although their France World Cup contingent are unlikely to appear.

PSG take on United three weeks on from the weekend of the World Cup final and third place play-off match, so Ousmane Dembele, Bradley Barcola, Desire Doue and Fabian Ruiz almost certainly won’t play.

United play Leeds at Croke Park in Dublin on August 12 before ending their pre-season schedule against Ruben Amorim‘s AC Milan in Wroclaw on August 15.

OFF THE GROUND

UNITED and Wrexham were locked in a race to get their private jets out of Helsinki last weekend, knowing losers would be kept waiting on the runway for up to 30 minutes.

Wrexham’s squad made a swift exit to their bus, though goalscorer Sam Smith did pause in the corridor to catch up with a family friend and Phil Parkinson spent the longest speaking to the media out of the managers.



United appeared to be in far less of a hurry, with their first-half players trickling through the mixed zone on Saturday and four stars stopping to chat along the way.

United lost the game, but won the race for take-off.

WILL-I-AM

THE same scout behind Ayden Heaven’s move to Old Trafford struck again.



Emerging Talent scout at United, Sam William, s worked alongside head of recruitment Christopher Vivell and director of football Jason Wilcox to seal Tynan Thompson’s transfer this week.

Williams rejoined United four months after Ineos took over football operations in February 2024.

He initially left United in 2022 to become recruitment head at Ipswich Town, supporting their promotion to the Premier League.

FINNISH LINE

CARRICK took a morning jog through the city centre before United’s opening pre-season friendly at the Helsinki Olympic Stadium.

Carrick and his 22-man squad, half of which were academy youngsters, spent time signing autographs for fans outside the team hotel in the Finnish capital on Friday afternoon.



Carrick thought a Finnish fan was handing him an item to sign, but it turned out to be a gift for him to keep.

JACE AGAINST TIME

CARRICK watched academy training sessions at Carrington the week before the senior players returned for pre-season.

Carrick, whose son Jacey has been confirmed as a first-year scholar this season, has been spending time assessing the development of players at Under-21 and Under-18 level.



In Helsinki, he fielded an entirely academy-produced side in the second half of the pre-season game against Wrexham and roughly the same group of players will be involved against Rosenborg in Trondheim on Friday.

United signed Spurs youth winger Thompson for £4million on Monday and are closing in on three 16-year-old midfielders, including Liverpool winger Isaac Konde.

OROZ-GOAL

COLOMBIAN defensive midfielder Cristian Orozco officially completed his transfer from Fortaleza CEIF following his 18th birthday.

The highly-rated U17 captain joined the club’s Under-21 setup in Germany for pre-season training.

Club officials hold the young leader in high regard, and this trip will act as a crucial testing ground.

Senior coaches and academy staff will closely assess his performances throughout the camp to gauge whether he is ready to make the leap toward the first-team fold.

He could well tread the same path as fellow South American teen Diego Leon, who was put with the U21s last summer after arriving from Cerro Porteno for an initial fee of £3.3million.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's private thoughts World Cup final players' behaviour revealed
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's private thoughts World Cup final players' behaviour revealed

Gianni Infantino praised Spain's players for their exemplary conduct - a stark contrast to Argentina's behaviour after their World Cup 1-0 defeat

View Image Luis de la Fuente has revealed Gianni Infantino's praise for Spain's players (Image: Getty Images)

Gianni Infantino has declared Spain a shining example to football, making the statement in the wake of the World Cup final's shocking scenes of violence triggered by Argentina's players. Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes was at the centre of the brawl, throwing punches and kicks at rival players as they celebrated the 1-0 triumph in New Jersey

‌



An extra‑time winner from Ferran Torres sealed the win for La Roja, who lifted the iconic trophy. Argentina were already down to ten men after Enzo Fernandez was sent off for a reckless moment late in normal time. Tensions then exploded after the final whistle, with violence breaking out across the MetLife Stadium pitch.

‌



Others were dragged into the chaos as the situation descended into mayhem, though calm was eventually restored before the medal ceremony and Spain hoisted the trophy. FIFA have subsequently launched an investigation into the distasteful scenes.

‌



Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage READ MORE :

Leandro Paredes speaks out on Argentina World Cup conspiracy theories after sparking Spain brawl READ MORE :

Infantino had previously met Spain boss Luis de la Fuente at the Olympic Games, where the Spain boss later disclosed the details of their discussion. Those views were repeated after the World Cup, with Infantino emphasising that his admiration for Spain's players remains valid today.

"I always say that private conversations should be private, but in this case, I think it's worth mentioning," he told Marca. "Why? Because it highlights the caliber of our players. Look, Infantino and I met at the Olympic Games, where we won the silver medal. The players' behaviour was spectacular.

"They put on their medals, they didn't take them off, they enjoyed the closing ceremony. When the ceremony was over, Infantino came up to me and said, 'Mister, your players are an example.'".

‌



"And many of those players were in this final. He reminded me of it the other day, saying, 'What I told you at the Olympic Games still applies today. What an example of everything: team spirit, camaraderie, generosity, sacrifice, and footballing greatness.' And that's something to be proud of. It's the greatest source of pride, beyond anything purely related to football."

This stands in sharp contrast to the conduct of certain Argentina players following the final whistle in the World Cup final - not only igniting confrontations on the pitch, but with multiple squad members also turning their backs as Spain received the trophy.

It's a moment that couldn't be further removed from the professionalism and dignity Infantino recognised in his exchange with De La Fuente, commending Spain's players for their collective spirit, humility and behaviour throughout both competitions.

‌

Sports.title: Ex-Man Utd star tipped for bright future by Alex Ferguson speaks out on being clubless
Sports.content:
Ex-Man Utd star tipped for bright future by Alex Ferguson speaks out on being clubless

Ben Amos, the former Manchester United goalkeeper, has been part of the PFA pre-season programme for the last month after his departure from Port Vale

View 4 Images Former Manchester United goalkeeper Ben Amos was at Port Vale last season but finds himself without a club (Image: Getty Images)

Ex-Manchester United goalkeeper Ben Amos is still searching for a new club after becoming a free agent. The 36-year-old, who made seven first-team appearances in 14 years at United before his departure in 2015, left Port Vale after his contract expired last month.

He had spent the previous two seasons at The Valiants, helping them win promotion to League One before the club were relegated straight back to League One. In that time, Amos kept 15 clean sheets in 41 matches and played a part in their run to the FA Cup quarter-final last term.

Although some Vale fans wanted to keep Amos, he left at the end of his contract in June and has since become a free agent. While waiting for his next club, Amos has been part of the PFA pre-season squad.

First launched as a pilot programme in 2023 for unsigned players to maintain fitness, the PFA put together a 10-week pre-season camp for the following year and they have been running it ever since. The camp - based in Leicestershire - is designed to help out-of-contract players regain sharpness and inevitably find their next club.

Former Sheffield Wednesday cult hero Fernando Forestieri, ex-Preston forward Will Keane and Ipswich Town's 2023/24 promotion-winning campaign Samy Morsy are among those with the PFA this summer.

Inside England's most dramatic title race and last day promotion shootout READ MORE :

FIVE Baller League footballers now punished by clubs as new sack statement drops READ MORE :

Amos is another involved and he has been at the PFA's Champneys Springs base for the last four weeks, featuring in pre-season matches against a free agents side from France and non-league Hednesford Town.

"It's been unbelievable," Amos said, when asked about his time at PFA pre-season. "I think this is like my fourth week I think I've been here. Obviously really hard work, they've pushed us every day.

"But just invaluable, like the sessions that they've put on, the games, obviously the facilities for recovery, everything has been laid on for us, so even to the food, the food has been unbelievable.

"When you're away from here, if you're not on the PFA camp, you just can't recreate it. You can do all the fitness work you want, all the ball work, but you just can't compare to this kind of training and service."

View 4 Images Ben Amos spent the last two years at Port Vale but left the club at the end of lasts eason (Image: Getty Images)

Amos turned 36 in April and is approaching the twilight of his career, but he still feels he can offer something to a club in the Football League ahead of the new season.

"I feel like I'm getting better all the time," Amos continued. "Yes, I'm without a club in 20-something of July, which I've never been in that position before, but I don't feel like I've ever been in a better position in terms of how I feel. It's just the dynamic at the moment, the market and what have you. Hopefully, I won't be waiting too much longer.

"I feel like I've got a lot more to give. I want to go until I'm 40 and maybe beyond. The market will dictate at the end of the day, it always does. The good thing is I know I'm in a great place, ready for whenever that happens."

Amos started his professional career at boyhood club United and came through the ranks at the Reds before making his first-team debut, aged 18, during a League Cup tie against Middlesbrough in September 2008.

At the time, Amos was United's fourth-choice keeper behind Edwin van der Sar, Ben Foster and Tomasz Kuszczak, but Sir Alex Ferguson spotted the talent and gave him a chance to impress.

View 4 Images Ben Amos (left) during his time at Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

Although Amos didn't do much wrong on his debut, he had to wait more than two years for his next competitive match for the Reds, when he featured in the League Cup against Wolves in October 2010.

Amos went on to play seven times in total for United - one of which came in the Premier League - before leaving at the end of his contract in 2015. He moved to Championship side Bolton Wanderers on a permanent deal, having spent the second half of the previous season on loan at the Trotters.

Reflecting on his time at United, Amos felt he should have left the Reds sooner than he did.

Amos said: "I've been a United fan since I started watching football. Obviously it was always my dream, Peter Schmeichel was my idol and all that stuff when we went to go and watch them when I was a kid. I just kept punishing, working my hardest in the academy. Then I think there was an injury or something and I obviously got an opportunity to play in the League Cup. I think I was 18, so that was amazing."

"I think I played seven times, but that was all under Sir Alex. If I was performing well, I'd normally get an opportunity in the Cups, League Cup," Amos added. "He played me in the Champions League and the Premier League. Just one of those things, really.

View 4 Images Former Manchester United goalkeeper Ben Amos during his time with the club (Image: Getty Images)

"I think [David] De Gea was bought for £20million, which was a big chunk at the time. And obviously a world-class keeper, so it's pretty hard to get in front of the likes of those guys. I definitely stayed a couple of years too long, with hindsight. I was still hoping for those opportunities, but when Sir Alex left, I didn't get any more.

"You don't have regrets if you can help it, but if I could have my time again, I think you'd do that. I'd probably have left when Sir Alex left, and go out and get some more experience."

Ferguson viewed Amos as "very talented goalkeeper" with a "good future" after promoting him to the senior set-up at Old Trafford. And while his time at United didn't go as he would have wanted, he has forged out a solid career in the EFL, making more than 350 appearances for some big clubs.

Charlton Athletic, Hull City, Wigan Athletic, Millwall, Cardiff City and Bolton count as some of Amos' former employers and he will be hoping to find his next club in the coming weeks.

Sports.title: Man Utd drop clearest hint yet over Marcus Rashford's future as club bosses reach out
Sports.content:
Man Utd drop clearest hint yet over Marcus Rashford's future as club bosses reach out

EXCLUSIVE: Marcus Rashford's future has been left up in the air by Barcelona's failure to sign the forward permanently but he could yet be offered a lifeline at Manchester United

View 2 Images Marcus Rashford could be offered the chance to resurrect his Manchester United career (Image: Steph Chambers/FIFA)

Manchester United bosses have invited Marcus Rashford to be part of a documentary about the club in a move which suggests they are prepared to perform a stunning U-turn and keep the outcast at Old Trafford.

‌



Rashford has not kicked a ball in anger for United since December 2024. The Red Devils were expected to sell him to the highest bidder, with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe keen to get him off the wage bill.

‌



But it has emerged that United executives have asked Rashford if he wants to be included in the fly-on-the-wall film the club has agreed with Amazon, in a multi-million pound deal.

‌



It's understood Rashford has not made a decision, as he continues to mull over his next move. But the invitation suggests United might be willing to head into the new season with Rashford in their plans.

Three Man Utd coaches have all given their opinion on JJ Gabriel READ MORE :

Rashford fell out with former boss Ruben Amorim after revealing he wanted to leave his hometown club, before being sent on-loan to Aston Villa and then Barcelona last season.

Barcelona rejected the option to make the move permanent in a £24m deal. It means Rashford will return to United following his summer break, in the wake of being involved in the World Cup with England.

‌



His future remains in limbo, with several clubs weighing up a move for the 28-year-old forward.

View 2 Images Rashford has been focusing on the World Cup with England (Image: Chris Arjoon/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Cameras have started rolling for 'All or Nothing - Manchester United' now some of Michael Carrick's squad have returned to pre season training. And will continue to do so until the end of next season.

‌



Amazon wanted to do the same project last season, but the then manager Amorim refused to co-operate.

United insist the documentary is "aligned with the club's desire to be as open and transparent as possible" with the club's billions of supporters around the world.

The film promises to give viewers unprecedented access to the inner sanctum of the Old Trafford dressing room and Carrington training complex.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca insists Man City won't repeat what Man Utd did after Sir Alex Ferguson
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca insists Man City won't repeat what Man Utd did after Sir Alex Ferguson

Enzo Maresca spoke to reporters for the first time since he was given the daunting task of replacing Pep Guardiola as manager of Manchester City

View 2 Images Enzo Maresca spoke to reporters for the first time as Man City boss

Enzo Maresca insists Manchester City won't do what United did - and go to the dogs in the wake of losing a legendary manager.

‌



Maresca is facing the almighty challenge of replacing Pep Guardiola at the Etihad. Guardiola won a staggering 20 trophies in a decade of dominance in English football.

‌



And the scenario Maresca is now facing is similar to what David Moyes did when he followed in the footsteps of Sir Alex Ferguson at United in 2013. Moyes found himself sacked inside 10 months.

‌



While United have not come close to winning either the Premier League or Champions League title since Fergie retired.

Three Man Utd coaches have all given their opinion on JJ Gabriel READ MORE :

But Maresca is relishing the challenge of filling Guardiola's boots - and reckons City have a structure in place to keep on winning with him in charge.

Maresca said: "I consider Pep to be the best coach in the world in the last 20-25 years, so it's a challenge. It's nice, its a privilege and also the history of the manager with many years in the same club always struggled a little, like after Sir Alex.

‌



"It's a big challenge for everyone. But I think the organisation is the main thing. This club has had three managers in 17 years.

View 2 Images David Moyes was sacked by Man United after just ten months (Image: 2014 Getty Images)

"This is not normal, it doesn't happen often so this is one of the things why I'm confident we can do a great job. And continue to do the job that has been done in the last 14 or 15 years."

‌



Maresca, meanwhile, admits he is unconcerned by all the speculation surrounding World Cup winner Rodri. The Spanish Ballon d'Or winner, who will have minor back surgery next week, has been linked with a move to Real Madrid.

But Maresca added: "Around big players there is always speculation. I'm not worried about that, it's normal. Every manager wants to have Rodri, but now surgery. He needs to rest and recover, and then he will be back here with us."
