Coffee Fest Sonidero Brings Specialty Producers to the Pyramid’s Shadow

Coffee Fest Sonidero will run from 10:00 to 21:00 on Sunday 26 July at the Museo Regional de Cholula, on Avenida 14 Poniente next to the Great Pyramid. Entry is free, with specialised workshops priced around 200 Mexican pesos (roughly US$10).

Around 15 specialty coffee bars and local producers from Puebla municipalities such as Naupan and Huitzilan will pour and sell their beans. The event targets families who may not yet know that Puebla grows high-quality specialty coffee.

A latte art competition with 16 baristas anchors the programme, alongside tastings, masterclasses on home brewing, and demonstrations of cold coffee cocktails. Sonidero music and dance will run throughout the day, and visitors can access the museum’s permanent and temporary exhibitions.

Festival “Puebla en Nogada” Aims for an Eight-Ton Record

The Festival “Puebla en Nogada” begins on 23 July at Parque Soria in San Pedro Cholula and peaks on Sunday 26 July. Ten traditional cooks, culinary schools, historians and artistic groups will anchor the gastronomic programme.

Organisers expect around 15,000 visitors across the four days, with an estimated economic impact of 5.5 million Mexican pesos (about US$275,000). Visitors can buy chile en nogada in various presentations and price ranges, from popular to gourmet.

On 26 July the cooks will attempt to prepare the largest chile en nogada in the world, with an estimated weight of around eight tons. As part of the celebration, 6,000 chiles en nogada will be given away free, following a specific distribution dynamic.

A Broader Push to Turn Gastronomy into Year-Round Tourism

Chile en nogada season runs from July to September across Puebla state, with multiple festivals in municipalities such as San Nicolás de los Ranchos, San Andrés Calpan and the city of Puebla itself. The Cholula events connect local producers of coffee, walnuts and fruits directly with consumers and international visitors.

Both festivals wrap gastronomy inside a full cultural experience that includes music, dance, artisan exhibitions and educational conferences. This model mirrors successful strategies in Oaxaca and Mérida, where food festivals have become reliable anchors for small-business revenue and real-estate demand.

For Cholula, which already draws visitors for its pyramid and colonial architecture, adding signature food-and-music events extends the tourist stay and spending per head. Local authorities are betting that a packed July calendar will strengthen the town’s brand as a weekend destination for Mexico City and Puebla capital residents.

What the Cholula Cultural Festivals Mean for Investors and Expats

Cholula’s property market has already seen rising interest from Mexican and foreign buyers seeking lower prices than Mexico City or San Miguel de Allende. Events like Coffee Fest Sonidero and Puebla en Nogada add cultural infrastructure that supports rental yields and hospitality ventures.

Specialty coffee is a high-margin sector in Mexico, with export potential and a growing domestic consumer base. The presence of 15 producers at a free-entry festival signals that Puebla’s coffee supply chain is maturing beyond raw-commodity sales into branded, direct-to-consumer retail.

For expats already living in the Puebla-Tlaxcala corridor, the festivals offer networking opportunities with local producers, chefs and artisans. The international participation from 35 countries at Puebla en Nogada also suggests that organisers are deliberately courting a global audience, which tends to raise service standards and English-language accessibility over time.

How to Navigate Both Cholula Cultural Festivals on 26 July

The two venues are roughly 15 minutes apart by car. Coffee Fest Sonidero at the Museo Regional runs from 10:00 to 21:00, while the record attempt at Parque Soria is a daytime affair on Sunday.

A practical itinerary would start with morning coffee tastings and the latte art competition at the museum, then move to Parque Soria for the giant chile en nogada attempt and free servings. Both sites sit near the Great Pyramid and Cholula’s central zócalo, making it easy to fill gaps with cultural sightseeing.

Parking will be tight. Visitors coming from Puebla city or Mexico City should plan to arrive early or use ride-hailing apps, as street closures around Parque Soria are likely during the record attempt.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Coffee Fest Sonidero in Cholula?

Coffee Fest Sonidero takes place on Sunday 26 July from 10:00 to 21:00 at the Museo Regional de Cholula, Avenida 14 Poniente, San Pedro Cholula. Entry is free, and specialised workshops cost around 200 Mexican pesos (US$10).

What is the giant chile en nogada record attempt in Cholula?

On Sunday 26 July at Parque Soria in San Pedro Cholula, cooks will attempt to prepare the world’s largest chile en nogada, weighing an estimated eight tons. As part of the celebration, 6,000 free chiles en nogada will be distributed to attendees.

Are the Cholula festivals suitable for families and international visitors?

Yes, both events are designed as family-friendly experiences. Coffee Fest Sonidero includes music, dance and museum access, while the Puebla en Nogada Festival features traditional cooks, artisan exhibitions and educational conferences on the history of chile en nogada.

World.title: San Miguel Comparte Aims to Make City Mexico’s First Conscious Gastronomic Capital
World.content:
Culinary Tourism & Social Impact

Key Facts —Initiative. San Miguel Comparte is led by the local organisation BASMA. —Core Mission. It rescues surplus food to reduce waste and support vulnerable families. —Distintivo BASMA. A recognition for restaurants and hotels that integrate food donation and sustainability. —Broader Goal. To position San Miguel de Allende as Mexico’s first conscious gastronomic capital. —Participation. The project invites restaurants, hotels, businesses, residents, and visitors to take part.

A new civic initiative called San Miguel Comparte is working to make San Miguel de Allende Mexico’s first conscious gastronomic capital by linking the city’s celebrated food scene to direct social and environmental action.

The Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel towers over San Miguel de Allende, a gastronomy and expat hub. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What San Miguel Comparte Actually Does

San Miguel Comparte is a project led by BASMA, a local organisation focused on food rescue and community support. It collects surplus food that is still fit for consumption and distributes it to hundreds of families in need.

The operation tackles two problems at once: hunger and food waste. Restaurants, hotels, and businesses donate excess food instead of discarding it, creating a direct link between the city’s high-end culinary economy and its most vulnerable residents.

Redefining What a Gastronomic Capital Means

San Miguel de Allende already enjoys international fame for its restaurants, cooking schools, and food festivals. The conscious gastronomic capital concept adds a new layer: culinary prestige should be measured by how much a destination contributes to local well-being.

The initiative argues that a truly great food city does not only serve world-class meals. It also ensures that food reaches those who need it most and that the environmental cost of dining is taken seriously.

The Distintivo BASMA and How Businesses Join

A central tool is the Distintivo BASMA, a recognition awarded to establishments that integrate food donation and sustainable practices into their daily operations. Restaurants, hotels, and other businesses can earn the distinction by committing to regular surplus food rescue.

The visible badge signals to diners and guests that an establishment is part of the solution. For business owners, it offers a way to differentiate themselves in a competitive market increasingly shaped by conscious consumer choices.

Why This Matters for Investors and Expats

San Miguel de Allende has long been a magnet for foreign residents and investors drawn by its colonial architecture, cultural life, and safety. The conscious gastronomic capital push adds a new dimension to the city’s value proposition.

Properties and businesses associated with verified sustainability and social impact programmes tend to hold value better over time. For expats considering a move, a city that formalises food rescue and community support signals a cohesive, well-managed civil society.

The Latin America Read-Through

Mexico’s tourism sector is under pressure to demonstrate that growth does not come at the expense of local communities. San Miguel Comparte offers a replicable model for other destinations across the region.

If the initiative succeeds, it could influence how cities from Oaxaca to Mendoza brand themselves. The idea that a place earns its culinary reputation partly through social responsibility is a quiet but significant shift in Latin American tourism thinking.

What to Watch Next

The project’s trajectory depends on how many restaurants and hotels 

Local government endorsement would accelerate the initiative, but the model is designed to work through civic and business channels regardless. Watch for data on tonnes of food rescued and families served as the key performance indicators.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is San Miguel Comparte?

San Miguel Comparte is a BASMA-led initiative in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, that rescues surplus food from restaurants, hotels, and businesses to distribute to vulnerable families. Its broader mission is to position the city as Mexico’s first conscious gastronomic capital by linking culinary prestige to social and environmental responsibility.

How does the Distintivo BASMA work?

The Distintivo BASMA is a recognition awarded to establishments that commit to regular food donation and sustainable practices. It serves as a visible signal to customers that a business actively contributes to reducing food waste and supporting the local community.

Why does the conscious gastronomic capital concept matter for San Miguel de Allende?

The concept redefines culinary excellence to include social impact, not just restaurant quality. For a city with a large expat population and a tourism-driven economy, it strengthens the brand, supports property values, and demonstrates that growth can benefit all residents.

World.title: Ilha Do Mel Hosts 12th Jazz a Gosto Festival This August
World.content:
Cultural Tourism

Key Facts —Dates. The festival runs every weekend in August 2026, starting 31 July, across five weekends. —Location. All events take place in Nova Brasília village on Ilha do Mel, Paraná. —Scale. The 12th edition features approximately 40 performances across main and off-circuit stages. —Cost. All musical performances are free; visitors cover only transport, lodging, and a small environmental fee. —Curatorship. The line-up is curated by bassist Glauco Sölter, prioritising musicians from Curitiba and Paraná.

The 12th Jazz a Gosto Festival will bring roughly 40 free performances to Ilha do Mel this August, cementing the car-free island as one of Southern Brazil’s most distinctive music destinations.

(Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

A Festival Rooted in Island Life

The Jazz a Gosto Festival began informally in the 1990s when bassist and current curator Glauco Sölter started bringing jazz performances to Ilha do Mel. What began as small gatherings has grown into a structured month-long programme that now anchors the island’s winter cultural calendar.

The 12th edition runs across all five weekends of August, starting on Thursday 31 July and continuing every Friday through Sunday. The main stage sits in Praça Felipe Valentim, the central square of Nova Brasília, while a parallel off-circuit places intimate shows inside the village’s pousadas, cafés, and bars.

The Curitiba Connection Driving the Jazz a Gosto Festival

The festival’s curatorial identity is firmly tied to Paraná’s capital. Sölter and his team deliberately showcase musicians from Curitiba’s robust instrumental, soul, and jazz scenes, alongside artists touring Brazil during the Southern Hemisphere winter.

This focus transforms the island into a temporary extension of Curitiba’s cultural life. For the capital’s residents, the festival offers a compelling reason to make the roughly two-hour drive to the coast, board a ferry, and spend a weekend immersed in music without the distractions of urban life.

A Broader Jazz Ecosystem on One Island

Jazz a Gosto does not operate in isolation. Ilha do Mel hosts two other jazz festivals during August — Ilha do Mel Jazz and Encantadas Jazz — which together generate more than 90 musical attractions across the island’s two main villages, Nova Brasília and Encantadas.

This clustering effect turns the entire island into a jazz hub for the month. Visitors can move between venues on foot along sandy trails, encountering everything from solo bass performances in a small café to full ensemble shows under the stars in the main square.

What the Festival Means for Local Business

August is traditionally a quieter month for Ilha do Mel’s tourism economy, which peaks during the summer months of December through February. The Jazz a Gosto Festival and its sister events inject consistent weekend demand into the island’s pousadas, restaurants, and boat services during the low season.

For small business owners in Nova Brasília, the off-circuit programme is particularly valuable. Hosting a performance draws patrons into a pousada’s restaurant or a bar that might otherwise sit half-empty on a winter evening, creating a direct link between cultural programming and commercial survival.

Practical Planning for Visitors

Reaching Ilha do Mel requires a boat crossing from Pontal do Sul or Paranaguá, as no cars are permitted on the island. The ferry ride takes roughly 30 minutes from Pontal do Sul, and visitors should budget for the crossing, accommodation, meals, and a small environmental preservation fee charged upon arrival.

Detailed schedules are typically released close to the festival’s start date on the official Instagram accounts @jazzagostoilhadomel and @ilhadomeljazz. Booking accommodation early is advisable, as the island’s limited pousada capacity fills quickly on festival weekends.

The Read-Through for Investors and Expats

The Jazz a Gosto Festival illustrates a broader trend in Brazil’s cultural tourism sector: well-curated, niche events in distinctive locations are proving capable of extending tourist seasons and generating reliable off-peak revenue. For investors watching Brazil’s hospitality and experience-economy spaces, the Ilha do Mel model offers a replicable template.

For expats based in Curitiba, the festival represents a high-quality, low-cost weekend escape with strong logistical simplicity. The combination of free music, car-free island atmosphere, and proximity to the capital makes it one of Paraná’s most accessible cultural offerings.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the 12th Jazz a Gosto Festival take place?

The festival runs every weekend in August 2026, starting on Thursday 31 July and continuing each Friday through Sunday. The full programme spans five weekends, with performances during both daytime and evening hours.

How do I get to Ilha do Mel for the festival?

Access is exclusively by boat from Pontal do Sul or Paranaguá, with the crossing from Pontal do Sul taking approximately 30 minutes. No cars are allowed on the island, and visitors should plan to walk between venues along the island’s sandy paths.

Are tickets required for Jazz a Gosto performances?

All musical performances at the Jazz a Gosto Festival are free of charge. Visitors are responsible only for their own transport, accommodation, meals, and the environmental preservation fee collected upon arrival on the island.

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Dates. The 20th edition runs from 15 to 26 July 2026 in Panama City. —Scale. More than 500 musicians from Panama and abroad will participate. —Venues. Concerts span the Teatro Balboa, Ciudad de las Artes, and Teatro Ateneo. —Highlight. Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 “Resurrection” closes the festival on 25–26 July. —Organiser. The non-profit Fundación Sinfonía Concertante de Panamá (FUNSINCOPA) leads the event.

The Alfredo de Saint Malo Festival returns to Panama City for its 20th anniversary edition this July, bringing over 500 musicians and dozens of international guest artists to venues across the capital for eleven days of concerts and masterclasses.

A Capital-Wide Celebration for a 20th Anniversary

The 2026 Alfredo de Saint Malo International Academic Music Festival runs from 15 to 26 July under the motto “20 años tejiendo cultura” — twenty years weaving culture. Organised by the Fundación Sinfonía Concertante de Panamá (FUNSINCOPA) with support from the Ministry of Culture, the festival will activate major venues across Panama City.

The Ciudad de las Artes serves as the academic campus for lessons and rehearsals. The historic Teatro Balboa hosts the flagship symphonic and closing gala concerts, while the Teatro Ateneo in the Ciudad del Saber and the Biblioteca Nacional Ernesto J.

Castillero R. provide settings for chamber and pedagogical performances.

Additional events are scheduled at the Museo del Canal Interoceánico, the Parlamento Latinoamericano y Caribeño (PARLATINO), the Hotel Santa María, and the Iglesia San Francisco de Asís. The city-wide footprint reinforces Panama City’s growing profile as a hub for academic classical music in the region.

International Guest Artists and Pedagogues

The festival’s 20th edition draws a large roster of international guest artists, consistent with recent years when roughly 40 foreign musicians travelled to Panama for the event. Confirmed names for 2026 include American orchestral conductor Christopher Russell, Uruguayan pianist Mariana Airaudo, and American saxophonist Preston Duncan.

Chinese conductor Hu Cheng Yun, Italian mezzo-soprano Benedetta Orsi, and conductor-pedagogue Daniel Rieppel also join the programme. The Argentine Cuarteto Gianneo and Venezuelan violinist Eddy Marcano with his Cuarteto Acústico add chamber-music depth to the lineup.

Panamanian and international performers including Luis Casal, Graciela Núñez, Stephanie Matthews, Reenat Pinchas, Hsin-Ni Liu, Juan Pablo Mora, Lacey Hays, and Jonathan Helton round out a faculty designed to deliver intensive masterclasses alongside public concerts.

Mahler’s “Resurrection” as the Artistic Summit

The 2026 Alfredo de Saint Malo Festival’s most ambitious project is a performance of Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 2, “Resurrection.” Organisers describe it as one of the greatest artistic challenges in the festival’s two-decade history.

The work will be performed at the closing concerts on 25 and 26 July at the Teatro Balboa. It features a large symphony orchestra, a full chorus, and international soloists, all under the baton of Christopher Russell.

The Mahler project exemplifies the festival’s dual mission: delivering high-level symphonic repertoire while offering intensive educational training for young musicians and choristers from Panama and beyond.

Education, Exchange, and the Read-Through for Panama

Beyond the concerts, the festival runs a 12-day academic programme for nearly 100 young musicians aged roughly 14 to 30. Masterclasses and seminars cover orchestral, chamber, and solo performance, with many activities open to the public and some offered free of charge.

For Panama, the festival is both a cultural asset and a soft-power tool. It draws international artists and audiences to the capital, supports the local hospitality sector, and positions Panama City alongside better-known Latin American cultural destinations.

For expats and investors, the festival signals a maturing quality-of-life infrastructure. A reliable calendar of international arts events adds to Panama’s appeal as a place to live, work, and raise a family, complementing its established strengths in logistics and financial services.

What to Watch Next

FUNSINCOPA is expected to release a detailed day-by-day schedule closer to the festival dates. Ticket information for the Teatro Balboa closing concerts and other venues will be published through the foundation’s official channels and the Ministry of Culture.

The 20th edition arrives at a moment when Panama is working to broaden its tourism offering beyond the canal and beach resorts. A successful anniversary festival could strengthen the case for increased public and private cultural funding in the years ahead.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Alfredo de Saint Malo Festival?

It is an annual international academic music festival held in Panama City, organised by the Fundación Sinfonía Concertante de Panamá (FUNSINCOPA). The event combines public concerts with masterclasses and intensive training for young musicians, and it is named after the Panamanian musician Alfredo de Saint Malo.

When and where does the 2026 edition take place?

The 20th edition runs from 15 to 26 July 2026 across multiple venues in Panama City, including the Teatro Balboa, Ciudad de las Artes, Teatro Ateneo, and the Biblioteca Nacional. The closing concerts featuring Mahler’s “Resurrection” Symphony are scheduled for 25 and 26 July at the Teatro Balboa.

How many musicians participate in the festival?

The 2026 edition brings together more than 500 musicians, including children, youth, and professional artists from Panama and abroad. The festival typically hosts several dozen international guest artists and pedagogues alongside a large contingent of Panamanian students and performers.

The Panama Book Fair 2026 returns to Atlapa from 25 to 30 August, bringing publishers, investors, and expat families a packed cultural programme anchored by the Panama Canal’s expansion anniversary.

A Canal-Themed Fair Anchors the Panama Book Fair 2026

The Cámara Panameña del Libro (CAPALI) has confirmed the 22nd Feria Internacional del Libro de Panamá for 25 to 30 August 2026. The Centro de Convenciones Atlapa on Vía Israel will again host the event.

The Panama Canal serves as guest of honour, exactly ten years after its multibillion-dollar expansion opened. Organisers have adopted the motto “La ruta de las mil historias,” framing the fair as a journey through literature, commerce, and national identity.

For the international business community in Panama, the canal theme carries weight. The waterway drives roughly a quarter of state revenue, and its anniversary will draw diplomatic and trade delegations alongside the literary crowd.

What the Activity Agenda Will Include

CAPALI has not yet published the hour-by-hour 2026 schedule. The detailed daily grid typically appears on the fair’s official website and social media channels a few weeks before opening day.

Based on the 2024 and 2025 editions, visitors can expect book launches and signings by Panamanian and international authors, conferences on literature and current affairs, and specialised seminars including the recurring International Copyright Law Seminar. Writing workshops, poetry readings, and a dedicated children’s programme with storytelling and cosplay contests will run across all six days.

The canal anniversary adds unique programming. Early announcements point to forums and tributes to architects and historians, a new book on the expansion, and a musical work titled “El sueño de un istmo” with free student access.

Live concerts, theatre, and folklore performances will fill the Teatro La Huaca and other Atlapa spaces each evening.

Tickets, Hours, and the Business Case for Attending

Admission pricing follows the established model. General adult entry is expected at $3, seniors at $2, and students with identification at $1.

A weekly cultural passport covering all six days should cost $18.

Pre-sale tickets will be available through Panatickets until 15 August 2026. Doors are likely to open from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. daily, matching the 2025 schedule.

For publishers, booksellers, and ed-tech investors, FIL Panamá is the region’s most important Spanish-language rights marketplace after Guadalajara and Buenos Aires. The fair draws distributors from across Central America, the Caribbean, and Colombia, making it a cost-effective entry point for companies eyeing the Latin American book trade.

Why the Panama Book Fair 2026 Matters for Expats and Families

Panama City’s expat population has grown steadily, drawn by the dollarised economy and the multinational corporate hub. The book fair offers a rare window into Panamanian literary culture that is both accessible and family-friendly.

The children’s pavilion runs dedicated programming throughout the fair, including bilingual activities that suit English-speaking families. School groups attend on weekday mornings, while weekends see heavier foot traffic from local and international families.

Atlapa’s location on Vía Israel puts it within a short drive of the banking district, Punta Paitilla, and the Corredor Sur. Parking is ample, and ride-share services operate reliably to and from the convention centre.

How to Get the Official Programme When It Drops

The most reliable source is the CAPALI website, where the full cultural programme and daily room-by-room grids will appear closer to August 2026. The chamber’s social media accounts on Instagram and X post real-time updates, schedule changes, and author announcements.

Local outlets including TVN, Ellas, and Destino Panamá typically publish daily breakdowns once the fair opens. The Panatickets event page will also carry basic schedule information and direct ticket links.

For business visitors seeking B2B meetings with publishers, contacting CAPALI directly through their official channels well before August is advisable. The fair’s professional networking opportunities often fill up before the public programme is released.

When exactly is the Panama Book Fair 2026?

The 22nd Feria Internacional del Libro de Panamá runs from Monday 25 August to Saturday 30 August 2026. The venue is the Centro de Convenciones Atlapa on Vía Israel in Panama City.

Doors are expected to open from 10:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. daily, consistent with recent editions.

How much do tickets cost and where can I buy them?

General adult admission is expected at $3, seniors at $2, and students with valid identification at $1. A weekly cultural passport covering all six days should cost $18.

Pre-sale tickets will be available through Panatickets until 15 August 2026, and tickets can also be purchased at the Atlapa box office during the fair.

The detailed daily programme has not yet been published. CAPALI will release the hour-by-hour agenda on its official website and social media channels a few weeks before the fair opens in August 2026.

World.title: Maquenque Lodge: Costa Rica’s Treehouse Haven for 590 Bird Species
World.content:
LIFE: San José, Costa Rica

Key Facts —Location. The lodge sits inside the Maquenque National Wildlife Refuge near Boca Tapada, about three hours north of San José. —Bird Species. Over 590 species have been recorded in the refuge, including the endangered Great Green Macaw. —Treehouse Rooms. Elevated canopy rooms sit roughly 12 metres above ground with private balconies and hammocks. —Access. Guests cross the San Carlos River by boat to reach the property, as it has no direct road connection. —Inclusions. Stays typically include breakfast, guided morning bird walks, and canoe use on the lagoon.

Maquenque Lodge Costa Rica delivers a genuine rainforest immersion where a weekend can yield sightings of over 200 bird species from a treehouse balcony, just three hours from San José.

(Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Getting to Maquenque Lodge from San José

The drive from Juan Santamaría International Airport or downtown San José takes roughly three hours north through Alajuela province. The final approach ends at the San Carlos River, where a boat ferries guests across to the lodge.

A rental car or private transfer is the most practical option for the journey. The lodge is not accessible by direct road, which adds to its secluded character and keeps the surrounding forest intact.

The Birdwatching Reality: More Than 590 Species

Maquenque Lodge sits inside the Maquenque National Wildlife Refuge, a protected corridor where over 590 bird species have been documented. The figure reflects updated counts from the lodge and recent birding reports, making it one of Costa Rica’s richest birding destinations.

The endangered Great Green Macaw is the signature species and a core conservation focus. Guests also regularly spot Scarlet Macaws, Keel-billed and Yellow-throated Toucans, King Vultures, and dozens of tanagers, honeycreepers, and hummingbirds.

A dedicated observation hide about ten minutes from the lodge offers close views of King Vultures. Typical sightings range from four to eight birds at distances of eight to fifteen metres, ideal for photography.

Life in a Treehouse at Maquenque Lodge

The treehouse rooms rise roughly 12 metres into the canopy, built directly among the branches. Each unit measures about 45 square metres and includes a private bathroom with solar-heated hot water, a ceiling fan, screened windows, and a balcony with a hammock.

Some newer treehouses add outdoor showers and jacuzzis, though air conditioning is generally absent in favour of natural ventilation. The elevated position means constant jungle sound and frequent bird activity at eye level, especially at dawn and dusk.

These rooms are not suited for guests with mobility limitations or small children due to the stairs and height. For those preferring ground-level comfort, bungalows near the lagoon offer air conditioning and easier access while still delivering excellent birding from the terrace.

A Practical Weekend Itinerary

Arrive on Friday afternoon, cross the river by boat, and check in by 3:00 p.m. Settle into the treehouse and explore nearby trails and the lagoon before sunset, then watch fruit-feeder birds around the restaurant during dinner.

Saturday starts with the 6:00 a.m. guided birdwatching tour through gardens, lagoons, and forest trails when bird activity peaks. Late morning can be spent birding from the treehouse balcony or using the lodge’s canoes on the lagoon.

An afternoon boat trip on the San Carlos River adds waterbirds, kingfishers, and raptors to the list. An optional night walk reveals frogs, snakes, and nocturnal birds before a final Sunday morning birding session and the drive back to San José.

What the Lodge Means for Sustainable Tourism Investment

Maquenque Lodge operates on roughly 68 to 150 acres of protected land with a clear eco-credential model: solar hot water, reforestation programmes, and direct investment in Great Green Macaw conservation. The lodge’s tree-planting initiatives and local school visits form part of a broader sustainable tourism package that appeals to international visitors.

Costa Rica’s eco-lodge sector continues to draw attention from impact investors and hospitality groups looking at Latin America’s green premium. Properties like Maquenque demonstrate that remote, low-density lodges with strong conservation narratives can command steady occupancy from high-value niche markets, particularly birdwatchers from North America and Europe.

The three-hour proximity to San José also makes it viable for weekend domestic tourism, a segment that proved resilient during past downturns in long-haul travel. For expats based in the Central Valley, it represents a repeatable escape rather than a once-a-year destination.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many bird species can you realistically see in a weekend at Maquenque Lodge?

A focused weekend with guided walks and boat trips can easily yield over 100 species, and dedicated birders often record more than 200 in peak conditions. The lodge’s refuge holds over 590 documented species, so the potential is exceptionally high for a short stay.

Are the treehouse rooms suitable for families with children?

The treehouses are not recommended for small children or guests with mobility limitations due to the height and multiple stairs. Families may prefer the ground-level bungalows, which offer air conditioning and easier access while still providing excellent wildlife viewing.

What is the best time of year for birdwatching at Maquenque Lodge Costa Rica?

Birding is excellent year-round, but the dry season from December to April generally offers more predictable weather and easier trail access. The green season from May to November brings lush foliage and high bird activity, though afternoon rain showers are common in this lowland rainforest climate.

What the Fortal 2026 micareta means for Fortaleza’s events economy

Fortal is Brazil’s largest off-season carnival and the biggest indoor micareta in the country. The 33rd edition lands in a symbolic year: Fortaleza marks its tricentennial in 2026, and city authorities are using the event to showcase the capital’s capacity for large-scale tourism.

Hotel occupancy is forecast to surpass 90% during the festival window. Local trade groups estimate the event generates roughly 40,000 jobs across hospitality, transport, food and beverage, security, and retail — a significant injection for a metropolitan region of about four million people.

Opening night sets the pace for the Fortal 2026 micareta

Thursday, 23 July, opens the Corredor da Folia with the Vumbora bloco, led by Bell Marques alongside Rafa & Pipo Marques, and the O Vale bloco, fronted by Alinne Rosa. The Camarote Mucuripe opens with Natanzinho Lima, Henry Freitas, Felipe Amorim, and Banda Eva.

The Arena Fortal stage begins with Filhos de Jorge, a band with deep roots in Bahian music. The simultaneous start across three venues — bloco circuit, camarote, and arena — is designed to disperse crowds and maximise early-weekend spending.

The full Fortal 2026 micareta line-up and new blocos

Friday brings Bell Marques back with the Siriguella bloco and Claudia Leitte with Largadinho. A new bloco, Beleza Rara, debuts with Banda Eva and Xanddy Harmonia — a pairing that targets the family audience and younger festival-goers.

Saturday features Ivete Sangalo with Se Lança and the debut of Alegria Original, commanded by Timbalada. Sunday closes with Sangalo again, Bell Marques on Siriguella, and the new Resenha bloco, which gathers Rogerinho, Tito, Núzio, Jotavê, and Thales Play — a move clearly aimed at the sertanejo and piseiro audience that has grown sharply in the Northeast.

The Camarote Mucuripe programme runs parallel: Xandy Avião, Wesley Safadão, and Rafa & Pipo on Friday; Matheus & Kauan, Zé Vaqueiro, Rey Vaqueiro, and Pedro Sampaio on Saturday; Durval Lelys, Syon Trio, Eric Land, and Litto Lins on Sunday. The Arena Fortal closes with Alexandre Peixe.

The satellite economy: Iate Clube, Portal IN, and the society circuit

Beyond the Cidade Fortal perimeter, the “Siriguella com Feijão” event at Iate Clube de Fortaleza on Saturday, 25 July, has become a fixture of the extended Fortal week. Durval Lelys and Timbalada lead the programme, drawing a premium crowd that overlaps with the city’s society and business networks.

Portal IN — founded by Pompeu Vasconcelos, a pioneer of digital society journalism in Ceará — and its Balada IN vertical provide intensive coverage of these parallel events. Their reporting functions as both a social record and a promotional engine, connecting Fortal’s brand to high-net-worth readers and potential sponsors.

What the Fortal 2026 micareta signals for investors and expats

Fortal’s consistent growth — now in its 33rd year — tracks the maturation of Northeast Brazil’s events infrastructure. Cidade Fortal is a purpose-built indoor venue, which reduces weather risk and allows for predictable operational margins that outdoor carnivals cannot guarantee.

For hospitality investors, the 90%-plus occupancy forecast and the 40,000-job estimate signal a market that can absorb large-scale events without collapsing supply chains. For expats and remote professionals based in Fortaleza, the festival week offers a concentrated window of networking, cultural immersion, and consumer activity that mirrors what Carnival delivers in Salvador or Rio — but in a more controlled, indoor setting.

The tricentennial overlay adds a layer of municipal and state investment in urban infrastructure — transport, security, sanitation — that should outlast the festival itself. Watch for post-event occupancy data and tax-receipt reports from the Ceará state government as concrete indicators of return on that public spend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Fortal 2026 take place?

Fortal 2026 runs from Thursday, 23 July, to Sunday, 26 July, at Cidade Fortal in the Manoel Dias Branco neighbourhood of Fortaleza, Ceará. The opening night begins simultaneously across the Corredor da Folia, Camarote Mucuripe, and Arena Fortal.

Who are the main artists performing at Fortal 2026?

Headliners include Ivete Sangalo, Bell Marques, Claudia Leitte, Wesley Safadão, Banda Eva, Alinne Rosa, Xandy Avião, and Pedro Sampaio. Three new blocos debut this year: Beleza Rara, Alegria Original, and Resenha, broadening the musical range from axé to sertanejo.

What is the economic impact of Fortal on Fortaleza?

Local trade groups project hotel occupancy above 90% during the festival and estimate roughly 40,000 direct and indirect jobs linked to the event. Sectors benefiting include hospitality, food and beverage, transport, retail, and security, making Fortal one of Ceará’s largest annual economic drivers.

Humberto Gessinger brings acoustic Engenheiros to the capital

Zé Vaqueiro and BaianaSystem lead the Na Praia festival

Outdoor options include sports events, workshops, and traditional festivals featuring forró, reggae, and folk culture in parks and open spaces. The “Vai de Graça” free-transport scheme on Sundays makes the entire programme accessible for cardholders using the metro and bus network.

What Brasília weekend events mean for visitors and expats

For expats and business travellers based in Brasília, the weekend offers a concentrated window into Brazil’s cultural breadth — from southern rock to northeastern vaqueiro music and Bahian sound-system innovation. The Pride Parade also signals the capital’s role as a stage for national social and political expression.

The mix of paid concerts and free public events reflects a city that, despite its reputation as a political machine, sustains a growing cultural infrastructure. Investors and long-term residents watching Brazil’s consumer and entertainment sectors can read the weekend’s density as a sign of maturing demand in the Centre-West region.

Where is the Brasília LGBT+ Pride Parade held?

The 27th edition departs from in front of the National Congress on the Esplanada dos Ministérios and proceeds along the Eixo Monumental. It starts at 2 p.m. on Sunday, 26 July 2026, and entry is free for all.

How can I get free transport to Brasília weekend events?

Humberto Gessinger plays two acoustic sessions on Friday at the Ulysses Guimarães Convention Centre. The first is at 7 p.m. and the second at 9:30 p.m., covering Engenheiros do Hawaii classics and solo work.

World.title: Costa Rica Lawmaker Revives Cable Car Idea for Chirripó Summit
World.content:
Costa Rica’s highest point is hard to reach, and for the past half-century that difficulty has been the policy. A proposal now circulating in the Legislative Assembly would change it. Álvaro Ramírez Bogantes, head of the National Liberation Party caucus and the deputy elected first on the party’s San José slate, said this week that he is evaluating a project to build a cable car to Cerro Chirripó, the 3,820-meter (12,533-foot) summit that crowns the Cordillera de Talamanca.

Ramírez said the idea is to widen access to the peak for more people, including those with different physical conditions, and that he has presented it to the Grupo de Acción Territorial de Pérez Zeledón, a civic organization headed by Antonio Mora. He described a group of business owners and community leaders with whom he has been discussing the concept, and said he has begun conversations with other legislative caucuses about it.

Beyond that, almost nothing about the proposal exists yet. There is no route, no engineering study, no cost estimate, no environmental impact assessment, no financing plan and no bill filed in the Assembly. Ramírez has not said whether the line would terminate at the summit itself, at the Base Crestones shelter, or somewhere below the park boundary — a distinction that would determine much of the project’s legal footing. What he has described is a conversation, and he has framed it as one.

The lawmaker said the concept borrows from a cooperation model developed for a proposed cable car to Turrialba Volcano, and that he wants to test whether the same approach could be replicated in Pérez Zeledón. That Turrialba initiative, promoted by former deputy Rosaura Méndez with support from then-legislators Alejandro Pacheco and Pilar Cisneros, is the furthest along of Costa Rica’s several cable car proposals.

Cisneros told reporters in February that the plan would stimulate tourism and improve park infrastructure. The initiative is budgeted at ₡2,053 million — roughly $4.5 million at current exchange rates — including ₡1,600 million from the Rural Development Institute for land purchase and ₡650 million from the Environment and Energy Ministry.

The Chirripó idea is not new either, and its earlier version collapsed on the same ground it would have to cross now. In February 2017 the Pérez Zeledón Municipal Council voted unanimously to declare a summit cable car a project of cantonal and public interest, and then-mayor Jeffrey Montoya asked President Luis Guillermo Solís to declare it of national interest. Montoya put the likely cost at around $20 million and said the municipality would seek a private partner.

Within weeks the plan drew organized opposition. Environmental attorney Álvaro Sagot argued that the National Parks Service Law expressly barred the kind of stations and infrastructure the municipality envisioned. Luis Diego Marín of Preserve Planet said the only route forward would be a bill amending that law, which he called very unlikely, and warned that the park supplies the water Pérez Zeledón residents drink. Osvaldo Durán of the Federación Conservacionista noted that no technical study had been produced before the council voted. The project went no further.

The legal question is genuinely contested rather than settled. The Parks Service Law restricts construction inside national parks, while Article 18 of the Forestry Law allows the state forestry administration to authorize recreation and ecotourism infrastructure within the State’s Natural Heritage under defined conditions.

Any Chirripó project would also have to reckon with the park’s international standing. Chirripó National Park sits within the Talamanca Range-La Amistad Reserves, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 and extended in 1990, and a major built structure inside a World Heritage property would attract scrutiny well beyond San José.

The practical arithmetic is equally unforgiving. Access to the summit today runs through a reservation system that caps overnight capacity at 60 people per night at the Base Crestones shelter, distributed across the San Gerardo, Herradura and San Jerónimo approaches, with bookings made through SINAC’s online platform.

Slots between December and April fill fastest. Critics of the 2017 plan argued that a cable car needs high throughput to pay for itself while Chirripó’s carrying capacity is deliberately low, and that the families around San Gerardo de Rivas who provide lodging, meals and porter services to hikers would lose the business that the overnight trek generates.

Neither SINAC nor the Environment and Energy Ministry, headed since May by Mónica Navarro Del Valle, has commented publicly on the Ramírez proposal. Both would be central to any serious evaluation, along with the National Environmental Technical Secretariat, which reviews environmental viability, and the park’s own management plan, which governs what activities are permitted where.

Two other cable car proposals have surfaced in recent years without producing anything built. The French group Poma pitched routes to the Cartago municipality in 2021, including Cristo Rey to Tierra Blanca and Tierra Blanca to Irazú Volcano. In 2022 then-deputy Carlos Andrés Robles, now Minister of Seas, promoted a line linking Quepos to Manuel Antonio National Park and proposed that the Rural Development Institute and the Costa Rican Electricity Institute fund a feasibility study.

For anyone planning a Chirripó climb anytime soon, nothing changes. The trek remains a reserved, multi-day hike, and any cable car — if it ever advances past conversation — would be years and several legal thresholds away.

World.title: Ministry of Health and Wellness launches Belize MOVES in Belmopan
World.content:
Ministry of Health and Wellness launches Belize MOVES in Belmopan

By Zoila Palma: On July 23, 2026, the Ministry of Health and Wellness officially launched Belize MOVES at Sir George Brown Park in Belmopan.

Belize MOVES is a national campaign promoting healthier lifestyle habits across the nation.

Developed in response to the rising challenges of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), the initiative encourages Belizeans to integrate manageable physical activity into their daily routines.

The program emphasizes that sustainable health improvements do not require strenuous regimens, but can instead be achieved through accessible, community-based activities.

World.title: Prime Minister and U.S. Deputy Secretary of State discuss bilateral cooperation and strengthening trade and commercial ties
World.content:
Prime Minister and U.S. Deputy Secretary of State discuss bilateral cooperation and strengthening trade and commercial ties

By Zoila Palma: On July 23, 2026, Prime Minister John Briceño met with United States Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington, D.C.

Discussions included areas of cooperation and reaffirmed the strong and enduring relationship between Belize and the United States.

The meeting highlighted the shared commitment to strengthening bilateral relations through enhanced collaboration in economic development, security, and regional stability.

Prime Minister Briceño welcomed the continued progress on the Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact (MCC), recognizing its potential to support Belize’s development priorities in education and energy security.

In addition, they discussed expanding cooperation to combat transnational organized crime and narco-trafficking, addressing irregular migration through coordinated regional efforts, and deepening trade and commercial relations to create greater opportunities for investment and prosperity.

Prime Minister Briceño expressed appreciation for the enduring relationship between Belize and the United States and reaffirmed Belize’s commitment to working closely with the U.S. Government to address shared challenges while advancing the prosperity of both countries.

World.title: Government of Belize participates in UNIDO Regional Conference for Latin America and the Caribbean
World.content:
Government of Belize participates in UNIDO Regional Conference for Latin America and the Caribbean

The Government of Belize, through the Ministry of Investment, was invited by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and the Government of Uruguay to participate in the UNIDO Regional Conference for Latin America and the Caribbean in Montevideo, Uruguay, from July 15 to 16, 2026. The event brought together government leaders, development partners, private sector representatives, and international organizations from across Latin America and the Caribbean to strengthen regional cooperation, share best practices, and advance sustainable industrial development.

The two-day conference provided a high-level platform to advance industrial policies that promote economic resilience, competitiveness, and inclusive growth, while accelerating green and digital transitions across the region.

Belize’s representation highlighted the work being done in the country to develop a national Industrial Strategy with Green and Blue Industrial Policies funded by UNIDO and the Government of Japan. This includes the ongoing diagnostic in Belize to prioritize economic activities in the agro-processing and manufacturing sectors that have been identified as having potential for growth.

Meetings were held with the UNIDO AIM Global Alliance to discuss how Belize could access AI training or applications for MSMEs in various industrial sectors. Belize was also introduced to representatives from the UNIDO SIDS Hub at the Barbados office, which is pioneering an initiative aimed at enhancing UNIDO’s work in Small Island Developing States (SIDS). Belize was invited to further discussions with the SIDS Hub to determine how it can access technical assistance for economic diversification and promote investment, particularly in the blue economy, digital, and green solutions, and leapfrog to innovative technologies.

The Ministry of Investment was represented by Lincoln Blake, Director of the Investment Policy and Compliance Unit.

World.title: Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 set to bring Livestock, food and family fun to Belmopan
World.content:
Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 set to bring Livestock, food and family fun to Belmopan

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo 2026 is set to take place on August 15, 2026, at the National Agriculture Showgrounds in Belmopan, bringing together livestock producers, food lovers, families and rodeo enthusiasts for a full day of entertainment and activities.

The event is being organized through a collaboration between the Belize Livestock Producers’ Association (BLPA) and the Wild West Rodeo Club.

Running from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., the festival will showcase Belize’s livestock industry while highlighting local food, agriculture and entertainment.

Among the featured activities will be the Belize Beef Fest Grilling Competition, the Belize Livestock Genetics Showcase, and an exhibition highlighting All Things Meat in Belize.

Visitors will also have the opportunity to enjoy a variety of Belizean cuisine and drinks, along with rodeo events for both children and adults.

The BLPA is inviting families from across the country to attend and experience a celebration of Belize’s livestock industry, local cuisine and rodeo culture. Booth spaces are available by calling 672-5275.

World.title: Fire up the Grill! Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo to host $1,000 Grilling competition
World.content:
Fire up the Grill! Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo to host $1,000 Grilling competition

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo will feature a grilling competition on Saturday, August 15, 2026, at the National Agriculture Showgrounds in Belmopan, giving grill masters an opportunity to showcase their culinary skills and compete for cash prizes.

The competition, organized as part of the Belize Beef Fest & Rodeo, will include three categories: beef, pork and lamb.

Participants will compete for a top prize of $1,000, while the second-place winner will receive $500 and the third-place winner will take home $250.

The Belize Livestock Producers Association (BLPA) says that cash prizes have increased, with the second-place prize rising from $300 to $500 and the third-place prize increasing from $200 to $250.

Registration costs $100 per category, and interested participants are encouraged to register by calling 672-5275.

The event is expected to bring together food enthusiasts, livestock producers, families and members of the public for a day celebrating Belize’s cattle and agricultural industries.

World.title: A New PolyClinic for Duck Run
World.content:
A New PolyClinic for Duck Run

For many of Belize’s rural communities, a trip to the doctor’s office is much more complicated than a simple walk-in or appointment. It often involves navigating public transportation schedules and long distances, and can sometimes require an entire day’s dedication. For decades, this has been the case for families living in Duck Run 1 and neighboring villages in western Belize. The recent establishment of a new polyclinic, however, is about to remove one of the community’s greatest barriers to healthcare.

Photo by Ignite Ltd. Aerial views of newly built Polyclinic in Duck Run 1, Cayo District

Constructed through funding from the European Union and the Government of Belize in partnership with the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the Duck Run 1 Polyclinic is fully equipped with consultation rooms, medical furniture, and all essential supplies needed to bring healthcare services closer to the people who need them. The facility will serve not only residents of Duck Run 1, but also neighbouring communities, including Duck Run 2, Duck Run 3, Santa Familia, and Los Tambos. In total, approximately 6,000 people are set to benefit. And while the polyclinic represents an important investment in healthcare for rural Belize, for the residents who have spent years traveling long distances to access medical care, its significance extends far beyond the building itself.

Ciriaco Castro has called the village of Duck Run 2 home for more than thirty years. During that time, visiting a doctor has, more often than not, meant traveling to San Ignacio or Belmopan. It’s a journey that he says has become increasingly difficult with age and without reliable transportation—and it’s an experience that reflects that of many others.

Families have often had to travel significant distances for routine medical appointments, sometimes facing long waits and even having to return home without being seen.

Photo by Ignite Ltd. Mr. Ciriaco Castro, Resident of Duck Run 2 Village, Cayo District

When asked what he thinks of the new clinic, Castro noted, “ I believe everyone is going to be happy about it, because we are all benefiting.”

That sense of shared benefit is echoed throughout the surrounding villages.

One of the first residents of Duck Run 3, Elvin Larios remembers when there were no roads connecting the growing communities. While infrastructure gradually improved over the years, access to healthcare remained a persistent challenge.

“More or less, we started it in 1985, and I came to this country in 1976,” he said. “We were working in Spanish Lookout, and then we came to this village and began building in the village. Three of us arrived at first, and from there we began to expand the place.”

Photo by Ignite Ltd. Mr. Elvin Larios, Resident of Duck Run 3 Village, Cayo District

Like Ciriaco Castro, Elvin, and other residents of Duck Run 2 have often had to seek out transportation for travel to San Ignacio, located about 14 miles away:

“And sometimes, when we arrived, the place was already full. Sometimes we went for nothing and had to return, then go back another day.”

With the new clinic, the residents will be able to rest easy knowing healthcare is just minutes away.

“This clinic that is being established, we will see quite a difference—maybe not everything we need, but we already have a beginning…it brings benefits to us, the community, and the communities in this area.”

Bridging the Gap

Before the polyclinic, community health workers like Ordel Alford, Sandi Castro, and Arcelita Perez worked hard to ensure that residents were not left without care. Through meaningful work like monitoring patients with chronic illnesses, checking glucose and blood pressure levels, carrying out home visits, and helping residents navigate the public health system, they have been helping to bridge the gaps between rural western Belize and essential healthcare services.

For many, they were among the first people to call whenever illness struck.

Ms. Ordel Alford recalls transporting patients herself when no other options were available:

“If they call me… I could bring them in my vehicle… If they don’t have a vehicle, I could assist them. That’s my job.”



Photo by Ignite Ltd: Ms. Ordel Alford, Community Healthcare Worker, Duck Run 1 Village, Cayo District

For Alford, the opening of the new polyclinic means residents will no longer have to rely so heavily on long journeys or the generosity of neighbours simply to receive medical attention. And, it also serves to strengthen the work that Alford and others like her have been doing. To Sandi Castro, that means being better able to serve her community—the main reason why she decided to become a community health worker. It’s a change that she is welcoming with open arms.

Photo by Ignite Ltd: Ms. Sandi Castro, Community Healthcare Worker, Duck Run 2 Village, Cayo Distric

“This polyclinic will be a big opportunity for my community and for me as well,” she said.

Much like Sandi, Arcelita Perez has dedicated herself to serving residents across rural western Belize. Perez, who has been a community health worker for ten years, believes that the polyclinic is “a blessing” and that its impact will certainly extend far beyond Duck Run 1.

Photo by Ignite Ltd: Ms. Arcelita Perez, Community Healthcare Worker, Duck Run 1 Village, Cayo District

“Everyone around the neighboring villages will be blessed because they can come here, and they can have their primary health care.”

Together, the three women represent years of dedication to ensuring their neighbours receive the care they need. Today, rather than replacing that work, the Duck Run 1 Polyclinic strengthens that dedication by giving them a permanent healthcare facility where they can continue serving.

Healthcare Closer to Home

Dr. Juan Carlos Sabido, Chief of Staff at the San Ignacio Hospital, understands just how important it is to reduce barriers to healthcare in rural communities. He also understands just how taxing it can be for families from those communities to access services. According to him, the new clinic is expected to ease not just the physical journey but the financial burden as well:

“For families in Duck Run 1, travelling to the community hospital usually took about 40 minutes, and reliable public transportation was limited. They had to plan their hospital visits around the bus schedule, hoping to be seen in time to catch the return bus. If they missed it, they often had to find a ride or pay approximately $60 for private transportation. By bringing healthcare closer to the community, this new polyclinic will save families both valuable time and as much as $60 in transportation costs each time they need medical care.”

Photo by Ignite Ltd: Dr. Juan Carlos Sabido – Chief of Staff at San Ignacio Community Hospital, Cayo District

The clinic has been designed as a comprehensive primary healthcare facility, providing services for patients of every age from Monday to Friday between the hours of 8 AM and 5 PM.

“We’ll be able to take kids all the way below one year of age, all the way up to the elderly and everything in between,” Dr. Sabido explained.

And, in addition to providing routine consultations, the clinic is also set to be a provider of National Health Insurance (NHI), offering residents a very broad range of services.

“We do welcome all of the neighboring communities to come and register so that they can start taking advantage of the NHI services as well. This clinic is an NHI provider, and with that, once we get that rolling, we’ll have internists, pediatricians, an OBGYN, and a nutritionist. “

“It’s a lot easier,” added Dr. Sabido. “You no longer have to plan your whole week or whole day because you need to go and see the physician or you need to take your kids because they’re feeling ill.”

For young parents like Juanita Sanchez, that comes as a much-welcomed relief. Living just minutes from the new facility with her daughter, she remembers when even routine medical visits meant travelling far from home.



Photo by Ignite Ltd. Ms. Juanita Sanchez, Resident of Duck Run 1 Village, Cayo District

“It’s better now, because my baby, if she gets sick, well, I could bring her here.”

All people should be able to live in dignity. Access to energy, healthcare, quality education, and water—among others—are essential rights. The European Union through its Global Gateway strategy continues to contribute infrastructure, capacity building, and other measures for reinforcing the capacities of Belizean public actors in the delivery of essential public services to the country’s population. This goes beyond just healthcare and includes access to electricity and justice as well.

The EU has been a steadfast partner of Belize in the health sector, supporting the strengthening of public health services. In recent years, the EU supported crucial renovations of some of the country’s most important infrastructure, including at the Central Medical Laboratory in Belize City, the Punta Gorda Community Hospital, and the Corozal Community Hospital.

Photo by Ignite Ltd. Interior shots of the Polyclinic: Waiting area (top left), Consultation room (top right), Pharmacy (bottom)

Thanks to the infrastructure improvements introduced, these facilities are now disaster-resilient, energy efficient, and “green”. Among many other initiatives enhancing the health sector in Belize, the EU has also supported the provision of specialized training for central and district level health sector managers and other personnel, strengthened health services organization and management in Belize, funded the development of key policies for the health sector, and supported the upgrading and expansion of the Belize Health Information System.

The new Duck Run 1 Polyclinic comes as part of a wider European Union-supported initiative to improve climate resilience and strengthen communities across western Belize. Alongside the new polyclinic, the project, implemented through the IOM, also delivered a hurricane shelter in Duck Run 1, completed right before the start of the hurricane season as well as hurricane shelters in the other communities targeted under the project.

Additionally, the EU funded the upgrading of water systems to ensure better water supply in the villages of Santa Familia and Los Tambos. Drainage infrastructure was also improved thanks to the establishment of 4 miles of drains and 12 culverts. The initiative also allowed for capacity development through the formation and training of community-level emergency response teams and firefighting brigades across six communities.

While these EU-supported initiatives reflect the strength of international partnership, their greatest impact will be measured by the lives touched. For the thousands of residents that they are set to serve, they mean better access to essential services, improved everyday quality of life, community resilience, and stronger support for community workers. For communities like Duck Run 1, that impact is already being felt, as access to healthcare will no longer be defined by the distance residents must travel.

World.title: Police seek man after iPhone stolen from Central Drug Store
World.content:
Police seek man after iPhone stolen from Central Drug Store

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are asking for the public’s assistance in identifying a man captured on surveillance footage in connection with a theft recently reported at Central Drug Store in downtown Belize City.

According to the report, an iPhone valued at $2,500 was stolen from the business. Investigators have released a still image from the store’s camera system showing the man they wish to identify and question. He is seen wearing a light colored baseball cap, dark sunglasses and a blue short sleeved shirt, and carrying a large gray and black backpack.

The man has not been charged with any offence, and police are seeking him for questioning as part of the ongoing investigation.

Anyone who recognizes the individual or has information that could assist is asked to contact the nearest police station. Tips can also be sent confidentially to Breaking Belize News and will be passed directly to the investigating officer. The identity of anyone providing information will be protected.

Businesses in the area are encouraged to review their own camera systems for footage that may assist investigators.
