World.title: $1.5-b pothole rescue
World.content:
Water has settled in this pothole on Fairdene Avenue in St Andrew on Thursday.

AS motorists across the island continue to face gaping potholes, minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has told the Jamaica Observer that the Cabinet on Monday approved a further $1.5-billion spend for patching and sheeting work on main roads across the island to bring some well-needed relief to drivers.

This brings the money allocated to tackle the persistent pothole problem to $3.1 billion for this fiscal year.

According to Morgan, the additional allocation was necessary based on the scope of the problem. He told the Observer that the money initially allocated for the pothole patching programme is already being spent.

“We are engaged in a $1.6-billion programme patching the roads. It’s really sheeting in many cases. Cabinet just approved another $1.5 billion to do more roads. We are doing the $1.6 billion now and then, before the end of the year, we are going to spend another $1.5 billion on road rehabilitation,” said Morgan.

But even as the minister promised relief, motorists across the Corporate Area were pointing the Observer to several roads where potholes are making driving almost impossible.

In downtown Kingston, where many large potholes pockmark the streets, motorists pointed to one on Orange Street, close to its intersection with Heywood Street, which they said is a source of frustration for many.

While an Observer news team was in the area on Thursday, motorists and pedestrians urged the team to take as many pictures and videos as possible to expose the failure of authorities to maintain roads.

In response, Morgan said that area could be fixed as early as next week as it is schduled for priority repairs.

He underscored that his ministry is responsible for fixing main roads through the National Works Agency, and not streets or lanes.

“Not all the roads are mine. I am strictly responsible for main roads; I am not responsible for avenues, lanes, and I am not responsible for crescents. I am not responsible for any of those community roads. None at all. My roads are roads like Washington Boulevard, Constant Spring and Barbican Road.

“Roads like Liguanea Avenue, Paddington Terrace, roads in Cherry Garden, and a lot of the community roads in downtown Kingston are not mine — they belong to the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation — but I have been getting blamed. Parish councils get a billion dollars a year and they need to fix those roads,” argued Morgan.

However residents of several Corporate Area communities only want their roads fixed, with no concern over which agency will do it.

On Fairdene Avenue in Ackee Walk, St Andrew, residents and passing motorists expressed their displeasure at the state of the road, which is littered with very deep and wide potholes..

“It is treacherous. It is dread. When the rain falls, pedestrians get splashed easily all the time. They need to fix the roads properly and done,” said one motorist.

He was supported by another motorist, who charged that the condition of the roads in Corporate Area forces drivers to make detours into areas where they would rather not drive.

In the meantime, one motorist complained about damage to his vehicle by the potholes.

“The road stay very bad, man. The road need to fix. It a mash up mi front end and we have to drive on the roads every day,” lamented the motorist.

World.title: Grief turns to protest in Troy
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents in Troy, Trelawny, on Thursday protesting againt the arrest of a man in connection with fatal mobbing following murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

TROY, Trelawny — Still mourning the murder of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke on Tuesday residents of the usually quiet district took to the streets on Thursday after one of their own was reportedly arrested by the police in connection with the mob killing of the man believed to have attacked her.

According to residents the man was taken into custody by the police who are probing the death of Shani and the fatal attack on the suspected child killer Delroy Coke, and the brutal beating of his father.

The placard-bearing residents used debris to block the Troy main road — which links part of south Trelawny to northern Manchester — as they charged that the police had no reason to arrest the man, whose identity has not been released.

The residents also expressed their anger at the murder of Shani.

“We want justice. Protect our children. Children are the future. Let us protect them. The justice system failed us. We want justice for the brutal murder of Shani,” some of the placards read, while other called for the freeing of the man they said had been taken into custody.

Some of the protesters also took to social media platform TikTok to express their frustration and disgust.

“We a protest, because the police lock up a man and we want him to be freed…. We want justice,” one of the protesting residents told the Jamaica Observer.

Shani partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday. Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on the father and son in the community.

Residents told the Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father was left with major wounds.

When contacted head of the police Area One Assistant Commissioner Glenford Miller said the investigators are seeking those involved in the mob attack.

“I know we are investigating to know who were the persons involved in that mob killing. I cannot say at this time if we have made any arrests,” Miller said mid-morning on Thursday. Subsequent efforts to get a further update were unsuccessful up to press time.

A heavy pall of gloom and anger clouded over Troy on Thursday with one resident telling the

Observer that the community remains grief-stricken.

“The whole of Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” said the resident who requested anonymity.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday, Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

On Wednesday relatives remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night [Tuesday] we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” her aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

World.title: ‘The best yet’
World.content:
Kevin Downswell.

Award-winning Jamaican gospel artiste Kevin Downswell says his upcoming album is the most personal project of his career, describing it as his “the best yet” and the most vulnerable he has ever allowed himself to be in his music.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer’s Spalsh ahead of his Pre-Album Launch Worship Experience on Sunday, July 19 at Victory Tabernacle, Bayside, Port Henderson Road, Portmore, Downswell revealed that the unnamed album was largely written during the COVID-19 pandemic, with its songs inspired by seasons of uncertainty, disappointment, perseverance, and renewed faith.

“I wrote most of these songs in the pandemic, when we were feeling all the pressure and the battles, the tears, the pain and the disappointment,” he said. “Wherever you are in your process, one song will connect with you.”

Asked to describe the album in three words, the gospel minister replied simply: “The best yet.”

Downswell said listeners can expect what he considers his strongest songwriting to date.

“I think this is the realest I’ve ever been in my songs,” he said. “This is the most vulnerable I’ve ever been with my tracks… and I think this is the best I’ve ever written.”

He added that fans will hear pieces of his own testimony throughout the album: “You’ll hear my story in every song. You’ll know that I couldn’t write like this if I hadn’t been through something like this.”

The first taste of the project came with the release of Higher (From the Fire) on Tuesday, July 14, an Afro-soca anthem centred on overcoming life’s trials.

“Sometimes what was meant to destroy you actually lifts you higher,” Downswell explained, pointing to the biblical story of Joseph as one of the inspirations behind the song.

The singer also disclosed that the album moves beyond traditional gospel, blending worship music with reggae, Afro-soca and calypso influences.

“I’ve always tried to stay away from limitations,” he said. “It’s a beautiful mixture.”

The event, which formed part of the Portmore New Testament Church of God’s 50th anniversary celebrations, served as an opportunity for fans to hear songs from the upcoming album before its official release.

“There’s nothing like live performances,” he said. “I’ve worked all my life to make the live experience better than the recordings.”

Beyond the music, Downswell said his greatest hope is that listeners encounter God in a fresh way.

“I’ve fallen in love with God all over again,” he said. “I just want people to experience His presence and His love. I want God to meet people wherever they’re at.”

World.title: BPO’S US$220-M SLIDE
World.content:
Key points:

Local spending fell 22 per cent from about US$1 billion to US$780 million as another 5,000 jobs disappeared.

Government data put employment at 50,000, while the GSAJ estimates about 40,000.

A working group is pursuing new investment, better skills and a shift towards higher-value KPO services.

JAMAICA’S global digital services (GDS) sector spent an estimated US$780 million in the local economy in the fiscal year ended March 2026, down US$220 million from about US$1 billion a year earlier as the industry lost another 5,000 jobs.

The estimate — which measures spending in Jamaica rather than export earnings — was higher than the US$612 million earned from bauxite and alumina exports in 2025 and was equivalent to about 47 per cent of the country’s US$1.65 billion in total merchandise exports.

The spending covered wages, office-space leases, utilities and other operating expenses.

Employment in the sector fell to approximately 50,000 in March 2026 from 62,000 two years earlier, while the number of companies declined from more than 90 to about 70.

The sector had already missed Government’s March 2025 target of 70,400 jobs by 15,400. By March 2026, the gap had widened to 20,400 jobs.

“This decrease in employment is attributed to a variety of factors which include: Onshoring/reshoring, geopolitical considerations, technological advancements, the impact of Hurricane Melissa and the local challenges of cost of doing business,” the Government of Jamaica stated in its annual report on Form 18-K for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission.

The report said Hurricane Melissa compounded those pressures.

“Hurricane Melissa, in particular, had a disruptive impact on Jamaica’s GDS sector, primarily through damage to critical infrastructure and interruptions to essential utilities. Widespread outages in electricity and telecommunications networks constrained business continuity across BPO (business process outsourcing) and other digitally enabled services, limiting firms’ ability to meet international client demands and maintain service-level agreements. In addition, damage to transportation networks and displacement of workers further affected operational capacity and productivity,” the annual report added.

However, Global Services Association of Jamaica President-elect Yoni Epstein has placed employment in the sector at about 40,000 for two consecutive years. The

Jamaica Observer reported on August 1, 2025, that Epstein said the sector employed about 40,000 people, a figure he repeated to the

Financial Gleaner earlier this month. The Government, by comparison, reported approximately 55,000 jobs in March 2025 and 50,000 in March 2026, leaving differences of 15,000 and 10,000, respectively. It was not immediately clear whether the discrepancies reflected different reporting periods, industry coverage or methods of counting workers. Epstein is the founder and CEO of Outsourcing Management Limited, trading as itel.

Since 2012, the Development Bank of Jamaica Limited (DBJ) has committed US$92.66 million in financing to the GDS sector and disbursed US$90.01 million to 20 BPO ventures covering approximately 1.18 million square feet of operating space. The ventures had a combined capacity for 27,513 jobs.

The report said DBJ financing also facilitated US$152.72 million in private-sector investment. However, the Government’s latest report gives a different account of the occupancy of the DBJ-funded projects.

The 2025 annual report said all 20 projects had been completed, leased and occupied and had reported total employment of 22,598. However, the 2026 report said only 19 projects were leased and occupied and had provided 22,598 jobs at their peak. It said the remaining project had been completed with capacity for another 1,200 jobs, but the developer was still seeking an operator. The reports do not explain the change in the stated occupancy of the projects.

The sector’s contraction has also affected the Port Authority of Jamaica (PAJ), which recently postponed plans to monetise its BPO real estate assets through an initial public offering on the Jamaica Stock Exchange.

A CariCRIS report on the PAJ noted, “The authority decided that prevailing market conditions were not conducive to achieving favourable valuation outcomes and therefore postponed the transaction.”

The Government has responded by establishing a working group comprising representatives of the GDS sector, the PAJ, Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) and the Jamaica Special Economic Zone Authority (JSEZA) to develop and implement an action plan aimed at growing the industry.

The working group’s mandate was limited to three areas in the Government’s 2025 annual report. The latest report expands the mandate to six areas. One of the six areas is changing the industry’s mix of BPO and KPO (knowledge process outsourcing) jobs from 80:20 to 60:40. This would reduce the sector’s concentration in basic queries and routine tasks while expanding its participation in more advanced, higher-value activities.

Other focus areas include enhancing job-readiness and digital-skills curricula, optimising processes, institutions, regulations and the incentives framework, strengthening the sector’s value proposition, and developing incubator and accelerator programmes for small and medium-sized enterprises. These initiatives build on work being done with the HEART/NSTA Trust, the United Kingdom Trade Partnerships Programme and the Inter-American Development Bank to better prepare GDS firms and their staff to take on new global opportunities.

“Jamaica, through Jampro (the government agency responsible for the promotion of business opportunities in export and investment), has actively engaged international KPO operators to get them to expand their business to Jamaica. Additionally, Jampro continues to work with local universities and key stakeholders, sharing opportunities for employment as well as establishing partnerships for training in the KPO and ITO (information technology outsourcing) space,” the annual report stated.

World.title: CASH SQUEEZE
World.content:
Jamaica Football Federation headquarters in New Kingston (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has outlined what he considers a harsh financial reality facing the body, which is managing a tight cash-flow situation after putting significant resources into national team programmes that ultimately missed out on major qualification payouts.

International football is a high-stakes business, and Ricketts says the JFF is counting the cost of an aggressive push for global recognition that fell short on the pitch.

Failing to qualify for the 2026 FIFA World Cup cost the JFF a guaranteed minimum payout of at least US$10.5 million to US$12.5 million (under J$2 billion) — a windfall tied to FIFA participation and preparation fees.

For a federation historically hampered by tight budgets, a capital injection of that size could have cleared existing debt, reduced reliance on government subventions, and fully funded grassroots facilities, coaching development, and youth travel across all age groups.

“Right now, it’s challenging,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “We would’ve invested heavily in so many of the World Cup qualifiers. The U-20s leave [today] to participate in the last round. The ladies will play their last game against Costa Rica in November, and of course the senior men’s team didn’t do as well as we would’ve thought; hence, we did not get the returns based on the investment.”

The immediate strain comes as national squads continue to compete. While the senior men missed their target, the federation must still fund ongoing campaigns, including the departure of the national Under-20 team and the senior women’s team’s crucial November fixture.

Should the Reggae Girlz win that Concacaf W Championship game against Costa Rica, they qualify not only for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but also for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil. At the latter, they would receive a financial payout for competing in the group stage at the very minimum. FIFA has however not yet shared an exact breakdown of monetary prizes for this tournament.

Ricketts defended the heavy spending as a necessary cost of doing business in modern football, where federations must spend aggressively across all age groups just to remain competitive on the world stage.

“There were so many teams vying for global recognition that it cost us a lot of money,” Ricketts said. “So, we are struggling right now financially, simply because we would’ve invested heavily in these programmes and the senior men’s team didn’t qualify.”

Despite the short-term financial challenge, Ricketts says staying visible on the global stage remains the JFF’s best path forward. Mentioning long-term commercial goals, such as Jamaica’s interest in hosting the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup, Ricketts says the high cost of international football is a necessary investment in the country’s social and technical future.

He believes the star power of players like Khadija “Bunny” Shaw and Jody Brown demonstrates the return on investment that numbers alone cannot capture.

“This is to ensure that we impact the lives of every Jamaican,” Ricketts said. “Everybody wants to be like Bunny Shaw, everybody wants to be like a Jody Brown, everybody wants to be like a Jamaican player. So, we’re very hopeful, we’re optimistic that this will, from a commercial standpoint, from a technical standpoint, from a social standpoint, certainly help our country.”

World.title: Addison adds up victory
World.content:
Chris-John Addison celebrates his second win in the Drift Ruption series at Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier on July 19.(Photo: Rory Daley)

Chris-John Addison was the winner of the second round of Drift Ruption, which was held on Sunday, July 19, at the Falmouth Cruise Ship Pier, Trelawny.

“This victory is a great feeling, because we were leading the competition from round one, and nevertheless we came out today to execute, and that’s what we did,” Addison told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Addison worked his way through a field stacked with major drift talent from across the island.

In the Drift Ruption format, entrants are whittled down to the highest-scoring eight, and then the highest-scoring four to determine the winner.

It is not a timed event, but a pure drift event in which the drivers have to display maximum slip angle while navigating and interacting with various obstacles for points.

So tough was the competition that several drivers posted perfect runs, leading to multiple ties. When it came to the final four Addison was tied with Sheldon Johnson at the very end. It was his consistently high scores throughout the event that eventually gained him the win.

“This round we didn’t do anything different, because we have an engine being built for high-speed drifting, so we decided to use the stock motor for this, the last car park event. Other than that, no major upgrades. That happens next event,” explained Addison.

Following Addison and Johnson were Cleve Ottey and Nicholas Barnes.

The current standings put Addison at the top of the leaderboard with 200 points. Johnson sits in second with 176 points. Barnes is third on 128 points, while Ottey is fourth on 124 points.

“The event went very well for me and my team,” said Kingsley Scott, event organiser and conceptualiser.

This event marks a change for Drift Ruption as it shifts to high-speed tandem drifting and a move to circuit venues, such as Dover Raceway in St Ann and JamWest Speedway in Westmoreland. The Drift Ruption finale is for a to-be-determined date in December.

World.title: WATCH: Troy residents protest amid man’s arrest following fatal mobbing over slain 10-year-old
World.content:
Placard-bearing residents protesting in Troy, Trelawny on Thursday morning.

TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Placard-bearing residents of Troy, Trelawny on Thursday morning mounted a roadblock as they demanded the release of a man who they say was arrested in relation to a fatal mobbing two days ago following the gruesome murder of 10-year-old Shani Coke.

The residents also protested over Coke’s death. The child’s partially nude body was found with her throat slashed in bushes on Tuesday.

Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on a father and son in the community.

READ: Family grieves bright 10-year-old killed in Troy, as man accused of her murder beaten to death by mob

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. They accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father, who was also attacked by the mob, was admitted to hospital.

Subsequently, police arrested a man in connection with the mob attack. However, residents are demanding his release as they claim he is innocent.

“We blocked the road this morning, and police came and clear most of it. The police came and lockup [a man] and he is innocent, because the guy never went to the mobbing with any machete,” a resident who requested anonymity told Observer Online.

“The whole Troy is in mourning. We can’t stop thinking about the little girl and how she died so awful,” added the resident.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: A light extinguished
World.content:
Shawna Williams-Stevens (left) shows off trophies her niece, 10-year-old Shani Coke, received from Troy Primary School. Looking on is Shani’s mother, Ackeem “Kim” Williams. Kasey Williams

TROY, Trelawny — Huddled on the verandah of their family home, relatives of 10-year-old Shani “Kaidra” Coke, whose partially nude body was found with her throat slashed on Tuesday, remembered the child for her brilliance and radiant smile.

“Shani was born here and lived [with her grandparents], because her [mother] has to work. When Shani goes to school she doesn’t play around. She took her education seriously. From Shani a go basic school she was always first [in her class]. She was always putting out her best. She is from an educated background. Her father is educated and so is her mother,” the child’s aunt Shawna Williams-Stevens told journalists on Wednesday as she stood beside her grieving sister, Shani’s mother Ackeem “Kim” Williams.

The aunt’s hands could not hold the many academic trophies and certificates earned by Shani during her tenure at Troy Primary School.

“From grade one her teachers rewarded her, whether with a stamp in her book or sweets, or you know the teachers always try to elevate her for her to know that she does good. Her mother would always buy her gifts to encourage her,” said Williams-Stevens.

“Right now she was [among] the top students at Troy Primary. If school was keeping it would have to lock today, because of Shani,” added the aunt, while pointing out that up to last Friday Shani was recognised for her participation in summer school.

“All last week she got her certificate to show her brilliance. When you look at her you see the next doctor, lawyer, and they just took her life, just cut her off. Right now we are devastated. Right now we don’t know our head from our feet. Last night we nuh sleep. This is traumatising. Maybe Kaidra was going to come and take her mother out of poverty and they cut her life short and kill her,” Williams-Stevens said before breaking down in tears.

According to a police report, as well as the account of residents, mid-afternoon Tuesday Shani was walking home from a shop along a roadway near her home when she was abducted.

Later, a farmer, who had gone in search of his cow after hearing strange sounds from bushes, made the grisly discovery and raised an alarm.

Police said following the discovery of the child’s body, there was a mob attack on a father and son in the community.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that the two men are Shani’s relatives. Angry residents accused the son of raping and killing the child. He was beaten, chopped and stoned to death, while his father, who was also attacked by the mob, was admitted to hospital.

Police identified the dead man as Delroy Coke, but did not provide any other information.

Shani’s father, Aston Coke, otherwise called Junior, told journalists that his daughter was well-loved and admired by many in her community.

“Her grandmother sent her to the shop and she did not make it back home. Someone stopped her on the street and disturbed her somehow and slashed her throat… She was loving and caring in the community growing up. Everybody knows her. She knows everyone. She can see you and call you by your full name. She had a sense of humour. She was doing well in school and she got a lot of academic awards,” said the heartbroken father.

“She decided that she wanted to make something out of herself growing up, because we were driving that into her head, but things just happened overnight,” added Coke as he alleged that the man believed to have killed his daughter was a habitual offender.

“It is an act that should never have happened in this neighbourhood,” declared Coke, who is battling his own health problems.

He recounted the last encounter with his daughter over the weekend.

“She came by Saturday afternoon and my uncle was putting on a back-to-school treat up by the community centre and she went there to get bags and food. She was very polite. She stopped by and I said to Kaidra, ‘What you doing here? Aren’t you supposed to be up by the treat?’ She said, ‘Yes, Daddy’ and she walked off and said, ‘Daddy, later when I am coming back I will show you what I get.’ I called her back and went in my wallet to give her money to buy juice,” Coke said.

“That was the first time my uncle and some of my aunts met her. I didn’t get to see her Sunday morning when she went to church and I didn’t get to see her yesterday (Tuesday), because she didn’t come all the way out here to the store,” he said as he reflected on the precious memories and proud moments he spent with his daughter.

“She was always smiling and you never saw her sad. You always saw her happy. Those are the things I remember about her at all times. When it comes to the academics you go by her grandmother’s house, trust me you will see a lot of achievements — trophies — that she got at school. Even sometimes when her mother and grandmother are not around I go by the church to collect them,” he said.

“It is a very sad story to know that this neighbourhood of Troy, Trelawny, has come to this. I don’t know if it is because it reached my doorstep [why] I feel it so pressuring, but things have been happening around here a long time and nobody gets justice,” charged Coke.

World.title: Governments criticize EU’s cash-for-reforms model in new budget
World.content:
It’s yet another thorny issue to solve for the EU's 27 countries racing to reach a deal before the start of 2027, when national elections are due in France, Italy, Poland and Spain, which could make discussions even more difficult.

Major contributors to the budget including Italy, France and Spain, and net recipients of EU funds such as Hungary, Malta and Poland, spoke out against the cash-for-reforms model during Wednesday's meeting. Critics say that the approach could increase the power of national governments at the expense of regions, and result in the EU imposing reforms with no political backing.

“We don’t want [the Commission’s] recommendations to become impositions,” said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this article, was granted anonymity to speak freely.

One the other hand, Netherlands defended the plan during the meeting, according to the diplomats. Other fiscally conservative states, such as Sweden and Denmark, have long argued that conditionality could help poorer EU countries become economically more efficient

But two EU diplomats from the rival camp argued that their real motivation is to slow down payments to less affluent regions.

The RRF model

The cash-for-reforms model was tested in the EU’s post-Covid recovery fund, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), where payouts were linked to judicial and pensions reforms among others.

World.title: World chess chief steps aside after EU sanctions
World.content:
Arkady Dvorkovich, president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), talks to media during the pre-tournament press conference on June 16, 2026. | Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

Arkady Dvorkovich stepped aside temporarily after the EU accused him of supporting policies that threaten Ukraine’s sovereignty.

Arkady Dvorkovich, Russia’s former deputy prime minister and president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), suspended his duties Thursday evening after the European Union sanctioned him.

In its latest sanctions package, the EU accused Dvorkovich of “supporting actions or policies which undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.” The FIDE chief pushed back, stating “unequivocally” that he considers the decision “unlawful and unfair.” “I am confident that justice will prevail,” he added.

Dvorkovich became FIDE’s president in 2018, drawing criticism over his closeness to Vladimir Putin’s regime. The Russian president appointed him as deputy prime minister from 2012 to 2018.

Dvorkovich said the decision would remain in effect for as long as he is subject to EU and Swiss sanctions. FIDE Deputy President Viswanathan Anand, a former world champion, will take over his duties. In 2022, Anand told AFP that Dvorkovich had “clearly demonstrated that he is independent of Kremlin influence.”

Under Dvorkovich’s leadership, FIDE’s Ethics and Disciplinary Commission largely overturned a 2024 ruling that had temporarily suspended the Chess Federation of Russia and reprimanded him for “improper association” with an organization or person whose activities conflicted with FIDE’s objectives or interests. The reprimand against Dvorkovich was rescinded.

World.title: China strikes back at EU sanctions targeting defense, tech firms
World.content:
A Bundeswehr truck with the logo Rheinmetall is seen in Unna on July 21, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them.

BRUSSELS — China announced it will add export restrictions on 14 EU defense and technology companies after the EU added 14 Chinese businesses to its Russia sanctions lists.

This marks Beijing’s most direct and forceful response yet to EU sanctions listings, which it denounced as “egregious.” Recent studies estimate that up to 90 percent of sanctioned goods still reaching Russia transit through China.

Germany’s rapidly expanding defense company Rheinmetall is among 14 firms that Chinese exporters are now barred from supplying with dual-use goods — products that have both civilian and military applications — China’s Ministry of Commerce said Friday. The list also includes Czech truckmaker Tatra, Dutch naval engineering firm IHC Merwede, and several optics and laser companies.

Exporters may apply for licenses permitting certain shipments when they are deemed “truly necessary.”

The announcement came a day after the EU added 14 Chinese and Hong Kong entities to its sanctions list, barring European companies from doing business with them. Most are not high-tech defense firms, but logistics companies that help Russian importers obtain Western technology.

World.title: Polish conservatives split ahead of 2027 election
World.content:
That clash at the top boiled over on Friday when Kaczyński expelled Morawiecki and some three dozen MPs for refusing to abandon an internal grouping in PiS that has been widely seen as Morawiecki’s attempt to build his own splinter party.

Kaczyński announced the expulsion after a midnight deadline he had given Morawiecki and his group to sign loyalty declarations.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign and at the same time everyone knew what the consequences of not signing were. And so they made the decision they made,” Kaczyński told a press briefing at PiS’s headquarters in Warsaw.

Morawiecki’s allies are now expected to establish a separate caucus in the Polish parliament, the 460-seat Sejm.

The departure of Morawiecki’s followers is going to reduce its parliamentary contingent to 140-145 seats, making it the second-biggest caucus after Tusk’s Civic Coalition.

While PiS was ahead of Civic Coalition in polls last fall, support has now dropped to 26 percent, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls, behind the Civic Coalition on 32 percent.

World.title: EU signals relief over new US tariffs as Trump respects transatlantic truce
World.content:
“The EU notes positively the fact that this outcome is in line with the U.S. tariff commitments agreed under the EU-U.S. Joint Statement,” said Olof Gill, deputy chief spokesperson for the European Commission.

While Brussels cautiously welcomed these new tariffs, it is still conscious that more investigations — looking at alleged industrial overcapacity in Europe and pharmaceutical pricing policies — are under way, meaning cumulative duties could ultimately breach the 15 percent cap. Those probes are conducted under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, a tool used by Washington to take action against unfair trade practices by other countries.

“Looking ahead, the EU expects the U.S. to continue abiding by the terms of the EU-U.S. Joint Statement, including as regards any remedies under additional Section 301 investigations,” Gill added.

The new U.S. tariffs follow a five-month investigation into efforts to crack down on imports of goods made with forced labor — a measure specifically combating manufacturing from America's trade rivals in Asia.

The EU’s own forced labor regulation will only apply from Dec. 2027. This is the justification cited by the U.S. Trade Representative for applying a 10 percent tariff on goods coming from the bloc.

The EU’s foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas struck a less diplomatic note, pushing back against Washington’s reasoning to impose the tariffs.

“We had a deal with America and we have kept to that deal, that side of the deal. That's why this is a negative surprise that this agreement is not kept,” she told Reuters on the sidelines of a meeting with ASEAN countries in the Philippines.

“If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labor conditions for our employees, so it's not really grounded.”

World.title: Merz seeks to revive political fortunes with cabinet reshuffle
World.content:
“These personnel changes follow a clear guiding principle,” he added. “We want a government that works with the greatest enthusiasm and joy, while also reflecting the diversity of our society and political landscape. We are a reform-oriented government, and we intend to continue demonstrating that.”

Merz has often been publicly criticized for surrounding himself with men at top adviser level. With the appointment of Nina Warken, the current health minister, as chancellery chief he is putting a woman in charge of the chancellery’s inner workings for the first time in Germany’s postwar history. The position is of strategic importance as it is key to behind-the-scenes brokerage work, for example when mediating between the chancellery and ministries as well as with lawmakers and at state level.

“She is assertive, and she is also well-versed in security policy issues, which are, after all, coordinated here in this house,” Merz said of Warken. “She will therefore be one of the most important — if not the most important— pillars of support for me in the day-to-day work of the government, as well as my primary point of contact.”

The cabinet reshuffle allows Merz to make a political reset before crucial regional elections in September. Polls show that the AfD has a chance of winning an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6 and is poised to perform well in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and Berlin later that month.

To fend off the rise of the far right, Merz has promised to bring much-needed reforms, for example to the pension system, through parliament this fall. In doing so, he would show voters that the political center is indeed the only viable option to get things done, or at least that’s how the thinking goes in the government.

The current general secretary of Merz’s CDU, Carsten Linnemann, is set to take over as health minister from Warken. He will be tasked with bringing one of the key reforms, the health reform, through parliament later this year.

World.title: Merz: Linnemann folgt „meiner Bitte“ und wird neuer Gesundheitsminister
World.content:
„Mir ist bewusst, dass das eine große Aufgabe ist“, sagte Linnemann auf der Pressekonferenz neben Merz und Warken. Er freue sich auf die Aufgabe. Der CDU-Politiker war bereits zu Beginn der Legislatur im Gespräch für ein Ministeramt. Der 48-Jährige sollte ursprünglich Wirtschaftsminister werden, lehnte die Position aber ab. Er wäre lieber Arbeitsminister geworden, wie er der „Welt“ sagte (hier). Das Ressort ging aber an die SPD.

Warken will Reformkurs fortsetzen

„Ich freue mich, den Reformkurs, den wir jetzt begonnen und gut auf den Weg gebracht haben, mit der Bundesregierung weiter voranzutreiben“, sagte die künftige Kanzleramtschefin Warken. Die CDU-Politikerin blickt auf einen steilen Aufstieg zurück. Erst vergangenes Jahr wurde sie zur Überraschung vieler Gesundheitsministerin, jetzt wechselt sie auf die Schlüsselposition im Kanzleramt und soll dort Merz bei den anstehenden Reformen helfen. Merz lobte, dass Warken auch mit den sicherheitspolitischen Themen vertraut sei. Es ist das erste Mal in der Geschichte der Bundesrepublik, dass eine Frau das Bundeskanzleramt leiten wird.

Doch noch ist der Umbau nicht abgeschlossen. „Es wird weitere Veränderungen im Bundeskabinett geben“, sagte Merz. Wen genau es betrifft, will er zu gegebener Zeit kommunizieren.

World.content:
Water Matters

Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. World.title: Edinburgh’s tourist tax has now launched. Here’s how much you have to pay
World.content:
Travellers to Edinburgh will now have to pay a tourist tax, starting Friday 24 July.

 

A 5% fee now applies to the cost of all paid overnight accommodation in Scotland’s capital.

Edinburgh is the first Scottish city to introduce such a scheme, and hopes to raise up to £50 million (€58 million) a year to invest in its worldwide appeal as a place to visit and live.

Edinburgh tourist tax comes into force

The visitor levy was formally agreed in January 2025, with councillors approving a proposal to charge guests at hotels, B&Bs, hostels and holiday rentals including Airbnbs.

The 5% fee has applied to all advance bookings made since 1 October 2025 for stays taking place on or after 24 July 2026.

The levy is capped at five nights in a row and charged at the same rate every day of the year.

“We know that the city’s popularity comes at a cost through the pressure it puts on our services and on the people who live and work here all year round,” says Council Leader Jane Meagher.

“This small new contribution from overnight visitors will help improve the services and public spaces we all depend on, while better managing the effects of tourism and major events.”

How will Edinburgh’s tourist tax benefit the city?

In February, councillors agreed the first full set of investment programmes using funding raised by the levy.

Worth more than £90 million (€105.3 million) over the next three years, the initial programmes fall under three themes: City Operations and Infrastructure; Culture, Heritage and Events; and Destination and Visitor Management.

Several 'early win' projects have already started, including a £132,000 (€154,400) contribution towards Edinburgh's Festival Carnival and Mardi Gras events and partnering with Police Scotland to create a City Centre Policing Unit, increasing public safety in the city centre.

There are several more initiatives to be delivered in the next three years. This includes £1.3 million (€1.52 million) for additional operations services in the city centre like waste, cleansing and patrols, and £2 million (€2.34 million) and £2.5 million (€2.93 million) respectively towards transforming the city's key coastal visitor attractions at Cramond foreshore and Portobello Promenade.

Parks will also be a key focus, with increases to repairs budgets, doubling the number of park rangers across the city, and additional investment in planting, such as floral gateways, to improve the look and feel of the city's green spaces.

"From revitalised public spaces to better visitor infrastructure and experiences, we're confident the levy can help Edinburgh stay welcoming, resilient and successful," says Julie Ashworth, Chair of the Edinburgh Visitor Levy Advisory Forum.

World.title: Spain sets global audience records after World Cup win
World.content:
Beyond the pitch, Spain's triumph in securing their second World Cup star has boosted the international profile of the Spanish national team, strengthening its presence and connection with supporters in recent months, ever since the official announcement of the World Cup squad.

 

This impact is also the result of the communication strategy developed by the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF), which has brought the team's day-to-day life closer to millions of followers throughout the World Cup. The national team’s social media accounts (@sefutbol) have gained 6.7 million new followers, a 31% increase in just two months.

The RFEF has strengthened its digital strategy through a model of constant communication based on exclusive content and a continuous presence on social media, showcasing the team's more human side and strengthening its bond with fans.

During the World Cup, the RFEF adopted new formats tailored to platforms such as Instagram and TikTok, producing more dynamic and emotionally engaging content. Some posts gained significant international traction and even went viral, including the tributes to Chattanooga and images of New York awash in red ahead of the final.

Among the RFEF’s standout content during the World Cup were the podcast La estrella que nos une and the World Cup vlog series, which brought fans closer to the players’ stories, emotions and experiences.

In addition, post-match interviews and title celebrations racked up millions of views on social media, including more than 25 million plays on Instagram. Overall, RFEF content generated 2.7 billion views on Instagram and more than 93 million interactions.

A docuseries set to reach more than 200 countries

In December, the RFEF and Prime Video will release a four-part docuseries on the Spanish national team's historic World Cup triumph. Featuring never-before-seen footage and exclusive interviews with the key protagonists, the series will reveal the story behind the team's journey to a second World Cup star. It will be available in more than 200 countries.

In a post on X, Spain’s men’s national football team announced the project as follows: “The @rfef and @PrimeVideo will release a docuseries about the triumph at the #FIFAWorldCup. It will be available in December and will consist of four episodes.”

The revamp of the national team’s visual identity also strengthened its image during the World Cup, with high-performing posts such as Campeones del Mundo, which generated 316 million views, A la final with 137 million, and the image of the trophy lift with 81 million.

An unprecedented media and digital impact

The RFEF’s and the national team’s activity during the World Cup generated 11.5 million media mentions between 25 May and 21 July, with an estimated advertising value equivalent (AVE) of €643 million and 41.4 billion opportunities to view.

TikTok was the fastest-growing platform, gaining 3.5 million new followers and recording a 470% increase in views. Overall, the RFEF’s social media profiles reached a combined 34.3 million followers, strengthening their digital presence through new content formats and daily tournament coverage.

Throughout the World Cup, the RFEF also carried out an extensive media operation, arranging 215 one-to-one interviews, 245 flash interviews, 34 press conferences and dozens of player appearances in mixed zones. The operation enabled the federation to meet the reporting needs of more than 215 accredited journalists during the tournament’s final stages.

World.title: Latvian foreign minister confirms consulate in Ukraine was hit by deadly Russian attack
World.content:
Latvia’s Foreign Minister Baiba Braze confirmed “with indignation” on Friday that a Russian attack had damaged the Baltic nation’s honorary consulate in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, killing at least six Ukrainian civilians and injuring dozens more.

 

“I have informed EU and NATO ministers and international organisations,” Braze said in an online statement. “Russia can destroy buildings, not Ukraine’s will and Latvia’s support.”

Latvian public broadcaster LTV Zinu dienests reported that Latvia’s Honorary Consul, Oleksandr Pavenko, was not harmed in the attack, which occurred in the Donbas region.

Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics described the attack on the consulate as a “war crime.” “Latvia stands with Ukraine. We will continue to support the work of our honorary consul, Oleksandr Pavenko, and all those who remain on the front lines helping their people,” he said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that guided aerial bombs killed half a dozen civilians on Friday, with more injured. In a statement posted online, he said that the attack damaged "ordinary homes, the consulate building, and vehicles."

"It is important that our partners fully understand that protecting lives also depends on them. Interceptors for Patriot systems are the number one priority," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this is another example of Russia's "blatant violation of international law" and its disregard for the protection of civilian and consular premises.

He urged "strong international responses" to the incident.

EU and Baltic outrage

Senior EU figures have also lent their support to Ukraine and Latvia.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen leads the charge by offering her condolences to families affected by the fatal attack, with the strike against Latvia's diplomatic outpost also showing Russia's "complete disregard for diplomacy.

"Russia is losing the war it started, and is increasingly targeting civilians in a desperate attempt to crush Ukraine’s spirit. But Ukraine’s spirit is unbreakable. And so is Europe’s resolve to support Ukraine’s defence," she said.

European Council President António Costa echoed these remarks, adding that Russia's attack on the consulate and the city of Sloviansk is a "grave and unacceptable act."

"I strongly condemn this strike, which claimed lives and left many injured," he said.

Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys denounced Russia's actions against Ukrainian civilians and Latvia’s political infrastructure, insisting they will not "break the courage, resilience, and determination of the Ukrainian people, nor the resolve of those who stand with Ukraine".

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna called the incident a “deliberate attack” on Ukrainians and European diplomatic offices.

“These attacks will not go unanswered. Pressure will intensify, and support for Ukraine will not waver,” he added.

In August last year, Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv "severely damaged" the EU's diplomatic offices, with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stating at the time she was "outraged" by the assault, which killed at least 17 Ukrainian civilians.

World.title: Poland's opposition PiS splits ahead of crucial 2027 elections
World.content:
The leader of Poland's right-wing opposition party Law and Justice (PiS), Jarosław Kaczyński, announced on Friday that more than 30 MPs have left the party following a bitter power struggle between him and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki.

 

The split is the biggest in Poland's main opposition party in more than two decades, and follows weeks of tensions over the future direction of PiS ahead of the 2027 parliamentary elections.

Kaczyński had demanded the dissolution Rozwój Plus, an association founded by Morawiecki and his allies, whom he ordered to sign a declaration pledging not to belong to internal political factions.

Morawiecki refused to sign what he described as a "loyalty declaration", arguing that it carried negative historical connotations. Instead, he proposed a compromise, including stepping down as one of the party's vice-president while remaining an ordinary PiS member.

But talks between the two camps ultimately failed to produce an agreement.

Kaczyński: 'It's all over'

Speaking on Friday, Kaczyński confirmed that the final number of resignations among the party's MPs was still being determined. He declined to confirm whether Morawiecki himself was among those leaving, saying only that "it's all over."

The dispute reflects a broader battle over the party's strategy after its 2023 election defeat. Kaczyński has steered PiS towards a more conservative course, while Morawiecki and his allies have argued the party should appeal to a broader centre-right electorate to improve its chances of returning to power.

The split could have major implications for Poland's next parliamentary election in 2027. Prime Minister Donald Tusk's governing coalition will hope that the breakup of its main political rival could weaken the opposition, dividing conservative voters and shifting attention away from criticism of the government's record.

At the same time, analysts say a separate political force led by Morawiecki could emerge as a powerful new player on the right, appealing to moderate conservatives and business-oriented voters. Rather than eliminating competition for the governing coalition, the argument goes, the split could reshape Poland's political landscape into a three-way contest for power.

Whatever the precise implications, the departures mark the most serious internal rupture in PiS since the party was founded in 2001, raising fresh questions about the future of Poland's largest opposition force and the balance of power ahead of the 2027 vote.

Recent opinion polls suggest that PiS remains one of the country's largest parties, though support varies widely across surveys, from about 19 percent to just under 30 percent. None of the latest polls gives the party enough support to govern alone, so it would likely need coalition partners to return to power.

A step to Polexit?

At the same time, Poland's right has adopted an increasingly confrontational stance towards the European Union. PiS rejects suggestions that it wants Poland to leave the bloc, but it nonetheless opposes several flagship EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal.

Przemysław Czarnek, who has emerged as a leading candidate to become prime minister if the conservatives return to power, has argued that Poland should withdraw from the EU's Emissions Trading System, saying the carbon market undermines the country's economic competitiveness.

Among those opposed to the ETS is President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has renewed his call for a referendum on EU climate policy.

The presidential office says the initiative is intended to give voters a direct say on EU climate measures, while politicians from Tusk's governing coalition argue it risks fuelling anti-EU sentiment and laying the political groundwork for a future debate over Poland's membership of the bloc.

World.title: Netanyahu orders 'firm' military action after deadly West Bank clash
World.content:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has announced that he has directed the Israel Defense Forces to take "firm measures against terrorism" following a deadly clash in the occupied West Bank on Friday.

 

Netanyahu's orders include demolishing "the home of the terrorist who carried out this morning’s attack near the village of Tell," carrying out "vigorous operations in villages that serve as centres of terrorism," and reinforcing the military "throughout Judea and Samaria."

He added that the IDF would "accelerate the legalisation of existing farms and the establishment of new ones."

Four Palestinians were killed and four others were injured by Israeli forces in the West Bank on Friday, the Palestinian health ministry said. An Israeli man was also killed in the incident, which occurred around the village of Tell, per Israel's Magen David Adom emergency service.

While exact details on what happened remain unclear, Israeli and Palestinian media reports suggest that Israeli settlers from Havat Gilad entered Tell and were met by locals.

The Palestinian News Agency WAFA reported that the Israeli group "attacked the eastern part of the village" and set fire to a shop, two homes, and agricultural land.

The IDF said that the Israelis were "were hiking in the area" and that one Palestinian resident had stolen a weapon from a security officer who arrived at the scene and opened fire at the Israelis.

Video footage circulating on social media appeared to capture the chaotic scene as it unfolded. It shows armed men moving towards a group of Palestinians before one is seemingly disarmed and gunshots break out.

The IDF said its forces had killed the person who allegedly took the weapon.

The West Bank

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 and has seen a surge in violence since the start of the war in Gaza, which broke out following the Hamas militant group's October 7 attacks in 2023.

According to a report from the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, there were around 737,000 Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as of October 2024.

Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.

In May, the EU agreed to new sanctions on Israeli settlers due to the increase in violence in the West Bank. It came as the bloc also announce fresh sanctions on leading Hamas figures.

In a statement at the time, the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said: "It was high time we move from deadlock to delivery. Extremisms and violence carry consequences".

According to the Palestinian health ministry, 87 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank in 2026.

World.title: EU seeks dialogue with US as tensions rise after Google fine
World.content:
The European Commission said on Friday it would engage with the US to de-escalate tensions after the EU executive fined Google on Thursday over its dominance in the EU's digital market, sparking an angry reaction from Washington.

 

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the EU's fine jeopardised dialogue between the two sides of the Atlantic on digital regulation, as well as the trade deal that the US and EU struck last year after tough negotiations.

The Trump administration has persistently railed against the EU's digital rules, accusing Brussels of imposing non-tariff barriers on US companies and disproportionately targeting American Big Tech.

However, the Commission's chief spokesperson, Paula Pinho, said on Friday that the US had left the door open for talks.

“There’s a call for dialogue which we fully embrace,” she said, adding that Brussels would engage while making sure to preserve the EU's regulatory “autonomy”.

'The EU undermines dialogue'

Earlier this week, 25 US lawmakers wrote to US President Donald Trump calling for a US investigation into EU trade practices in advance of the anticipated fine against Google.

The fine was duly announced on Thursday, penalising the tech giant to the tune of €890 million under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which Washington has relentlessly criticised over the past year, along with the Digital Services Act – an EU regulation targeting illegal content on large online platforms.

“We are trying to resolve our concerns with the EU’s Digital Markets Act and other actions through responsible, constructive dialogue,” Greer said in a statement after the fine was announced. “The EU’s recent actions undermine these efforts and pose a real risk to the continuation of transatlantic stability with respect to trade,” he added.

German Socialist MEP Bernd Lange, the European Parliament's trade chief, told Euronews that he feared further escalation in transatlantic relations and expected additional action from the US.

The EU lawmaker was at the forefront of the negotiations to implement the EU-US agreement struck in July 2025 by Trump and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen after weeks of trade disputes. Yet despite the deal, EU officials still consider transatlantic relations volatile.

On Thursday, the White House announced a new tariff regime targeting its trading partners, including the EU, over forced labour allegations. While insisting it has stringent rules to combat products made with forced labour, Brussels chose not to retaliate, arguing that the new tariffs respected the 15 percent cap on EU goods set out in the trade deal.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Europe wildfires: Many flee by boat as fires spread, merge
World.content:
Tens of thousands hopped onto cars and boats to escape southwestern France's wildfires. In the Madrid region, authorities declared a national emergency as at least two fires merged.

Wildfires continued to rage through parts of France and Spain on Friday, forcing tens of thousands to evacuate and authorities to ask European Union neighbors for help.

French authorities ordered the total evacuation of the tourist Cap Ferret peninsula off the Atlantic coast, with many boarding boats to flee.

In Spain, two fires converged near the capital, Madrid, with authorities declaring a national emergency, the first over a wildfire.

Heat waves fuel wildfires across southern Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about France's Cap Ferret fire?

Over 60,000 people evacuated the area in and around Cap Ferret as the blaze consumed some 100 square kilometers (38 square miles) of land.

Authorities sent boats to help with the evacuation, with many others using small water taxis.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television that a fire that erupted in Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, was the largest so far this season in France. It was threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula.

"It's quite impressive and even frightening," the Associated Press quoted Laurent Moretti, a resident in the town of Ares, as saying. "An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

Tens of thousands had to evacuate the tourist area of Cap Ferret as wildfires continued to rage Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

Some 1,500 of those who fled the peninsula arrived in the city of Arcachon by sea. They were met with coffee, fruit and water in a reception area prepared by town officials.

In the Gironde department, Nunez said 40,000 people have been evacuated, with 23,000 more in the Landes department.

French President Emmanuel Macron said the country will receive EU reinforcements to help put out the blaze, after calling for the neighbors' help.

At least 2 fires merge in Madrid

As Spanish authorities declared a national emergency over the wildfires, two fires converged despite the deployment of over 2,000 personnel and 10 aircraft in an effort to control the blaze, according to Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska.

Over 19,000 people were ordered to evacuate from towns in the mountains west of Madrid, where many of the capital's residents sport second homes. The area is densely populated.

Only emergency vehicles were allowed on roads near the blaze, the AFP news agency reported. Police set up checkpoints to prevent unauthorized access.

Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters a third fire in nearby Avila province was about to also merge with the other fires, or may have already done so.

Residents had to flee to shelters in the area west of Madrid to escape the fires Image: Pierre-Philippe Marcou/AFP

"I've lived here for 36 years and I've never seen anything like it. ​Nor did I expect it. I thought they were going to get it under control last night, but it was already late, and it was all out of control," local resident Javier Martin told Reuters.

Spanish authorities declared a national emergency on Thursday in the Madrid region and the Avila province.

"We are experiencing a dramatic situation, not just in several Spanish regions but also in neighboring countries," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez wrote on X.

World.title: Three years under military rule: Niger still seeks stability
World.content:
The military government in Niger had promised social, security and economic improvements when it usurped power in 2023. Three years down the line, there are mixed reviews on its performance.

The military seized power in Niger on July 26, 2023. General Abdourahamane Tiani, who became head of state, justified the coup by citing the poor security situation, which he said persisted despite international support.

In the weeks that followed, themilitary government announced a transitional period that was to last a maximum of three years.

However, the political promises made upon taking office have not been fulfilled: The transitional government continues to hold all the reins—and the security situation in the Sahel country remains fragile.

In the Tillabery region in southwestern Niger, attacks by jihadists are on the rise. Thousands of people have been forced to flee their villages, plunging the region into a severe humanitarian crisis.

Niger's military government has struggled to end an Islamist insurgency despite promises to do so Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

"Today, attacks on the armed forces and the civilian population are significantly more frequent and violent than they were three years ago," Maiga, a resident of the city of Tera, which has a population of 30,000, told DW. Maiga wished to remain anonymous for security reasons.

"Life used to be better despite the insecurity; the weekly markets operated normally and supplies arrived regularly," he said, adding that at the moment entire villages had fled and schools are closed.

The nongovernmental organization ACLED also says thethe security situation has deteriorated since the 2023 coup.

According to the organization, the Tillabery region remains the main hotspot for clashes between two rival Islamist groups, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and the so-called Islamic State in the Sahel Province (ISSP—formerly ISGS). This rivalry has resulted in numerous casualties among soldiers and civilians.

In 2025, nearly 1,200 deaths were recorded in the region. For Heni Nsaibia, a staff member at ACLED, these figures attest to the scale of the security crisis affecting Niger.

The most recent major attack, on July 17, claimed the lives of at least 16 soldiers, according to Niger's state media, ANP. 15 terrorists were killed in that attack, ANP said. "The situation in Niger has worsened, particularly in the Tillabery region, where the death toll is the highest in the central Sahel," Nsaibia told DW.

Insecurity taking a toll on civilians

"We live in makeshift shelters and are defenseless against the elements; we take on small odd jobs to survive," a woman told DW. A herder adds: "I used to be able to live with dignity from my work, but right now it's very difficult; even [portable] drinking water is a problem for us," he added.

Young Nigeriens are torn between disappointment and optimism: In the youth assemblies, known as "Fadas," the topic continues to spark discussion. Some—like Fadila—believe that the situation is gradually stabilizing after the turmoil of the first few years.

There was much optimism in Niger after the military took over power three years ago Image: AFP/Getty Images

"For a while, it wasn't easy at all: Salaries weren't paid on time, food supplies… that wasn't easy. But for some time now, things have been going pretty well overall," Fadila told DW.

Abdurahmane emphasized that young people can once again participate in politics: "Before the coup, young people were excluded from decision-making bodies." But in the meantime, he said, an advisory commission has been established that includes young people. "So that means the concerns of young people are now being taken into account in decision-making bodies."

Just two days after the ouster of President Mohamed Bazoumin 2023, junta leader Abdourahamane Tiani announced plans to combat corruption and boost the economy.

But three years later, the people of Niger are no better off, Tahirou Garka, a close ally of Mohamed Bazoum, noted. He is the spokesperson for the G25, a movement advocating for a return to constitutional order in Niger.

"They have failed economically and socially," he said, referring to the military government. "People are struggling to find drinking water; there is no water, no electricity, no fuel."

What is the Alliance of Democrats for the Sahel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, Hamani Oumarou of LASDEL, a social sciences research institute based in Niamey, takes a different view. According to him, the socioeconomic situation has improved for a large portion of Niger's population, especially for those who are not part of the middle class or the elite.

"Households with low incomes have more money left over to feed their families," Oumarou told DW. However, Niger is also forced to import food at certain times of the year, which leads to a sharp rise in prices.

Rebuilding ties with ECOWAS

Along with Mali and Burkina Faso, Niger is a founding member of the Alliance of Sahelian States (AES), which was formed in 2023 after all the three countries subsequentlywithdrew from the West African regional organization ECOWAS.

The AES has distanced itself from Western partners and is seeking closer ties withRussia.

Pape Ibrahima Kane, an expert on international organizations, now hopes for a rapprochement between the AES member states and their longtime allies in West Africa.

The military leaders of the Sahel Alliance support one another militarily and economically, but they still face political sanctions by the African Union (AU) Image: Mahamadou Hamidou/REUTERS

He sees a positive sign in the fact that Guinean Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate was elected chief negotiator forECOWAS a few days ago. According to Kane, Kouyate seems to have been accepted by the AES.

"We are at the beginning of a promising process, as both sides are truly on the same page when it comes to starting talks," he told DW.

For him, economic negotiations should also play a role. Niger depends on access to the port of Benin and on its electricity supply from Nigeria and Benin, both of which are ECOWAS member states.

Reliou Koubakin and Ali Abdou contributed to this article.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: UNESCO adds Lebanese, West Bank sites to endangered list
World.content:
Israel has rejected the listing of a Lebanese castle and an occupied West Bank archaeological site. UNESCO added both sites to its World Heritage in Danger list in the context of Israeli activity.

The United Nations cultural agency on Friday updated its list of World Heritage in Danger, with locations including a Lebanese castle that Israeli forces recently captured as well as an archaeological site in the occupied West Bank, amid Israeli objections.

The decision was made during a UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) meeting in South Korea's Busan.

Members agreed that five castles in Lebanon's Mount Amel, including Beaufort Castle, and the West Bank's Sebastia would both go on the agency's World Heritage List and List of World Heritage in Danger.

The decision came after reviewing the nominations on an emergency basis, citing ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

Israel's Foreign Ministry had urged the committee to reject the designation efforts, calling the nominations a "weaponization of cultural heritage."

Israeli forces occupied Lebanon's Beaufort Castle in May Image: Stringer/REUTERS

What do we know about the UNESCO-designated sites?

Beaufort Castle is a Crusader fortress also known as Qalaat al-Shakif. Israeli forces captured the fortress in May amid their military operations in southern Lebanon as part of the fight against Iran-backed Hezbollah militants.

The mountainous area where Beaufort and the other five Jabal Amel listed castles are located has come under repeated Israeli bombardment during the war.

UNESCO said the fortresses had sustained damage and faced ongoing threats from the conflict "serious enough to justify resorting to an emergency procedure."

Lebanese Culture Minister Ghassan Salame told the French AFP news agency that only two of the castles were "within the Lebanese government's reach" and accused Israel of having already destroyed Shamaa Castle and of threatening to demolish Beaufort.

Salame described the UNESCO listing as a "remarkable achievement in the effort to protect these important Lebanese historical landmarks."

Israel seizes strategic castle in Lebanon in deep incursion To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meanwhile, Sebastia, the other site added on Friday, lies near the West Bank city of Nablus. It is thought to be the ancient Israeli and later Roman city of Samaria, with archaeological remains spanning the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods.

Israel still uses the name Samaria to refer to the northern West Bank.

Israeli authorities have developed an interest in the site in recent years, in 2025 taking control of around 200 hectares of Palestinian land nearby for what it calls preservation and development purposes.

The site is important to the Palestinian tourism industry and threatened by the recent Israeli actions, including an Israelis-only road, a fence and entry fees.

"The integrity of the site is currently threatened by an expropriation project aimed at subdividing the property and creating the 'Samaria' (Shomron) National Park," UNESCO said.

Sebastia is thought to be the ancient Israeli and later Roman city of Samaria, with archaeological remains spanning the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods [FILE: Feb 12, 2026] Image: Zain Jaafar/AFP

Sebastia's nomination to the UNESCO list was first submitted by the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO in 2012. It argued the site remains largely undeveloped under Israeli control and requires additional conservation despite attracting tourists.

Adel Naim Daoud Atieh, a member of the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO, said the World Heritage designation rewards the perseverance of Sebastia's residents "who have protected this extraordinary site through generations, despite occupation, restrictions and repeated attempts to separate them from their own heritage."

How has Israel responded?

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar slammed UNESCO for the listings, calling that of Samaria in particular an attempt at "erasing and denying the Jewish connection to this land."

A member of the Israeli delegation, attending the Busan meetings as an observer after Israel withdrew from the organization in 2019, said it was a "shame politicization has ruined UNESCO and led to mockery of history."

In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli Foreign Ministry accused the Palestinian delegation of waging a "hostile, one-sided campaign" at UNESCO by falsely portraying Sebastia as an area facing an emergency.

Addressing the listing of the Lebanese Beaufort Castle, the Israeli Foreign Ministry alleged that Hezbollah turned it into a military stronghold by building tunnels beneath the site and launching rockets from the area.

Sebastia is an important site for the Palestinian tourism industry that is threatened by the recent Israeli actions, including an Israelis-only road, a fence and entry fees [FILE: Nov 20, 2025] Image: Nasser Nasser/AP Photo/picture alliance

At Friday's meeting, a Lebanese delegate said the castles have been used "only for cultural and tourism purposes" since Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 and accused Israeli media of circulating images of tourist facilities as military tunnels.

Israel's withdrawal from UNESCO was owed to what it called bias against it, accusing the UN agency of downplaying its historical ties to the Holy Land.

Edited by: Sean Sinico
