World.title: Ukraine hits ‘Russia’s Amazon’ warehouses outside St Petersburg
World.content:
Saint Petersburg – Ukrainian drones Friday hit warehouses for Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries for a third time in six days, this time near Saint Petersburg, triggering a fire that sent smoke pouring over the historic city.

Kyiv has accused Wildberries — Russia’s largest online retailer often known as the Russian equivalent of Amazon — of storing drone parts and helping the Russian army.

Ukraine has targeted Saint Petersburg as it steps up long-range drone strikes on Russian energy, military and logistics sites in recent weeks, calling the attacks justified retribution for Moscow’s nightly drone and missile barrage of its cities.

Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down some 571 drones overnight over more than a dozen regions and Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that Russia annexed in 2014 — one of the largest one-night barrages of the war.

In Saint Petersburg, an AFP reporter saw grey smoke rising into the morning sky over high-rise residential buildings in the city, President Vladimir Putin’s hometown that is more than 800 kilometres (500 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

Wildberries said two of its logistics facilities in Saint Petersburg and one in Simferopol, in Moscow-annexed Crimea, were hit.

“Rapid evacuation was carried out at all the warehouses … according to preliminary data, there are no casualties,” Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim said on social media.

Alexander Drozdenko, governor of the surrounding Leningrad region said three people were wounded in the attack, which saw at least 59 drones fired towards Saint Petersburg.

It was the third overnight attack by Ukraine on Wildberries’ sites in the past week.

Last weekend, eight night-shift workers were killed in attacks on Wildberries sites that saw one of the company’s main warehouses outside Moscow burn to the ground.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alleged after the first attack that the facilities were used to “supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment.”

Hundreds of small businesses saw their inventories wiped out in the strike, triggering angry comments on social media.

Kyiv calls its strikes “long-range sanctions”, saying the attacks are justified retribution for Russia’s more than four-year offensive and nightly attacks on its cities.

The campaign has triggered nationwide fuel shortages and, Kyiv says, dented Russia’s financial war chest.

– ‘Escalation’ –

Columns of thick black smoke were still billowing into the sky from one of the factories hours after the hit, an AFP reporter saw.

Russian President Vladimir Putin spent the first years of the war trying to shield the population from the fall-out of his decision to launch the offensive on Ukraine.

But the strikes on oil refineries have triggered fuel shortages and big attacks near major cities have brought the dramatic visible consequences of the war into the homes of many Russians.

Firefighters and investigators had been deployed to the sites in Saint Petersburg as the blaze raged through the morning, Russian officials said.

Saint Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport suspended flights during the attack, resuming operations around 06:00 (0300 GMT), with around 50 departures disrupted.

Both Russia and Ukraine have escalated their long-range strikes in recent months.

Moscow’s forces have fired increasing numbers of ballistic missiles at Kyiv — killing dozens and ripping open apartment blocks.

US President Donald Trump has appeared to give his backing to Ukraine’s counter-attacks on Russia — calling the strikes “an escalation that can lead to an end”.

Washington’s attempts to mediate a peace deal between the warring sides have largely stalled with its own war on Iran raging.

The United Nations has reported a surge in civilian deaths in 2026, saying June was the deadliest month since mid-2022.

Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and tens of thousands of civilians have been killed since Russia launched its full-scale offensive in February 2022 — though there is no precise toll with neither side routinely revealing the number of their losses.

World.title: South Korean tycoon ordered to pay $644m in divorce
World.content:
Seoul – A South Korean court ordered an AI chip-manufacturing tycoon on Friday to make a trimmed-down $644 million divorce payment to his former wife.

Chey Tae-won, 65, is the chairman of the SK Group, which owns world-leading memory chipmaker SK hynix — a pillar of South Korea’s tech-led economy.

Seoul High Court in 2024 had told him to pay 1.38 trillion won ($940 million) to his ex-wife Roh Soh-yeong, daughter of a former South Korea president.

The sum — equal to more than $1 billion at the exchange rate at the time of the ruling — led local media to dub it the “divorce of the century”.

Chey appealed to the Supreme Court, which told the high court to reconsider its 2024 decision and led to the tycoon’s reduced divorce bill of 944 billion won ($644 million).

The settlement is not yet final, however, as either side may refer it back to the Supreme Court.

The acrimonious case centres on the definition and valuation of the couple’s shared assets, including Chey’s lucrative stake in the SK Group.

Seoul High Court ruled Friday that Roh was entitled to a cash payout worth one-third of the couple’s marital assets.

“The defendant’s shareholdings increased substantially during the marriage through his management activities,” the court said.

“The plaintiff contributed to that increase through homemaking, childcare and public-facing activities related to SK Group.”

Chey and Roh married in 1988, but the couple are believed to have lived apart for more than 15 years. In 2015 he admitted to fathering a child with his lover.

With SK hynix selling vital memory chips to AI computing company Nvidia, Chey’s stake is now worth roughly $5.5 billion, according to regulatory filings and public data.

Roh, 65, has three children with Chey and has built a career in the cultural space, running a digital art museum.

– Bribes –

The pair were wed in Seoul’s presidential Blue House when her father Roh Tae-woo led the country from 1988 to 1993.

They have battled over the split in the courts since 2022, after Chey filed for divorce in 2017 and mediation broke down.

The court’s original 2024 ruling ordering the payout to Roh cited a 30 billion won slush fund her ex-president father used to propel SK Group’s growth.

The court said at the time that could be counted as her contribution towards the couple’s shared assets.

But in October last year the Supreme Court quashed that argument, saying that any such cash likely stemmed from illegal bribes and therefore should not be counted.

Another question was whether the dramatic increase in SK Group’s value since the couple’s separation, on the cusp of the AI boom, should be reflected in the asset division.

“The court took into account the sharp rise in the value of the defendant’s shareholdings when determining the property division ratio,” Friday’s court statement said.

SK Group shares have more than tripled in value since December 2015, when Chey publicly disclosed his extramarital affair.

The Supreme Court had already separately ordered Chey to make an alimony payment to Roh of 2 billion won.

World.title: PepsiCo deepens Iraq partnership with manufacturing, agriculture deals
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – PepsiCo has inked agreements with two Iraqi partners to increase food and beverage production, boost agricultural supply chains, and create employment, adding to a string of US investments announced during Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington.

The agreements, inked during the U.S.-Iraq High-Level Business Summit organized by the US Chamber of Commerce, strengthen PepsiCo’s collaborations with Baghdad Soft Drinks Company (BSDC), its long-standing bottling partner in Iraq, and Green Iraq Company (GICO).

According to the deal with BSDC, PepsiCo will aim to increase yearly production capacity to more than 250 million beverage cases, maintaining Iraq’s position as one of the company’s major manufacturing and bottling centers in the Middle East.

The expansion is planned to create new employment in manufacturing, engineering, logistics, and distribution, as well as teach and provide technical skills to Iraqi engineers and technicians.

A separate deal with GICO seeks to increase food production capacity and agricultural productivity by bringing advanced irrigation methods and farming practices to local farmers, therefore boosting Iraq’s goal to become a regional food and beverage export center.

According to PepsiCo, the program aims to boost domestic supply chains by encouraging more local procurement and assisting Iraqi farmers in improving yields and sustainability.

The deals were part of a series of commercial understandings struck at the summit, in which US and Iraqi firms announced commitments in energy, banking, aviation, infrastructure, and manufacturing as Baghdad strives to diversify its economy away from oil and attract foreign investment.

Baghdad Soft Drinks Company has been working with PepsiCo for over four decades, and both agreements were signed on behalf of BSDC and GICO by majority stakeholder Tarek Al Hassan.

The investment demonstrates global firms’ rising interest in Iraq’s consumer products industry, as improved economic circumstances and government reforms stimulate more private sector investment and industrial growth.

World.title: Socceroos star Volpato allegedly tests positive for cocaine
World.content:
Sydney – Australian World Cup star Cristian Volpato allegedly tested positive for cocaine after he was pulled over for speeding in Sydney on Friday, police and reports said.

A New South Wales police statement said a 22-year-old man — widely identified as Italy-based Volpato by local media — was allegedly caught speeding twice overnight.

He passed a roadside breath test on the first occasion and was issued an infringement notice before being pulled over again two hours later.

This time he was drug tested and returned a positive result for cocaine, police claimed, with a second sample sent for further analysis.

“His international driver’s licence was suspended for a period of six months, withdrawing his driving privileges in NSW,” police said.

Volpato, who plays for Serie A side Sassuolo, made three appearances for the Socceroos at the World Cup after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia shortly before the tournament.

He was born and raised in Sydney before moving overseas and represented Italy at various youth levels.

Tony Basha, a Sydney-based coach who trained Volpato before he moved to Italy and remains a mentor, told the Sydney Morning Herald the attacking midfielder denied taking cocaine or any other illicit substance.

“He was adamant he didn’t touch it,” Basha said. “He was shocked. I’m shocked because it’s a big allegation.”

World.title: Volkswagen profit plunges as carmaker weighs mass job cuts
World.content:
Frankfurt – Volkswagen said Friday that its net profit plunged in the second quarter as the crisis-hit carmaker, weighing up to 100,000 job cuts worldwide, grapples with increasing competition in and from China.

Net profit for the three months to the end of June came in at 1.54 billion euros ($1.75 billion), the 10-brand group said, a fall of 32.9 percent on the same period last year. Last year’s figure was itself a decline of almost 37 percent on 2024.

The result was hit by a 500-million-euro charge the carmaker booked for stopping US production of its electric ID.4, Volkswagen said, as well as “negative mix effects”, meaning the automotive giant sold more lower-margin products.

The firm, which in addition to its own brand also includes the likes of Lamborghini, Audi, Skoda and Porsche, also cut its guidance for the year and said it now saw sales flat or falling up to three percent. It previously expected growth of up to three percent.

The results pile pressure on the beleaguered group, which has been suffering from slimmer margins from the sales of electric cars, US tariffs and above all intense Chinese competition.

“We must accelerate efforts to structurally lower our cost base and sustainably improve our earnings quality,” Volkswagen finance chief Arno Antlitz said. “What matters now is swift and consistent implementation.”

World.title: Iraq border in focus as Kuwait reports drone attack
World.content:
Dubai – Here are the main events related to the war in the Middle East:

– Iran blasts Trump assets threat –

Tehran said Friday that US President Donald Trump’s threat to pay for shipping damage with Iranian assets was an “incendiary precedent”.

Trump had said that Washington would start using frozen Iranian assets “that the United States has in its possession, and controls” to pay for “any and all damages done to Ships, Cargo or anything related” in the region.

– New US strikes –

The United States military said Thursday it was attacking Iran for the 13th night in a row, adding that strikes were aimed at military targets with the goal of diminishing Iranian ability to attack shipping.

Iranian state media reported that US missiles had hit the city of Ahvaz, near the border with Iraq, and explosions were heard in the port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz and in Omidiyeh.

– Kuwait under attack –

Kuwaiti air defences have opened fire on incoming Iranian missiles and drones, hours after reporting a new drone attack at the border crossing with Iraq.

“Kuwaiti air defences are currently intercepting hostile missile and drone attacks following the wrongful Iranian aggression,” the general staff said in a message posted on social media.

– Trump rebuked –

The US House of Representatives passed a largely symbolic resolution calling for President Donald Trump to halt military action against Iran, delivering another congressional rebuke as the Middle East war escalates.

The measure directs Trump to remove US forces from hostilities against Iran unless Congress explicitly authorises the war.

– Houthi attacks ‘illegal’ –

Attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea by Yemen’s Houthi militants have drawn condemnation from around Europe.

Germany said the attacks risked escalating conflicts, Britain condemned the group’s “reckless actions” and EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said the attacks were “unacceptable” and “illegal”.

– UN chief warning –

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the Middle East conflict was “getting out of control”.

“It is teetering on the edge of the unimaginable,” he said.

– Oil passes $100 –

The price of the benchmark international oil contract, Brent North Sea soared more than eight percent to reach $101.93 a barrel after Yemen’s Houthi rebels struck oil tankers in the Red Sea.

The main US oil contract, West Texas Intermediate, rose 7.6 percent to $93.44 a barrel.

– Island strike –

Iranian news outlet Tasnim reported that a US missile had hit a site near the town of Suza on Qeshm Island, in the disputed Strait of Hormuz.

– Trump threatens Houthis –

Trump threatened Yemen’s Houthi rebels with “major military punishment” after they launched missile and drone strikes at oil tankers in the Red Sea.

“The US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis themselves” should the rebels launch further attacks, Trump said on his Truth Social network.

– Britain withdraws Iran staff –

Britain said it had withdrawn remaining diplomatic staff from Iran.

“Due to the security situation, UK staff have been temporarily withdrawn from Iran. Our embassy continues to operate remotely,” the foreign ministry said on its website.

World.title: Kuwait blames Iran afters drones hit border with Iraq
World.content:
Kuwait City — Kuwait on Thursday said drones hit its side of the border with Iraq, with one Kuwaiti official telling AFP Iran was to blame.

“The Al-Abdali border crossing was attacked this afternoon by hostile drones, resulting in material damage, but thankfully no casualties,” defense ministry spokesman Col. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Atwan said in a statement.

An Iraqi security source also confirmed the incident prior to the ministry’s statement.

World.title: Iraq, Iran sign transport, rail deals after Tehran talks
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq and Iran inked an agreement and three memorandums of understanding on transportation, rail connection, and government collaboration as Prime Minister Ali al-Falih al-Zaidi wrapped up an official visit to Tehran aimed at improving bilateral relations.

According to the Iraqi Prime Minister’s office, Al-Zaidi met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and conducted extensive conversations with key Iranian officials such as Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Judiciary Chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Eje’i.

The two sides signed an agreement on international road freight transport and shipping, as well as memorandums of understanding to extend a railway connecting Kermanshah, Khosravi, Khanqin, and Baghdad, establish a twinning agreement between Baghdad and Tehran municipalities, and collaborate on government administration and human resource training.

Iraqi ministers in charge of foreign affairs, electricity, and finance, as well as the head of the Planning Commission, signed the agreements in the presence of Al-Zaidi and Pezeshkian.

The proposed railway extension would improve overland transportation links between Iraq and Iran, as part of Baghdad’s larger plans to expand regional trade corridors and improve cross-border connectivity through investments in rail, road, and logistics infrastructure.

The visit takes place as Iraq aims to retain tight economic and political connections with neighboring Iran while simultaneously developing partnerships with the United States and Gulf nations as part of a larger drive to diversify investment and boost regional cooperation.

According to the New York Times, Iran rejected a US cease-fire proposal delivered by Al-Zaidi during the visit, while Iraqi authorities made no public comment on the claim.

World.title: PM Modi gains 1 million Instagram followers overnight after selfie video amid NEET protest
World.content:
PM Modi gains 1 million Instagram followers overnight after selfie video

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi gained around 1 million Instagram followers overnight after he released his selfie video on Thursday night addressing concerns of the NEET paper leak.Currently PM Modi has 102 million followers on Instagram. His video captioned: "More strict actions against paper leaks to come in tomorrowâs Cabinet!" has garnered 271 million views so far along with 15 million likes and 1.3 million comments on Instagram.In the video, he announced that the government would introduce tougher measures to tackle examination paper leaks. He also informed about the Union Cabinet meeting agenda held on Friday."I know that paper leak is not an ordinary issue. It is very painful for lakh of students and their guardians," he said."Numerous effective measures have been taken in the past two and a half months since the paper leak incident. The culprits have been caught and are in jail. Our most important responsibility was to ensure that students' year is not wasted. The government used all its might to ensure that 22 lakh students could take their exams in the shortest possible time," he added.The Union Cabinet on Friday cleared amendments to the anti-paper leak law, proposing stricter punishment for those involved in examination paper leaks. Sources said the revised law prescribes up to 10 years in prison and a fine of as much as Rs 10 crore, while raising the minimum jail term from three years to five years.

World.title: Trinamool Congress appoints Saugata Roy as Lok Sabha deputy leader after Satabdi Roy joins rebel camp
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Trinamool Congress (TMC) on Friday appointed veteran parliamentarian Saugata Roy as its deputy leader in the Lok Sabha, filling the post that fell vacant after Satabdi Roy joined the rebel camp that later aligned with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI).

The appointment comes amid a major organisational reshuffle in the TMC's parliamentary ranks following the rebellion by 20 MPs, prompting changes in the party's leadership structure in Parliament.

Satabdi Roy, who had been serving as the TMC's deputy leader in the Lok Sabha, was among the MPs who joined the rebel camp, necessitating the appointment of a new deputy leader.

Saugata Roy is one of the TMC's most senior parliamentarians and has been a prominent voice for the party in the Lok Sabha on political and policy issues.

A retired physics professor, Roy is a five-time Lok Sabha MP and currently represents the Dum Dum constituency in West Bengal.

He first entered the Lok Sabha in 1977 from Barrackpore. He later served as an MLA for five consecutive terms between 1987 and 2009 before returning to Parliament in 2009 from Dum Dum, a seat he has retained in successive elections.

Before joining the Trinamool Congress, Roy was associated with the Congress.





During his political career, Roy served as the Union Minister of State for Petroleum and Chemicals in the Charan Singh government and later as the Union Minister of State for Urban Development in the UPA government led by former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.

He has also been a five-time member of the West Bengal Legislative assembly.

World.title: Why the world is coming to India for medical treatment — and not just because it is cheaper
World.content:
People coming from various countries to get treatment in India

What is medical tourism?

Government focus

India ranks 10th on medical tourism index

Why patients are choosing India

Beyond affordability

Areas for improvement

The next phase of growth

A hip replacement in Vadodara. A dental procedure in Chennai. An IVF treatment in Delhi. Every year, hundreds of thousands of patients travel to India not for its monuments or beaches, but for its medical care.What was once driven largely by patients from neighbouring countries seeking affordable treatment has evolved into a broader medical travel ecosystem.Industry estimates cited by the Economic Survey 2025â26 and the government project India's medical tourism market to grow from around $8.7 billion in 2025 to $16.2 billion by 2030. Over the same period, the global Medical Value Travel market is projected to expand from $115.6 billion in 2022 to$286.1 billion by 2030. Additionally, India's broader hospital and healthcare delivery market is expected to grow at 10â12 per cent annually, reaching nearly Rs 12 trillion by FY30, with private hospital chains projected to expand capacity from around 70,000 beds to more than 108,000 by 2030.India ranks 10th among the world's 46 medical tourism destinations, according to the Medical Tourism Index 2020â21.Letâs dive deep into the medical world and see how much potential India offers to tourists.Medical tourism refers to patients travelling outside their home country to seek planned medical treatment. While lower treatment costs remain a major factor, patients also consider waiting times, access to specialists, quality of care, language support and post-treatment follow-up when choosing a destinationFor India, the demand spans a wide range of services, from cardiac surgery and joint replacements to cancer treatment, fertility care, organ transplants, dental treatment, cosmetic procedures and neurological interventions.Improvements in digital consultations and easier access to treatment information have also made it simpler for patients to compare hospitals and plan their care before travelling.The Union Budget 2026â27 has proposed the development of five Regional Medical Hubs in partnership with state governments and the private sector. These hubs will combine medical, educational and research facilities, along with AYUSH centres and dedicated Medical Value Tourism facilitation centres.To further facilitate such travel, India offers e-Medical Visa and e-Medical Attendant Visa facilities, which have been extended to nationals of 172 countries, along with newer e-AYUSH Visa categories for those seeking traditional Indian systems of medicine. The government is also upgrading its Heal in India (Medical Value Travel) portal into a single platform for hospital discovery, treatment planning, bookings, payments and post-operative care, while airport concierge services have been proposed to assist international patients on arrival.Notably, according to government data, India has 69,364 hospitals; including 43,486 private and 25,778 public facilities, along with around 1.2 million registered doctors and more than 1,299 NABH-accredited hospitals as of 2026. Several hospitals are also accredited by the Joint Commission International (JCI), with most located in Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad.For patients who make the journey, affordability is often only part of the story.India recorded 507,244 foreign arrivals for medical treatment in 2025, accounting for about 5.5 per cent of total foreign tourist arrivals that year; as compared to about 112,000 in 2009. Bangladesh was the largest source market with 3,25,127 arrivals, followed by Iraq (30,989), Uzbekistan (13,699), Somalia (11,506), Turkmenistan (10,231), Oman (9,738) and Kenya (9,357).People have given various reasons for choosing India.American traveller Charlie Evans, who sought treatment for seasonal flu and an ear complaint at a hospital in Rishikesh, said he was initially hesitant about seeking medical care in a foreign country. However, he described being greeted by English-speaking staff, facing almost no waiting time and receiving treatment using equipment comparable to what he had seen in the United States.Evans said his consultation, medication and treatment cost around $10â20, compared with an estimated $150 for a similar visit in the US. "I got better care in Rishikesh, faster and cheaper, than I've ever gotten at home," he said.Beyond the lower cost, Evans said what stood out was the professionalism of the medical staff. "The doctor who treated me could have easily been practising in the US," he said, adding that healthcare in India felt to him less like a profit-driven system and more focused on patient care.The experience reflects a broader trend, where patients increasingly weigh convenience and quality alongside costs.American content creator Kristen Fischer, who lives in India, has also praised the country's healthcare system. While she believes the US offers a better overall hospital experience, she said she prefers India's healthcare system because it is "simple, affordable, fast" and offers "quality treatment.""One thing I love about Indian healthcare is that you pay before treatment. Then after you leave the hospital you never have to pay or worry about anything else again," Fischer said, contrasting it with the US, where patients can receive bills "for months after" treatment. She also argued that India's upfront pricing makes costs more transparent, unlike in the US where insurance often shields patients from the true cost of treatment, contributing to higher healthcare expenses."The cost is clearly defined before treatment. This allows people to shop around for a good deal according to their budget," she said.Fischer, in her series of social media posts, has also highlighted the accessibility of healthcare in India, saying patients can often see a doctor the same day without an appointment, unlike in the US where consultations can take weeks. She has described Indian doctors as "way less rushed and more attentive to your needs" and recounted receiving treatment for a thumb injury at a Delhi hospital in about 45 minutes for just Rs 50.The cost advantage is evident even for routine procedures too. Sej, who lives in Utrecht in the Netherlands, said she schedules her dental appointments around her trips to India. "A 30-minute teeth cleaning costs around 185 euros near where I live. In Lucknow, I pay about Rs 3,000 for the same treatment," she said.Aditya Oza, CEO of CureMeAbroad, which connects international patients with accredited hospitals, said India is beginning to attract patients who once favoured destinations such as Turkey and Thailand.He cited a case where two people who had earlier travelled to Turkey for treatment but chose India for their latest procedure. "Patients who've already been through this once, who know what to look for, are increasingly landing on India specifically. The accreditation is there, the specialist experience is there, and the cost gap is often the widest of any destination," he said."What's changed is that patients now have a way to verify all of that upfront instead of guessing."Hospital executives believe India's competitiveness will increasingly depend on the overall patient experience rather than just costs.Dr Sonia Lal Gupta, joint managing director of Metro Group of Hospitals, said accreditation, transparent clinical outcomes and accountability remain important differentiators."What we haven't fully built yet is the trust and the experience around that care, and that is where the real opportunity lies," she said.She added that support should extend beyond the hospital stay, covering everything from the first enquiry and medical visa assistance to treatment, recovery and follow-up consultations after patients return home.Meanwhile, Dr Sharan Shivaraj Patil, founder and chairman of SPARSH Group of Hospitals, said providers are investing in dedicated international patient services to make treatment easier from the first inquiry through recovery. It includes pre-arrival teleconsultations, medical visa assistance, transparent treatment plans with cost estimates, airport transfers, accommodation support, language interpretation, culturally appropriate meals and post-treatment follow-up. "As the expectations of international patients continue to evolve, the focus remains on delivering world-class clinical outcomes complemented by personalised, culturally sensitive and compassionate care," he added.Meanwhile, UK content creator Reuben Charles, who is currently in Guwahati, said he was impressed by the convenience and professionalism of his healthcare experience in India after using an at-home medical service to get some blood tests. He said the healthcare professional who attended to him was knowledgeable, spoke fluent English and took the time to explain the procedure in detail."The service was great. It was very, very quick as well. It came right to my house," Charles said.He believes India's combination of quality, accessibility and convenience makes it an attractive destination for medical tourism, particularly for international patients who can afford private healthcareBritish traveller Jenny Mowbray, who spent five months in Kochi, also said India's healthcare system stood out for its speed, affordability and flexibility. Unable to easily access a second neurological opinion through the UK's public health system, she chose to undergo consultations and diagnostic tests in India."For me, the biggest attraction is the combination of accessibility, speed, quality, cost and choice," she said, highlighting the specialists' consult within a day, complete MRI scans and blood tests almost immediately and receiving results within hours.While describing her overall experience as "efficient, patient-centred and highly accessible," Mowbray said better access to verified information on hospitals, specialties and treatment costs could make India's medical tourism ecosystem even more attractive for international patients.Recounting her experience she said, " Before coming to India, I had already used healthcare services in Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Tunisia for a range of issues including my neurological concerns, gynaecological care and knee cartilage damage. During my five-month stay in Kochi, I wanted to have a mole checked and also revisit my neurological symptoms for peace of mind. "I was able to make appointments with both a dermatologist and a neurologist for the very next day.The dermatology consultation was extremely thorough," she added.Sharing another perspective, Jai Prakash, founder of Health Voyage Global, a medical tourism consultancy, said patients often come to India after struggling to get the right diagnosis. "Many patients believe they can receive the right diagnosis and treatment in India at a fraction of the cost they would pay elsewhere," he said. "Indian doctors are exposed to advanced medical equipment and global treatment protocols, allowing them to offer high-quality care with shorter treatment timelines and lower overall costs,â he added.Not every patient travels to India purely for lower costs or better hospitals. For some, crossing borders also offers privacy. A Delhi resident recounted how her neighbour had travelled alone to India from Nepal for IVF treatment because she faced social stigma and family pressure back home over fertility issues. Seeking treatment away from her community allowed her to undergo the procedure without the scrutiny and judgement.Despite rising patient numbers, hospitals say access to care remains uneven across the country.Dr Bharat S Mody, chairman of Welcare Hospital in Vadodara, said India attracts a steady stream of patients from neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan, as well as from Africa and parts of Central Asia. However, he believes the country has yet to realise its full potential in attracting patients from Europe, the US and other developed markets.Mody said international patients are drawn by India's competitive pricing and medical expertise, but most treatment remains concentrated in metro cities, even though tier-2 centres can offer comparable quality at lower costs.Apart from this, he emphasised the medical visa process remains another hurdle for overseas patients."Our experience has also been that the government portal which issues the medical visa is not user-friendly," he said, adding that it "frustrates a potential patient wanting to come to India for medical treatment."He cited the example of Marco Bellaro, an Italian living in Indonesia, who travelled to Vadodara for a total hip replacement after finding the hospital online. Although Bellaro initially had concerns about hygiene standards and hospital infrastructure, Mody said those were addressed during consultations. The surgery was successful, but the medical visa process proved cumbersome, reiterating that simpler visa procedures and stronger global branding could help India attract more overseas patientsDr Alok Khullar, Group CEO of RJ Corp Healthcare, also emphasised on simplifying medical visa procedures, increasing the number of internationally accredited hospitals, improving coordination between airports and hospitals, and expanding multilingual support remain key priorities."Greater transparency around treatment costs and clinical outcomes will further strengthen confidence among patients and their families," he said.Patients, too, gave suggestions to fill out gaps beyond treatment itself. Charlie Evans, the American traveller, said a dedicated website or app for international patients, featuring hospital rankings, verified patient reviews and guidance on where to seek treatment for specific conditions, would make it easier for foreigners to navigate India's healthcare system with confidence.Adarsh Yadav, founder of healthcare companion platform CARESY, also emphasised on holistic services and care, saying India already has the clinical expertise to compete globally but must also focus on the patient journey. "If we can combine this with a smoother and more reassuring patient experience, India can become an even stronger destination for medical travellers," he said.India already has the ingredients - a large healthcare network, skilled medical professionals and a growing international patient base. As demand for cross-border healthcare grows globally, industry stakeholders believe India has the potential to attract even more.However, realising that opportunity, will require more than competitive treatment costs. The next phase of growth will depend on how effectively hospitals, governments, airlines, hotels, insurers and digital platforms work together to create a seamless patient journey.

World.title: Protests fallout: NTA sacks 47 officials in big overhaul, some to face criminal action - top developments
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The stand-off between the Centre and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over the alleged NEET paper leak continued on Friday, with no breakthrough on the protesters' key demand for the resignation of union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

While the government sought more time to respond after the second round of talks, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi renewed his attack on the Centre, reiterated the students' demands and accused the government of using force against peaceful protesters.

Meanwhile, the National Testing Agency (NTA) has terminated the services of 47 officials as part of a major overhaul following the controversy over alleged paper leaks and examination-related irregularities.

The move is part of a wider restructuring of the NTA aimed at strengthening accountability and restoring confidence in the examination system.

Here are the top developments:

Major NTA reshuffle likely

The National Testing Agency (NTA) has begun a major overhaul following the controversy over the alleged NEET paper leak and other examination-related irregularities. As part of the exercise, the services of 47 officials have been terminated, and legal and criminal action will be initiated against some of them, according to sources.





"The NTA is set to undergo an overhaul and more reformative actions will follow. At least 47 officials have been terminated, and legal and criminal action will be initiated against some of them," a senior official said.

Officials said the NTA will undergo a complete overhaul, with further reformative measures expected to strengthen the functioning of the examination body and restore confidence in the system.

Second round of talks ends without breakthrough

A CJP delegation held a nearly two-hour meeting with Union Ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh at the Constitution Club in New Delhi.

The delegation submitted three key demands and a five-point reform charter, but the meeting ended without a final decision.

Addressing reporters, Nadda said the government would respond after internal consultations.

"The meeting went on for almost two hours. They had three main demands and five reform suggestions for exams. We have told them that we will meet them again tomorrow afternoon and tell them about the discussion we had within the government," he said.

The next round of talks has been scheduled for Saturday afternoon.

Centre seeks more time on Pradhan's resignation

CJP leaders said the Centre had sought time till Saturday afternoon to respond to their demand for Pradhan's resignation, which they described as non-negotiable.

CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka said the government had expressed in-principle approval to the other two demands.

"The government has asked for time till tomorrow afternoon on our demand for Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation.

We hope the government will remove him soon," he said.

CJP leader Saurav Das said the delegation had also sought Rs 1 crore compensation for the families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide, withdrawal of FIRs and legal cases against protesting students, and a written sovereign guarantee that similar action would not be taken against peaceful protesters in the future. According to the delegation, the government accepted the compensation and FIR-related demands in principle.

Rahul Gandhi reiterates students' demands

Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi renewed his demand for Dharmendra Pradhan's removal, alleging that the education minister was responsible for the crisis.

"Dharmendra Pradhan is a criminal education minister. He has to be removed. He is a symbol of the collapse of our education system. He has to go," Gandhi said.

He said students were demanding the removal of the education minister, action against those responsible for the alleged pellet gun use and lathi-charge during the protests, and an apology from Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

During the press conference, Rahul also presented a protester whom he alleged had suffered pellet gun injuries during the Jantar Mantar protest.

"His eye has suffered damage, and he has lost his vision," Gandhi said, while alleging that the government had falsely denied using pellet guns against protesters.

The government has denied using pellet guns during the protest.

Cabinet approves tougher anti-paper leak law

The union cabinet approved amendments to the Prevention of Paper Leak law, proposing stricter punishment for those involved in examination paper leaks.

According to sources, the proposed amendments provide for a maximum jail term of 10 years, a fine of up to Rs 10 crore and an increase in the minimum imprisonment from three years to five years.

Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said the government would introduce the Bill in Parliament soon and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had directed that there should be no delay. Rijiju also criticised the Opposition for disrupting Parliament and urged members to allow a discussion on the issue.

Supreme Court to hear police action pleas; CJI clarifies earlier remarks

The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear on July 27 two petitions alleging excessive police action against students protesting over the alleged NEET paper leak.

Earlier in the day, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant clarified that reports claiming he had refused to hear a petition on the issue were incorrect.

"In the last two days, a completely false statement was made that a matter was filed," the CJI said, adding that only a representation had been submitted at that stage and describing the reports as "irresponsible and reckless".

PM Modi promises stricter action

A day before the Cabinet decision, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that the government would introduce legislation providing for fast-track courts and stricter punishment in paper leak cases.

"Paper leaks are not an ordinary matter. For lakhs of students and their parents, it is extremely painful," Modi said.

The Prime Minister said the government had ensured that nearly 22 lakh students did not lose an academic year by conducting the examinations again. He also welcomed activist Sonam Wangchuk's decision to end his 26-day hunger strike, while the CJP maintained that its protest would continue until Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

World.title: 'There are Chinese projects on territories in J&K that belong to India': MEA objects to illegal occupation
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Friday accused China of violating India's sovereignty and said that it is "illegally occupying" Indian territories in Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh.

During a weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that the government objects to the Chinese projects in Jammu and Kashmir.

"EAM said that when it comes to sovereignty issues, it is actually India that should be and is raising them. India does not violate Chinaâs sovereignty in any manner and has been consistent," Jaiswal said.

"But China has been in illegal occupation of Indian territories in Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh since 1963, where Indiaâs right is officially acknowledged even by China.

There are Chinese projects on territories in Jammu and Kashmir that belong to India, and we object to that," he added.

This comes a day after external affairs minister S Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi on the sidelines of Asean summit in Manila,

According to the Chinese foreign ministry readout, Wang said the meetings between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Kazan and Tianjin had "guided China-India relations onto the right track of improvement and development."





"China and India are partners, not competitors, and opportunities, not threats, for each other," Wang said, adding that institutional exchanges between the two countries had gradually resumed, border areas had maintained peace and tranquillity, and bilateral trade had reached a new high.

"These achievements have not come easily and should be cherished," he said.

Calling China and India representatives of emerging economies and key members of the Global South, Wang said the two countries should "prioritise human well-being, demonstrate their responsibility as major powers, consolidate the positive momentum of bilateral relations, strengthen coordination and cooperation in international and regional affairs, and make positive contributions to promoting multipolarity and the democratisation of international relations.

"

He said China was willing to work with India to implement the consensus reached by the two leaders, maintain close high-level exchanges, expand cooperation in trade, media and people-to-people exchanges, properly handle sensitive issues, and "explore a correct way for neighbouring major powers to coexist peacefully, based on mutual respect, mutual trust, common development, and common prosperity.

Cabinet clears tougher anti-paper leak Bill with stricter penalties

At least 13 people, including a six-month-old infant, are feared dead after a taxi was struck by falling boulders on the Sansari-Killar-Tandi road in Himachal Pradesh's Lahaul-Spiti district. Weakness in heavyweight stocks such as Infosys and HDFC Bank added to the decline.

Bangladesh President Shahabuddin resigns ahead of Hasina's planned return

Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin has resigned nearly two years before the end of his term, according to local media reports cited by Reuters. His resignation follows reports of differences with the government and comes days after former prime minister Sheikh Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh later this year. Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad will serve as interim president until a successor is elected.

World.title: Instagram vs WhatsApp: How CJP protests are different and why that matters
World.content:
has ended his 26-day hunger strike after government assurances on paper-leak cases, examination reforms and protections for peaceful protesters, prompting PM

to wish him a quick recovery and promise fast-track courts and tougher punishment for offenders.

The story so far

Wangchuk said his decision followed lengthy negotiations and concerns about possible violence. He also urged supporters to remain peaceful.

Sonam Wâangchuk ended his fast after 26 days

A reshuffle of the education bureaucracy was also under way: New secretaries were appointed for higher and school education, while the incumbent handling both departments was moved to the panchayati raj ministry.

Union minister JP Nadda laid out what the government is actually offering: No cases against those who protested peacefully at Jantar Mantar or marched to Parliament on July 20, a parliamentary discussion on paper leaks and exam reforms, and "positive consideration" of compensation for NEET paper-leak suicide victims.

For a government that has publicly ruled out education minister Dharamendra Pradhanâs resignation, these shifts are a way of signalling change.

But for now, Cockroach Janta Party has vowed to continue protesting until education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

representatives and ministers have met today to arrive at some kind of settlement.

That, in brief, is the story so far. A satirical social-media page created barely two months ago has developed into a youth movement powerful enough to force a direct intervention from the PM himself.





Although its immediate cause is the NEET paper leak, the anger on the street is about something much larger.

Why CJP protest is different

Earlier protests against the Modi government could usually be placed inside identifiable social or geographical categories. The anti-CAA mobilisation came to be portrayed largely as a Muslim protest. The farm agitation remained largely concentrated among agricultural communities and in north India.

CJP protest is harder to categorise. Examination anxiety cuts across caste, religion and region.

More importantly, the movement has found resonance among aspirational middle-class families, including those that have traditionally been receptive to the BJPâs message of merit, mobility and a better future.

It is a protest that does not look political in the traditional sense. One does not need to attend party meetings or be bused to a rally to participate. Posting a reel, designing a meme, sharing a police-action video or changing a profile picture can make you a part of the protest.

You can join it from anywhere. Not necessarily be present at Jantar Mantar. That informality makes the movement easier to join and harder for established institutions to understand.

Instagram takes on WhatsApp

The CJP has unsettled the BJP by challenging it on terrain the party has dominated for over a decade: The digital public square of X and WhatsApp. The BJPâs communication model relies on organised networks, centrally crafted talking points and mass WhatsApp forwards.

Similarly, older protest movements largely lived on WhatsApp forwards and TV debates.

But CJP speaks the native language of Instagram: Reels, memes, remixes and short videos that are decentralised, irreverent and difficult to control. Students, comedians, rappers and amateur creators can produce content faster than an official communication team can rebut it.

Police action, in this case, does not necessarily suppress the movement.

It produces content for it. Every baton charge and crying student becomes distributable evidence for an online audience. Wangchukâs forcible hospitalisation similarly transformed a weakening hunger strike into a fresh source of mobilisation.

PM Modi goes selfie-style

Interestingly, the governmentâs response eventually borrowed from this new media language. PM Modi did not depend on an official statement or formal televised address.

In a selfie-style, self-recorded video released around midnight, he spoke directly to young people about paper leaks, fast-track courts and stringent punishment.

The format mattered almost as much as the announcement. It showed that the protest had forced the government to change not only its message but also its medium. To respond to the Instagram generation, Indiaâs most formidable political communicator picked up a phone, looked into the camera and spoke in the informal style of a social-media creator.

The oppositionâs awkward embrace

The protestersâ appeal comes partly from their distance from conventional politics.

But Congress, AAP and other opposition parties naturally see an opportunity. CJP, however, presents them with a dilemma. If they stay away, they surrender a rare wave of anti-government mobilisation. If they embrace it too tightly, they risk making an organic youth movement look like another opposition-sponsored campaign.

That tension was visible when Wangchukâs wife, Gitanjali Angmo, described Rahul Gandhiâs protest near the PM residence as âinsincereâ, arguing that opposition leaders should have joined the students at Jantar Mantar instead.

She also took a swing at the BJP directly, saying there was "nothing Hindu or nationalistic" about how the government had handled young protesters.

Why it matters

It would be premature to liken the cockroach protests as Indiaâs version of the Gen Z rebellions seen elsewhere in South Asia. India has always followed its unique path; democracy flourished in India when no one gave a chance after Independent.

CJP is not likely to become another JP Movement or even another Anna Hazare agitation.

Its internal contradictions could eventually weaken it. Social-media enthusiasm can disappear as quickly as it arrives, while public attention can move on to the next crisis.

But CJP has delivered a message no government can comfortably ignore: Indiaâs aspirational youth will no longer accept repeated institutional failure as an unavoidable part of growing up.

Something has already changed. A generation routinely described as distracted, politically disengaged and mainly glued to its phone has used that very phone to create a national protest.

For a generation raised on the promise of âNew Indiaâ, the last few months have been a crash course in the limits of that story.

The government, that built its brand on youth aspiration, now finds itself being judged, liveâstreamed and factâchecked by those very aspirants.

The opposition, meanwhile, is playing the catch-up game.

World.title: CJP students protest: RAF probes excessive force, pellet gun charges in July 20 crackdown
World.content:
The violence erupted during CJP-led 'Chalo Sansad' march on July 20. (ANI photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your opinion on RAF personnel social media activity regarding controversial issues? They should avoid commenting They have the right to express 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: The Rapid Action Force (RAF) has begun an internal verification of the conduct of its personnel during the July 20 student protests in Delhi, amid allegations of excessive use of force and the use of pellet guns to disperse demonstrators, officials told news agency PTI on Friday.The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), under which the RAF functions, has directed the inspector general of the anti-riot unit to verify the sequence of events involving its teams during the protest, including the actions taken to control demonstrators and instances where RAF personnel themselves came under attack, officials said.A formal Court of Inquiry has not yet been ordered. According to CRPF officials, such a probe will be initiated only if the ongoing verification establishes grounds for further investigation.The violence erupted during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led 'Chalo Sansad' march on July 20. Students had marched from Jantar Mantar towards Parliament, demanding Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the alleged NEET question paper leak. The protest ended in clashes with security personnel, who used batons and tear gas to disperse the crowd.Officials told PTI that the RAF has taken cognisance of multiple videos and photographs circulating on social media showing personnel in the force's distinctive blue camouflage uniforms using lathis and firearms during the operation.The footage also includes visuals of RAF personnel allegedly being surrounded and attacked by protesters."All legal procedures stipulated to examine the conduct of personnel during such operational duties will be followed," a senior officer told PTI.Officials said the RAF is equipped with 12-bore pump-action guns, commonly referred to as pellet guns, as part of its standard riot-control equipment. Under the force's standard operating procedure (SOP), these weapons may be used only in extreme situations where personnel face a serious threat to their lives.The SOP also requires the weapons to be fitted with a deflector so that the metal or rubber pellets cause limited injuries and are aimed only below the waist, officials said.The verification assumes significance amid allegations that at least two students sustained pellet injuries during the July 20 clashes and were admitted to hospitals.While the Delhi Police has denied possessing pellet guns and termed reports suggesting their use as misleading, neither the CRPF nor the RAF has publicly confirmed or denied whether RAF personnel fired pellet ammunition during the protest.Apart from the allegations of excessive force, the verification will also examine videos showing RAF personnel allegedly being attacked by protesters, footage of an RAF uniformed man appearing to trip a running protester, and another clip that purportedly shows a stun gun being used during the clashes, officials said.The CRPF has also instructed commanders of RAF and other units deployed during the protests not to speak to the media after comments made earlier this week by a woman RAF officer were considered "undesirable", officials said.Separately, the force is examining social media posts allegedly made by RAF assistant commandant Sonia Sehrawat through her Instagram account to determine whether they violated the CRPF's social media policy, according to officials. The paramilitary force's 2023 guidelines prohibit personnel from commenting on controversial or politically sensitive issues online.

World.title: Set up dedicated bureau for traffic management: CM
World.content:
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy directed officials to establish a dedicated bureau for traffic management and road safety to ensure scientific planning and continuous monitoring of traffic across the State.

Reviewing traffic management measures with senior officials, he said the organisational structure of the proposed bureau should be designed after a comprehensive study, enabling it to address emerging traffic challenges through a long-term institutional framework.

Mr. Reddy instructed officials to conduct a review every two to three months to assess traffic conditions and evaluate measures required for better traffic regulation. He asked officials to prepare traffic management plans by taking into account factors such as changing weather conditions, office working hours, peak traffic periods and local travel patterns.

He further called for the development of a signal-free traffic system in Hyderabad by constructing underpasses and elevated corridors wherever required.
